title: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
description: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial Image source, Addenbrooke's Hospital Image caption, Tony Chapman, 75, from Corby in the East Midlands was one of the 1,100 melanoma patients enrolled on the vaccine trial By Jim Reed Health reporter Published 3 hours ago A new personalised cancer vaccine given alongside a widely used immunotherapy drug has cut the risk of patients dying or their skin cancer returning by 42% in a major clinical trial. The researchers involved say the results could mark a turning point in cancer treatment, bringing personalised medicine a step closer. The trial also found that the new drug combination reduced the risk of melanoma, a type of skin cancer, spreading by 38% over two years compared to immunotherapy alone. The drug manufacturers MSD and Moderna say the same approach is already being tested against other tumours, including kidney, bladder and lung cancer. Independent cancer experts described the results as impressive but said longer-term studies were still needed to establish whether the treatment really helps most patients live longer, on average. Personalised vaccine The new approach is aimed at cancer patients who have already had their tumour removed through surgery. In the trial, 1,137 adults were given Keytruda, an established immunotherapy drug which helps the body's immune system find and attack cancer cells. About two-thirds also received an experimental vaccine with the rest being given a placebo or dummy drug. The vaccine, called Intismeran, uses the same mRNA technology as some Covid jabs. It is personalised to each patient, using information from their own tumour to help train their immune system to recognise cancer cells and target them if they return. Two years after starting the treatment, the patients who received the jab were far less likely to have had melanoma come back or see it spread across the body. "Personalisation is the next step up and it's really exciting, it's a fabulous technology," says Prof Pippa Corrie, a consultant medical oncologist who helped run part of the study with patients at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. "The question is how much can we really demonstrate it's worth and this trial was the first proof of principle." Image caption, The latest checks show that Tony Chapman is cancer free three years after he was first told melanoma skin cancer had spread to his lymph nodes 'What's to lose?' Prof Corrie worked with patients enrolled in the trial including 75-year old Tony Chapman, who was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019. He had the tumour removed from his chest but a lump later appeared under his arm. He was told his cancer had returned and he needed a second operation. He then volunteered to take part in the study but, like all the other participants, he still doesn't know whether he was given the experimental vaccine or a placebo alongside his immunotherapy treatment. "This just seemed like a really good example of moving science forward, as well as getting some benefit for yourself, so what's to lose?" Tony said. Three years on he is now having checks every six months and remains cancer-free. Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer. But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial. Both companies said they were now "engaging with authorities" suggesting they could file for approval from medicine regulators as soon as next year. Widespread NHS use will also depend on cost, given that each individual patient will need to have their tumour genetically analysed and a personalised vaccine made for them. The trial will continue so that the patients involved can be monitored â both to see if the cancer returns over time and to assess whether the drug ultimately helps them live longer. Professor Alan Melcher from the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn't involved in the research, described the results as "very impressive". "It is an important proof of principle for the field, although we shouldn't get ahead of the evidence," he said. "We can't assume from one melanoma trial that the same approach will work across all cancers, and longer follow-up will be important to understand the effect on overall survival." The full trial results are due to be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) cancer conference in Madrid on Saturday. They have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, where they can be scrutinised by independent experts. title: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
description: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting Image source, AFP Image caption, Photos of one of the suspected attackers were shared by AFP news agency By Tom Bennett Reporting from Jerusalem Published 23 October 2026, 10:25 BST Updated 37 minutes ago Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say. Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron. In response, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had ordered the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The attack comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time. The two injured Israelis are in critical condition, according to Israel's ambulance service. The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there. Unverified CCTV footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire. The Israeli military said it had begun raids on the homes of the attackers, while far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said he had ordered the demolition of several Palestinian buildings adjacent to the site of the attack. It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis. Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security for Israelis, said that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says. title: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
description: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich - his lawyers have said he denies concealing his fortune By James Oliver Â and Â Rory Tinman ,Â BBC Panorama Published 52 minutes ago Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax. Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ). A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit. Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws". The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering. The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed. Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (Â£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents. Image caption, Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation. A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months. When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved." He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated." Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune 12 October Watch on iPlayer Watch now on BBC iPlayer Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts. Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over â¬25m in unpaid VAT. Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it. title: Detective raped by colleague says Met handling of case 'like being raped again'
description: Detective raped by colleague says Met handling of case 'like being raped again' To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Met chief Rowley not fit for job, says Linda Williams By Daniel De Simone ,Â Investigations correspondent Â and Â Nalini Sivathasan Published 6 hours ago A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again". Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - a serial abuser jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 other women. Linda has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the attack and sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick. The lengthy civil case left her feeling suicidal, she says. The "worst thing", she says, was when lawyers acting for the Met commissioner challenged the severity of her PTSD on the basis that she had been raped only once. The Met has told the BBC it "tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams' welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible". "We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer," the force added. "Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable." Linda, who has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak to the BBC, has settled her civil case and the Met has now paid her compensation without acceptance of liability. In an unprecedented move for a serving officer, she is now calling publicly for Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley to resign. She believes he has failed to change police culture as promised and she still does not trust her own force to handle cases like hers. When he took on the most important job in UK policing in 2022, Sir Mark pledged to change the Met. At the time, the force was viewed as being in crisis - following Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer and other scandals including officers sharing photos of murdered sisters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Met Police commissioner Sir Mark Rowley has promised to get rid of officers unfit to serve After Carrick was jailed in January 2023, Sir Mark praised the victims and said: "We have failed and I'm sorry. He should not have been a police officer." Two months later, in an official report by Baroness Casey, the Met was described as a "boys' club", that was institutionally misogynistic and had failed women. Linda contacted the BBC, after seeing Panorama's report last year into a hidden culture of misogyny and racism inside the Met . Since reporting the rape by Carrick in 2021, Linda says it has been "horrific" and she would not report a rape to the Met today "because I don't trust the police and I don't think they deal with it correctly". Carrick was brought to justice by Hertfordshire Police, which investigated the rape of Linda. She reported it to the force after seeing media coverage of the news that Carrick had been charged with raping another woman. Linda was herself a rape investigation officer in the early 2000s. "I supported victims through rape but didn't report myself. I think that says loads. "I'm asking members of the public to report, and I'm there to support them, but I wouldn't do it myself and I didn't do it." She says if a similar attack happened to her tomorrow, she would not report it to the Met, because she has "no faith" that the force would deal with it correctly. Carrick raped her while she was on a three-month attachment with him in south London - miles from where she was normally based. One night, Linda says, Carrick suggested she should stay at his home, so she did not have to drive far late at night only to return early the next morning. He then raped her. When Linda told him no, she says Carrick replied: "It's what I do. I'm going to carry on." She knew that if she fought back then Carrick was going to get violent, she says. Image source, Linda Williams Image caption, Linda has been a Met Police officer for 27 years Afterwards, Linda says she "never told a soul". She says she felt unable to report the rape then, or for years afterwards, because of the culture in the Met. Reporting the rape "would have been the end of my career", she says, because Carrick would not have been charged and she would have been shunned. "I would imagine that if Carrick had been arrested, he probably would have been interviewed and then no further action. So then mud sticks, doesn't it? "Then I'd be the officer that alleges rape, and who's going to want to work with me?" The "very sexist" culture she says she experienced included having her forehead stamped with the words "Property of the Met" and being locked in the boot of a police car for the duration of a shift. Linda, now 60, says the mental and emotional impact of the rape has been vast. She has led a lonely life, she says, focused primarily on her work and pets. She has not had a relationship with a man since the day she was attacked and says she has missed out on having a family. "I still don't feel I could have any relationship," she adds. She feels guilty at not having come forward earlier to report Carrick, she says. Since his conviction, she says the Met's culture has not changed as much as it should have done. title: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
description: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018 Image source, Getty Images By Freya Scott-Turner Published 23 October 2026, 10:56 BST Updated 37 minutes ago The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018. In a statement, Meghan said a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police that year and subsequently shared with her. Her comments come after reports that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to her father had been found at his former home in the Philippines, which she said were "deeply" distressing. In an interview with the Daily Mail, Thomas Markle denied possessing child sex images, calling the accusations "sick lies". The duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed." She said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated". She added she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children". This was "to protect them", she said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families". Meghan described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children". title: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted
description: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access after row By Gabriela Pomeroy Â and Â Hafsa Khalil Published 22 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits on the satellite uplink had been reversed by Elon Musk. The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations. The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back". Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations. The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks. They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted". Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said. Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield , which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues. The White House has since repeatedly denied deliberately placing limits on the network in Ukraine. Trump refused to say whether he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service when asked about reports to that end on Thursday, but said: "Bottom line, he put it back." Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Published 15 October Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. Ukrainian reports of a slowdown to the service came during a tense diplomatic row between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war . Zelensky said the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump later denied. The row prompted a war of words between the two world leaders, with Trump suggesting it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and Zelensky implying Trump was not a real leader. Earlier on Thursday - before Trump's comments - Zelensky had said the speed of the system had still not been restored fully. "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so." The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had told Musk that he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped, and that the system was working closer to normal following that conversation. title: Final James Bond screen tests to take place this weekend, reports say
description: Final James Bond screen tests to take place this weekend, reports say Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden are both thought to be part of the final auditions to play James Bond By Helen Bushby Culture reporter Published 1 hour ago Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor are among the actors thought to be taking part in final auditions to play James Bond, according to reports. Screen tests are said to be taking place this weekend, possibly as early as Friday, according to the Hollywood Reporter , external , with between three and five actors understood to have reached the last stages of the process. The finalists are said to be taking part in auditions with three components - stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Deadline reported the screen tests , external had been due take place in early October, but had been delayed by scheduling conflicts, while Variety said Turner and Lowden , external "appear to be in the mix" to replace Daniel Craig. British actors Aaron Taylor-Johnson and James Norton were previously connected to the role, while Irish actor Paul Mescal's name had also been thrown into the mix. Other actors now appear to be in the frame, but reports on the current casting situation vary. Variety suggested Slow Horses star Lowden may now be edging ahead, while Masters of the Air star Turner was speculated about earlier this year, with some fans suggesting his wife Dua Lipa could sing the Bond theme song. Sources told Deadline that at least four final screen test offers have been made, and while unconfirmed, "three of the four expected to test are Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor". O'Connor is best known for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and for starring in 2025's Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, with Craig. Jack O'Connell had been thought to be in the mix, but sources said this may no longer be the case, while Euphoria and Wuthering Heights Star Jacob Elordi is not thought to be testing. Other stars who were previously linked with the role include The King's Man star Harris Dickinson, along with SAS: Rogue Heroes' Jack Barton. Deadline said: "Even with the tests wrapping next week, there is no timeline for when a final decision will be made." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Daniel Craig served as James Bond across 15 years and five films Amazon MGM Studios, who now control the Bond franchise, announced in May , external that the casting process was under way, but had no further comment at the time. In August, Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, told Deadline , external the "end of the year is a good bet" for possible news on who would be playing Bond. "We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow," she said. "And it's got to be something really different that is a stirring and exciting and different." The BBC's Lizo Mzimba reported in September that "for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen". He added: "As the 007 team themselves have explained , external in the past: 'Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors'." The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered Search for new James Bond officially kicks off as auditions begin Image source, Reuters Image caption, Writer Steven Knight said in September the first draft of the Bond script was done Only six actors have ever played novelist Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series - Sean Connery, Roger Moore, George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. The last announcement of a new Bond was in 2005 with Craig, who last starred in the role in 2021's No Time to Die, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga. During the equivalent stage of the audition process two decades ago, Superman actor Henry Cavill was widely thought to have also been in the running. "They told me I was close," Cavill told the Happy Sad Confused podcast in 2022. "They told me it was ultimately down to, and this is what I've been told, it was just down to me and Daniel, and I was the younger option. "They obviously went with Daniel and I think it was an amazing choice to go with Daniel," he said. "I probably wasn't ready at the time and I think Daniel did an incredible job over the past movies, so I'm happy they made that choice." The forthcoming film, reportedly out in 2028, will be directed by Dune's Denis Villeneuve , with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight writing the script . Knight told Zoe Ball on Greatest Hits Radio , external in September that the first draft of the script was completed. Amazon bought MGM for $8.5bn (Â£6.3bn) in 2021 , which included the rights to distribute James Bond, and they are reported to have paid at least $20m (Â£14.9m) more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future. Pascal and David Heyman are producing the film, while Tanya Lapointe is executive producer. Knight's final words on the film were about how much he was enjoying working on it. He told Ball: , external "I'm absolutely loving doing it. It's an honour to be asked. And believe it's going to be so good. I really do believe it's going to be amazing." title: Earnings limit of up to Â£140K for first-time buyers loan scheme
description: Earnings limit of up to Â£140K for first-time buyers loan scheme Image source, Getty Images By Paul Seddon Political reporter Published 10 minutes ago The government is expected to allow households earning up to Â£110,000 to apply for its new loan scheme to help first-time buyers in England. As first reported by The Times , external , a higher earnings limit of Â£140,000 is expected to apply to those purchasing properties in London. The Your First Home scheme will offer government-backed equity loans worth 20% of new-build properties purchased from participating developers. The loans, which will also be subject to an initial interest-free period, are designed to help people buy a home with deposits as low as 2.5%. Previous schemes to help first-time buyers did not restrict eligibility by income but faced criticism for stoking house prices by allowing relatively wealthy households to borrow more. Unveiling the Your First Home Scheme at last month's Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it would focus on those who "really need support". Details of the changes, including salary caps, are due to be confirmed at next week's Budget. The Times reported that ministers had initially decided to set the earnings limits at Â£90,000 for homes outside outside London and Â£110,000 in the capital, before concluding this would deny access to too many middle-earning couples, such as teachers and nurses. The government has also argued that the scheme will help to boost housebuilding, after ministers conceded they are set to miss a target to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election. Help to Buy Labour has said the scheme will be funded by within existing government budgets, but is yet to provide details of which other areas will see their spending cut. Developers taking part in the scheme will also be asked to contribute towards running costs. Like the Help to Buy scheme launched under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, the scheme will use equity loans, which are linked to changes in the value of properties they are used to purchase. That scheme, which initially ran between 2013 and 2021, enabled all home purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home worth up to Â£600,000. Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years. A second version of that scheme, which ran from 2021 to 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties could be bought under the programme. title: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
description: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning Image caption, Father Roy Snipes is known locally as the Cowboy Priest - he resisted plans to seize chapel land to build Trump's border wall By Gary OâDonoghue Chief North America correspondent, in the Rio Grande Valley Published 1 hour ago It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel. The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself. As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest. "I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname. In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys. During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). "There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Donald Trump campaigning in Texas earlier this month - the close Senate race is being hotly contested Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project. "They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing. "But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight." After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said. "The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added. Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy. This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year. Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered. Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate. Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem. "I remember I put out a videoâ¦ thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all." But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added. Image caption, Mario Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November Recent polls suggest much of Trump's support among Hispanic voters has ebbed away since 2024. Surveys taken since late summer indicate a majority of Texan Hispanic voters disapprove of the president. They also suggest Hispanic voters are favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin. "When I voted for President Trump, I voted for him because we saw an influx of immigration during the Biden administration," said Mario Guerrero, a young Mexican-American businessman who leads the South Texas Builders Association. It needed to be fixed, he said. "We thought that we were in the right by voting for Trump, and that he was going to do what was best in order to fix the crisis on the border. "And I think to myself, we were really not told the extreme that they were willing to go to make a point," he added, before referencing recent shootings involving ICE agents in US cities. Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues. A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration. Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown. "There's a man that I know thatâ¦ last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work."...

title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC finds
description: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC finds Image source, Saudi Hospital medics Image caption, Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed By Barbara Plett Usher ,Â Africa correspondent Â and Â Mohamed Madi Published 23 October 2026, 00:16 BST Updated 33 minutes ago A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago. UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings. The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government dismissed the allegations as propaganda. Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud said it was a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation. Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times. Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict. The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted. "The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC. "The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned." The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military. Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities. Image caption, El-Fasher residents had little access to healthcare during the long siege of the city In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility. But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query. UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city. The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city. A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan Published 13 November 2025 Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past Published 31 October 2025 Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say Published 2 days ago Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023. Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city. Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies. The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher. In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city. The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman. The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says. On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added. The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist. But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office. They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs. "There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners. Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead. "They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me." That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said. The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated. Dr Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base. According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy". In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains...

title: I thought I was dying but it was health anxiety - here's how to recognise the signs
description: I thought I was dying but it was health anxiety - here's how to recognise the signs Image source, Hollie Sharman Image caption, Hollie Sharman spent hours searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated By Emily Holt Published 23 October 2026, 00:20 BST Hollie Sharman was convinced she was dying. She would go to hospital "four to five times a week" complaining of excruciating chest pain. "I think the longest I spent in A&E was 13 hours," says the 25-year-old. But despite numerous tests, doctors could never find anything wrong. Sharman says she had "always worried" about her health as a child and remembers "making up any excuse" to get sent home from school and get into bed. Her 22nd birthday meal was spent in the restaurant toilets "having the worst panic attack I've ever had". That triggered years of health anxiety, with hours spent searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated. Constantly Googling symptoms "I was constantly Googling and using ChatGPT, every source I could get that could tell me what was wrong," she says. "I spent so long in the hospital. They'd tell me it's nothing, they'd check everything. "I'd go home, but then my legs would feel weak, so I'd Google that and then it would say it's a sign of heart failure. So I'd go back, it was literally a constant cycle." At its worst, she "completely disconnected from everyone" and wouldn't reply to messages from family to avoid repetitive conversations. Sharman says her health anxiety also had an extreme affect on her relationship. "It got to the point that nothing he said would be the right thing. "I would get upset because he didn't understand what was going on inside my own head. How can you tell someone everything's fine when I think I'm actually dying?" Image source, Dr Kirren Schnack Image caption, Dr Schnack says health anxiety is an "obsessional worry" about being seriously ill Clinical psychologist Dr Kirren Schnack says health anxiety is "a constant worry about being seriously ill or becoming seriously ill when you are not". Key signs can be "checking" behaviours, such as frequently examining your body, taking your temperature, blood pressure or researching symptoms online. Another is constantly asking the internet, friends or family for reassurance that you are safe and healthy, she tells Complex with Kimberley Wilson . Others may experience "avoidance" - not looking at their body or going to doctors appointments because they fear "the worst". Some may "take on the persona of somebody who has an illness", she adds. "You may slow down your movements and stop exercising, you're treating yourself and your body and mind as if you are already ill." Image source, Hollie Sharman Image caption, Sharman says her parents understand her condition more after watching the videos she makes about health anxiety on TikTok Sharman was eventually diagnosed with health anxiety and health-related obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD). She says her family and partner have been "incredibly supportive" and have helped her get to a "better place" with techniques to manage her anxiety. "I'd write down my symptoms like 'chest pain, excruciating'. And then at the end of the day, I'd write that I was fine. "And then next time I'd have it, I'd have something to read and I'd be like, but I thought I was dying then and I wasn't." Sharman says her health anxiety "doesn't control her life any more". "You need to push yourself and do things when you're anxious, don't put your life on hold because I did for so many years." Complex with Kimberely Wilson How to deal with health anxiety. Listen now. Listen on Sounds How to manage health anxiety Dr Schnack says if you have a symptom that is "new, concerning or doesn't go away", it is "responsible health behaviour" to check the NHS website. If a symptom has not gone away within two weeks, she advises making a GP appointment. Here's when to call 111, 999 or go to A&E. And here are some tips from Dr Schnack that might help: Challenge worst-case thinking - give your brain other explanations for physical sensations; a stiff back might be poor posture rather than a serious illness. Limit reassurance-seeking - set rules and time limits on how often you ask friends or family about symptoms, and stick to them. Burn off anxious energy - take quick bursts of movement, like jumping jacks, to help process adrenaline and cortisol. Ground yourself - use strong sensory experiences such as holding an ice cube or tasting something sour or spicy. Breathing techniques - take a long breath through your nose, add a second inhale at the top and release it with a long sigh through your mouth. Get in touch Do you experience health anxiety? Share your experience. title: Are Man Utd the unmanageable club?
description: Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club? Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Manchester United are without a win in seven games in all competitions By Phil McNulty Chief football writer Published 4 hours ago The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip. Carrick recreated a familiar scene - the same one acted out by predecessor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after a 4-1 loss at Watford in November 2021 cost him his job - by raising his hands in apology to supporters who had just seen United humiliated by the same scoreline at Como in the Champions League. Carrick is the seventh full-time manager since Ferguson stepped down in 2013 after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge. Since then there have been days of success under Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Erik ten Hag, and moments of hope, but the final outcome is always the same - dismissal. Carrick will need something miraculous to change that storyline, with results poor and revolt within the dressing room as defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the tactics in Como. It hints at something rotten in the state of United. So should it really be crestfallen managers standing in front of those disappointed supporters? Can it really be United's managers every time? Should not even more scrutiny now be aimed at those who appointed them, then decided the direction of the club? Have United effectively, through years of decay, decline and appalling decision-making, become the unmanageable club? There have been those seven full-time managers - David Moyes, Van Gaal, Mourinho, Solskjaer, Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick. There have also been spells as interims for others such as Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher. United's leaders, from former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward to the ruling Glazer family and now part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, have effectively tried every trick in the book to recreate the Ferguson era. And failed miserably. Moyes, an ill-starred appointment led by Ferguson, found the job too big for him after leaving Everton . Van Gaal and Mourinho were tried and trusted operators with stellar track records of success at Europe's superpowers. Solskjaer was effectively the anti-Mourinho without any sort of managerial track record that suggested he would succeed at United, but appointed after a successful spell in temporary charge. Ten Hag got the job on the back of leading a superb young Ajax side to the Champions League semi-final. Amorim was regarded as European coaching's hottest young property when he was lured from Sporting in Lisbon. All ended up sacked. All eventually found the unwieldy beast that is United impossible to tame. Van Gaal won the FA Cup in 2016. Mourinho won the League Cup and the Europa League in 2017. Ten Hag won the FA Cup in 2024 with a landmark win against Manchester City . Slim pickings compared to previous glories. United, however, have not become a bad or dysfunctional club overnight. They have been heading towards this point ever since the succession plan to Ferguson - not easy, admittedly - was botched so badly. Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp all felt able to resist the lure of Old Trafford, leading to what should have been red faces all round in December 2019, when they were all managing within 35 miles of each other in the north-west but none were at United. Ancelotti was at Everton , Guardiola was at Manchester City . Klopp was at Liverpool . United had Solskjaer, an over-sentimental choice made on the back of a feelgood interim spell. He lasted less than three years. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer adopts a similar pose to Carrick after his final game in charge in 2021 With every passing day, Carrick looks like Solskjaer Mark II. Carrick is a former fan favourite who did well in temporary charge, but whose previous managerial career was a sacking at Championship club Middlesbrough. Solskjaer shared that same unwanted distinction, sacked by Cardiff City in September 2014 after only nine months in charge as they struggled in the Championship. It has all brought United to the point where the question must be asked. Since Ferguson's departure, has it ever been worse than it is now? In recent times, has there ever been less hope than there is now? Has morale ever been lower than it is now? United will always find a manager should they require one, but their current parlous circumstances mean they are no longer the attraction they once were. They will not have the pick of the globe's finest. They will need to persuade someone that there is a future at Old Trafford that contains something other than future dismissal, a sobering state of affairs for the self-styled "biggest club in the world". Given the current state of United's squad, there is no guarantee a manager with a high-class track record would have a quick fix, or any fix at all, without huge investment. Carrick is front of house and, on current evidence, will pay the price for United's failings. He is a repeat of the Solskjaer mistake, an easy choice made after taking them back into the Champions League, a comfort blanket with supporters that has now been torn away by poor results. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Manchester United part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in heated discussion with director of football Jason Wilcox - with CEO Omar Berrada in between - at Wolves in December 2025 There are significant culprits elsewhere, led by Ratcliffe. United fans have held regular protests against the Glazers since they took control in 2005, their leveraged purchase loading debt on to the club. They have remained majority owners, despite the level of angered aimed towards them from supporters, unmoved by years...

title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
description: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow Image source, BBC/Getty Images Image caption, Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow By Liza Fokht Senior reporter, BBC News Russian Published 23 October 2026, 00:16 BST "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 to 2025, tells the BBC. US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War. But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year. The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion. They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials. Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed. Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia. "There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty." The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023 Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater. "Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow. Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission. The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution". Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials. One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy. Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia Published 4 days ago Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect Published 4 September They fled Russia, but the West sent them back Published 7 days ago Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police. One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear. Not everyone can deal with the pressure. One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months. 'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats' In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy. He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be. The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible. And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies. Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country. But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Pierre LÃ©vy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024 After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers. One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'." Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses. A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase. "It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US...

title: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok
description: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok Image source, Grandma Droniak Image caption, Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media By Yasmin Rufo BBC News Published 23 October 2026, 00:20 BST Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties. The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that allowed her to keep partying â but not supply alcoholic drinks. With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (Â£9,000) a month. The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren. From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life. 'I'm showing it's not that bad to get old' "I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom. She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older. "They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes." Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren. Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok." 'I'm very picky about brand deals' On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff. She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits. Image source, Viv Truran Image caption, Viv Truran shares her colourful outfits with her more than 800,000 followers Now she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves. "I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that." She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views â and is now on book five. Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad". Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective. She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities like Age UK who paid her several thousand for a recent campaign. "I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand." 'I cry when people send me messages from around the world' Naomi Baker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium". Image source, Nonna Gracie Image caption, Nonna Gracie has been dubbed "the internet's Italian grandma" Grace Geramita, 85, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades. Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job. Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off. "I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says. Much of her content is about more than food â she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table". 'Virtual grandma' for followers Baker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world". Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says. Image source, Barbara Costello Image caption, Barbara Costello says many people see her as the mother or grandmother they never had That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts. Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had". "Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy." Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on. She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children. "It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life." title: Call of Duty promises a return to form - but can it compete with GTA?
description: Call of Duty promises a return to form - but can it compete with GTA? Image source, Activision Image caption, Modern Warfare 4 is released on Friday after its predecessor "missed the mark" last year By Yasmin Malik Â and Â Tom Richardson ,Â BBC Newsbeat Published 23 October 2026, 00:20 BST Updated 2 hours ago Call of Duty is back - and it's got a lot to prove. Last year was a low point for the video game juggernaut, with poor reviews for its single-player campaign mode and multiplayer fans defecting to rival titles. So for latest instalment, Modern Warfare 4, publisher Activision is pulling out all the stops to bring fans back on board. But with increasing competition for fans' time and attention, and the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 just weeks away, can Call of Duty still cut through? BBC Newsbeat spoke to some of those behind the game to find out, and why they see the upcoming release of GTA 6 as an "opportunity". Since 2009, Call of Duty has been at the top - or a close second-place - in the US video game sales charts every year. But 2025's edition, Black Ops 7, dropped to seventh place in America, according to data from analytics firm Circana. In the UK, it was the eighth best-selling game , external . Itâs thought the gameâs inclusion on Xboxâs Game Pass subscription service, where it wonât appear on release this year, hit sales. But competition from long-running rival Battlefield 6 and new release Arc Raiders - a surprise success from Swedish studio Embark - put the behemoth on the back foot. Fans also complained about the inclusion of novelty skins, which change the appearance of characters during multiplayer games, based on cartoons , external and other pop culture crossovers. Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, admits it was a tough year for the series. "I think we missed expectations with our community last year," he says. "So we took a step back, we listened to them." Players now have the ability to switch off controversial cosmetic changes, and Bahl says Modern Warfare 4 is a "return to form". It's a message they've been keen to get out. Image source, Activision Image caption, The game locates players in a war between North and South Korea Newsbeat meets Bahl in a corner of Shoreditch, London, that's been turned into a convincing replica of a South Korean street complete with noodle bars and convenience stores. It's inspired by Modern Warfare 4's storyline, which depicts a North Korean invasion - a decision that provoked a mixed reaction in the lead-up to release . A similar installation to promote the game has been built in downtown LA - but it's far from the only extravagant promotional attempt to generate buzz around the game. Back in July, Activision recruited Obsession star Inde Navaratte - who streamed Call of Duty on Twitch before becoming one of Hollywood's hottest young stars - to publicise the game at sports convention Fanatics Fest , external . It's also struck a sponsorship deal with six-a-side football competition Baller League and worked with world's biggest YouTuber Mr Beast to showcase the game's new DMZ multiplayer mode , external . Bahl says the events and collabs are designed to demonstrate Call of Duty's "stature, swagger and scale" - something he admits does not come cheap. He says he's always thinking of ways for Call of Duty to leverage its position and "show up in culture in a really big and innovative way" to reach "as many people as possible". Call of Duty does have some strong competition in that space, however. Image source, Activision Image caption, Members of the Modern Warfare 4 cast also visited the South Korean pop-up This year it's launching just weeks before GTA 6 - arguably the most anticipated video game of the decade. Despite rising console prices, there's hope that the massive interest in Rockstar Games' ultra-blockbuster will convince people to buy a new console or return to the hobby. Bahl says GTA 6 and Call of Duty are "the two biggest games of the year" but they're not necessarily in direct competition. "More people dusting off their Xbox or their PlayStation, starting to play for the first time, it gives an opportunity for more gamers to come in and play both of the games," says Bahl. GTA 6 will only be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox consoles at first, and multiplayer modes won't be available at launch. "So we feel like this is differentiated enough to really stand out," says Bahl. The game itself sells for about Â£70 in the UK, but Bahl points out it can be a year-round hangout space for many fans. "The number one reason people come to Call of Duty is not just for the combat or the gunplay, but it's actually because their friends are there, right? "And so that social connection is so powerful." Image source, Activision Image caption, Mads Mikkelsen plays mysterious enemy The Archer in the new game One of the biggest criticisms of last year's Call of Duty was its single-player campaign mode. The short, cinematic adventures are rarely the main reason players pick up the latest title, but are nevertheless popular. Alternating titles in the series follow different storylines, and the Modern Warfare strand has produced some of Call of Duty's most beloved characters. Activision has said Modern Warfare 4 is the "epic conclusion" to the story of fan favourite Capt John Price, played by British actor Barry Sloane. "It's a lot of surprises, a culmination of all those pieces that we've been putting together coming together," he says. Sloane tells Newsbeat he's not too intimidated by the weight of expectation. "I've been greeted with love from the fan base since the get-go," he says. "I only feel excitement." title: Gasps as Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
description: Gasps as Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show Image source, PA Media By Emer Moreau Published 22 October 2026 The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize. During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize. As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa, to cheers and gasps from the audience. They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet". The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films. William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely. There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives Â£1m. The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November. Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro. The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability. At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible". The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday. title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says
description: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says Image source, Getty Images By Nick Triggle Health correspondent Published 23 October 2026, 00:20 BST Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's plan to create a universal care service , the regulator says. The Care Quality Commission's annual report , external highlights how a rising share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest increased their share by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors, and now own one in seven homes. While there can be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in quality. The regulator said rapid changes to the market, including the fragmentation of home help into more smaller services, needed monitoring and clearer planning. The CQC said the changes to at-home care, which covers support to help people wash and dress, could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people. In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care. Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter. Clearer vision needed The CQC said the funding system remains fragile â people using care services either self-fund or, for the poorest, the state helps to pay for their costs. And in some areas, providers are increasingly turning to self-funders, making it more difficult for councils to buy the care they need for those relying on state help. CQC chief inspector of adult social care Chris Badger said the reshaping of the market was happening "largely by accident rather than design", driven by a combination of economic pressure and the problems some councils were having in buying services for those relying on state-funded care. He said this government's renewed focus on social care â Andy Burnham made it one of his key priorities when he became prime minister â was welcome. But he said it was important the market was "shaped around what's best for people". "A clearer vision is needed," he added. Hugh Alderwick, of the Health Foundation think-tank, said the report by the CQC "lays bare the massive challenges" facing the government. "The prime minister's commitment to reforming the sector provides an opportunity to fundamentally redraw the state's offer on social care. "But change is needed now to strengthen the fundamentals of the system. "Councils need enough funding, the right skills and strong leadership to shape services around people's needs." Prof Martin Green, of Care England, which represents care providers, said: "If the government and regulators are concerned by consolidation in the care sector, they need to take some clear and tangible action to support smaller care home providers." He said changes to employer national insurance contributions, inflation and the rising cost of energy was making smaller homes unviable. "Unless we get some real progress in a funding settlement, the trend of smaller homes closing will be a trend that will continue." The Department of Health and Social Care said the report demonstrated the "scale of the challenge this government inherited", but said it was committed to overhauling social care.
