title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
description: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns Image source, EPA By Tara Mewawalla Published 22 October 2026 Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said. Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them. He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies. Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more". Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime". Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households. He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter. Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists". The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems. In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed. "It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time. "In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences." Image caption, The defence secretary on Thursday spoke at the opening of the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford, Shropshire The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states. Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet. The "Be Ready" campaign , external encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items. It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news. Asked by a Question Time audience member whether the campaign amounted to scaremongering, Streeting said the government want "people to be alert but not alarmed". He said that there was not a "specific thing we've got in mind" when putting out the advice. But, he added that the supplies on the list "might help you through some power cuts, or might also help you through if... your local shop's subject to a cyber-attack and your card isn't working at the till". Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation". It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added. Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean. She said the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient. Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather. The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden. The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario". It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil". The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis". title: Give more people weight-loss jabs on the NHS, say MPs
description: Give more people weight-loss jabs on the NHS, say MPs Image source, Getty Images By Nick Triggle Health correspondent Published 23 October 2026, 00:06 BST Hundreds of thousands more people should be given access to the weight-loss injection Mounjaro on the NHS in England, a cross-party group of MPs says. The Health Committee said the current plan for 220,000 people to have this jab for free on prescription in 2028 was a "woefully small number" and "unambitious". This represents only around 6% of eligible people and is a key reason why more than a million have been paying privately for weight-loss injections, including Mounjaro and Wegovy. The committee says a two-tier system is emerging in which only the wealthy can get good access to the medication that curbs appetite. Rollout too slow Due to costs, the NHS is currently working on a 12-year rollout for Mounjaro - although this is being reviewed. It is estimated that if all 2.8 million people eligible for the drug were given it immediately, it would cost the NHS Â£15.2 billion over five years. Some of that expense is linked to the NHS relying heavily on GPs to oversee the prescribing and monitoring. MPs say the NHS must learn from private providers who often use digital platforms to do some of this work. The MPs said streamlining the process of support for patients could reduce that bill â and they said it also made financial sense because of the overall cost of obesity to the economy â estimated to be around Â£75 billion a year. Another weight-loss injection, Wegovy, is available on the NHS, but only through specialist weight management services. Dangerous market The committee also called for a crackdown on the black market for weight-loss drugs, saying the lack of availability on the NHS had driven people to buy unlicenced products online. It wants a public awareness campaign to warn about the dangers, along with a review to look at how better to regulate online advertising. The MPs also criticised the wider system of weight-loss services, saying they were poorly designed and resourced. They want people to have better access to diet and lifestyle courses and bariatric (obesity) surgery. Moran said obesity should be treated as a serious health condition, like diabetes. "People can spend their entire lives battling with their weight. We say the NHS should provide effective, structured support to beat obesity for all those who seek it. Instead, those people are repeatedly failed," she said. Jack Doughty, of the Obesity Health Alliance, said people living with obesity were being "let down by a fragmented and overstretched treatment system". "The reality is that the existing treatment services, from behavioural support to weight-loss medications and bariatric surgery, remain patchy and unequal." NHS England said it was looking at ways to  accelerate roll out weight-loss drugs, but was currently ârightly prioritising these treatments for those with the most severe and complex needsâ. title: Lights will stay on this winter, grid operator says after concerns
description: Lights will stay on this winter, grid operator says after concerns Image source, Getty Images By Michael Race Business reporter Published 23 October 2026, 00:04 BST Updated 4 hours ago The lights will stay on this winter, the body in charge of Britain's electricity network has said after concerns were raised by some of its engineers. The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months. However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation. NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days". It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine. "While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO. In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables. Supply under scrutiny The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears. The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations. Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas. However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator. 'High levels of stress' Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced. It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult". The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership. Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said. The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run". One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June. This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation. Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right". Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them". "I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added. title: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to Â£800m
description: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to Â£800m Image source, PA Image caption, John Healey becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to cut red tape for businesses ahead of his first Budget By Claire Keenan Â and Â Nick Eardley Published 5 hours ago The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to Â£800m. Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses. The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs. In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses. "Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said. Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses. He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs. The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said. Ministers have claimed this will save almost Â£800m in administrative and tariff costs. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North. Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses. "If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said. The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament. The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform. Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the employment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency". "John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said. Get in touch Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story? title: Gianni Infantino: Asian football chief gives Fifa president re-election lift
description: Infantino re-election hopes boosted by Asia support after u-turn Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (left) had previously criticised Gianni Infantino over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme By Dan Roan Sports editor Published 4 hours ago Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president have been given a major boost by an endorsement from the head of the Asian Football Confederation. President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa told the confederation's Congress in Tokyo - which was attended by Infantino - that "we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you as you seek a new mandate as president". Sheikh Salman's backing represents a significant u-turn just two months after he signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf criticising Infantino over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. At the time the three confederations accused him of breaking trust "through deception" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, and "a profound failure of judgement...these are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership." But in what appears to be a blow to the rebellion against Infantino, Sheikh Salman told the meeting in Japan it was time "to move forward". "I've spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear," he added. "Yes, we had some issues, we spoke about them in the past, but let's not relate the two things together... "As one Asian family, we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni." Alongside Infantino's power base in Africa and South America, Sheikh Salman's endorsement could be crucial in ensuring the Fifa president secures a fourth and final term. At the election in Rabat in March, Uefa will have 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10. Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents Published 3 days ago Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency? Published 15 October The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed. Potential rivals such as Victor Montagliani, the president of Concacaf, and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders. "You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my dear Salman," Infantino said in an address to the confederation's delegates. "You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years." Asked later about Sheikh Salman's comments, Infantino said: "I feel great about the AFC's support." At a meeting of Fifa's Council last week, Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan , but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. He also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (Â£2.6bn). Uefa has since told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by 2 November. Related topics Football

title: Dream night for Bournemouth - how did the Premier League come to dominate Europe?
description: Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bournemouth have beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now AC Milan in the Europa League By Alex Brotherton ,Â BBC Sport journalist Â and Â Andy Cryer ,Â BBC Sport senior journalist Published 22 October 2026 At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation. That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture. Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final. Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008 , not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts. "It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports. "So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special." To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two). While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point. In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A. The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years. For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare? Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance? Bournemouth sweep aside 10-man Milan in Europa League Premier League sides make strong start English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once. In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them. In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them. Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21. The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams. But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years. So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory? Money talks Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List. It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League. Premier League clubs earn more than Â£1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined. Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30. Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'. Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final. In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively. In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League. All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates. The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of Â£3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues. Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight. You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings. Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent. "With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August. "A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer." title: Katie Boulter reaches Japan Open semi-final to reclaim British number one ranking
description: Boulter into Japan semis and back as British No 1 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Katie Boulter is through to her third WTA semi-final of the 2026 season Published 27 minutes ago Katie Boulter has reclaimed the British number one ranking after fighting back to beat Antonia Ruzic in three sets in the quarter-finals of the Japan Open. The 30-year-old was dethroned on Monday following Sonay Kartal's run to the final in Wuhan but knew she could overturn the 55-point deficit by reaching the last four in Osaka. Eighth seed Boulter trailed world number 91 Ruzic by a set and a break but recovered to win 3-6 6-3 6-3 in two hours to reach her first semi-final since Queen's in June. She will face Czech Katerina Siniakova in the last four and whatever the result will climb above Kartal and back into the world's top 50 when the WTA rankings are updated on Monday. "[Ruzic] is a really good player, full credit to her," said Boulter. "I tried to hang tough and find a way. I was a bit lucky in the middle of the second [set] but I feel I did really well to stay there." On facing Siniakova for a spot in the final, she added: "She's one hell of a player, extremely dangerous. It's going to be who gets the first strike in. "I've got nothing to lose. She's been building extremely well this week, so I'm going to have to come prepared." Inside British number one Kartal's remarkable comeback Published 4 days ago Boulter struggled on serve in the opening two sets, winning just 60% points behind her first serve, hitting four double faults, and facing seven break points, but grew into the match, finding success when stepping inside the baseline to put pressure on the 23-year-old Croat. Broken in her opening service game, Boulter was gifted a route back into the first set at 4-2 when Ruzic double-faulted on break point. However, Ruzic immediately hit back, winning the next four games. Boulter wrested back control in an increasingly scrappy second set, saving two break points in the third game to avoid going a double-break down before coming up with a crucial hold in the seventh after the pair had exchanged three successive breaks. That hold proved the second of eight straight games for Boulter, who raced into a 4-0 lead in the decider. Although she failed to serve out the match at 5-2, she broke her opponent to love to wrap up the win. title: World Treadmill Championship: Where amateurs compete against the elite
description: The World Treadmill Championship - pitching elite runners against amateurs To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Treadmill World Championship - what are they and how to compete? By Sarah Dawkins BBC Sport senior journalist Published 4 hours ago For decades, treadmill running has been viewed as little more than a training tool for outdoor runners. But that could be about to change, with the launch of the World Treadmill Championship. In this new World Athletics-sanctioned competition, runners around the world log 5km on a treadmill and compete for a prize pool of $100,000 and the title of world champion. Known as Run X, it pitches everyday runners against elite athletes. BBC Sport was invited along to a qualification event at a gym in Southampton to observe runners logging their times on the global virtual leaderboard. Image source, Run X Image caption, The finals for the first ever Treadmill World Championship will take place in Italy in March Among them is British marathon runner Charlotte Purdue. "I think it's good to get people into running. 5km is obviously not too far so people can have a shot at it, there's no pressure," she tells BBC Sport. Purdue, who holds the third fastest British female marathon time, believes the treadmill has been long misunderstood. "I personally love the treadmill and I've always used it in my training. We've got one at home and I find it easy at home and I really enjoy it." But does she think she's got what it takes to be the first ever treadmill world champion? "It's definitely added motivation," she adds. "But I wish it was a marathon on the treadmill, I think I'd have a better chance!" Image source, BBC Sport Image caption, Elite marathon runner Charlotte Purdue logged her 5km time at 18 minutes 15 seconds Runners have until 24 January to complete 5km, for free, at an official Run X centre. They can make multiple attempts, but only their best time will count. There is no official 5km treadmill world record recognised by World Athletics. The men's 5,000m track record is 12 minutes, 35.36 seconds, while the women's is 13:58.06 The men's road record for the distance stands at  12:49, with the women's at 13:54. The top 25% of runners in age categories from 18 to 75+ will represent their nation at the regionals, before the 10 best men and women in each category advance to the world finals in Italy next March. The $100,000 prize pool is split between the men's and women's overall podiums, across seven age-group categories. The exact distribution has not been published. There are currently 20 countries taking part and the list of elite runners registered has not yet been disclosed. Organisers hope to entice more participants with wildcard entries to events like the 2027 World Road Running Championships in China. Despite the treadmill sometimes being referred to anecdotally as the 'dreadmill' due to the repetitive and monotonous nature of indoor running, World Athletics president Lord Coe told BBC Sport it's a "great opportunity" to introduce a new audience to running. "It's across a whole range of age groups. It's very important that we continue to innovate and it's really important that when we innovate, we use technology that attracts more young people into our sport," he says. The ambition for treadmill running doesn't stop there, with hopes the discipline can also be included in Esport competitions in the next five years. "We know there are a lot of long-distance challenges but nothing at that 5km mark which is more accessible and that's the real big starting point," Luke Townsend, education manager at Technogym UK, the co-organisers of the competition, tells BBC Sport. Alongside professionals like Purdue on the treadmills in Southampton were members of the 'She Strides' run club. They usually opt to run together outdoors but wanted to take part in Run X to highlight how important treadmill running is from a safety point of view. "Unfortunately, so many women in the winter have to change their routines of running outside because they don't feel safe," says Hollie Thackway, founder of She Strides. With the clocks going back this weekend, many runners will soon be spending more of their training time in the dark. Thackway added: "By being able to run inside on a treadmill, it means you don't have to stop your training, you can still be on a programme, achieve your goals and not stop running altogether through the winter, so I think this event is great to highlight that." title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
description: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday By Koh Ewe Published 2 hours ago Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast. Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday. One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate. Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El NiÃ±o heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far. On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) . After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island. Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan. However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches. Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said. Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains. Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island. Taiwan's $5tn (Â£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather. Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual. In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company. More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines. Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan. Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties. Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane. While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea. This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms. The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El NiÃ±o - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons. title: England v Australia rugby league: What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas
description: What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas for England Image source, Getty Images Image caption, England will face Australia for the first time since a 90-4 loss in March 2025 By Emma Smith ,Â BBC Sport journalist Â and Â Steve Sutcliffe ,Â BBC Sport journalist Published 4 hours ago Mention of Las Vegas is enough to send a shiver down the spine of any England women's rugby league supporter. Not because of lost life savings on the slot machines or undercooked food at the buffet, but because England fell to a record 90-4 defeat by Australia at the Allegiant Stadium in Nevada. The meeting between England and Australia in March 2025 had been touted as the first in a three-match Test series. It was meant to be the beginning of a regular Women's Ashes competition between two historic rivals and form a large part of world rugby league's charm offensive in the US. Instead it served up a sobering reminder of the gulf between the Jillaroos - the winners of the previous three World Cups - and England, who shipped 17 tries in a lopsided affair. The sight of Georgia Roche, who scored England's only try, in tears at the final whistle and being consoled by her opponents only added to the suffering of English fans who made the trip. The outcome also led many to believe the game in the northern hemisphere had reached a new nadir - with England's World Cup prospects almost dismissed out of hand as a result. However, it has also delivered a seismic shift in England head coach Stuart Barrow's thinking. Few of those selected for this tournament bear the scars of that encounter, with a youthful and dynamic squad featuring only six of the team from the Sin City debacle. And Barrow says excitement, not trepidation, is the feeling in the England camp as they get ready to face the World Cup co-hosts in Perth on Saturday (10:05 BST). "The youngsters coming in think that they can do better than what we did last time and I fully back that and believe them as well," Barrow said. "I don't think they've [Australia] been beaten internationally for a long time, but that's exciting. "If you're a young player coming into this group and coming to represent your country in a World Cup on the other side of the world, you want to play the best. "People were saying, 'do we want to avoid teams?' When you come all this way, you want to pit yourself as an athlete against the best. So there is excitement among the group but they're all very aware and very respectful of who we're playing." Rugby League World Cup: Australia v England Saturday, 24 October: 10:05 BST HBF Park, Perth Listen on Sounds Listen to live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app. England need to step up Image source, SWpix Image caption, Stuart Barrow was appointed as England women's head coach in November 2022 While England thrashed Wales 70-6 in their World Cup opener, Barrow acknowledged their preparations to face Australia were dealt a "devastating blow" when Jasmin Strange picked up a serious knee injury in training on Tuesday, ruling her out of the rest of the tournament. The absence of the Sydney Roosters second-row forward will be sharply felt by Barrow's squad as they take on opponents who have lost just once since 2016 and remain the benchmark at international level. And Barrow insists that while their most recent encounter is "buried" and "in the past", he is using the chastening loss to help ensure England's readiness for this competition. "We learned a lot from it," he added. "We've built on that through all our training over the last 18 months. "We've got some senior players who were in that group at the time and it allows them to talk about what happened in that game to our young group. It allows them to talk about the difficulties, challenges and we can draw on the experience mainly from player to player." With Australia opening their campaign with a 40-0 win over Samoa, Barrow says his side will have to step things up from last weekend. "We came up with some unforced handling errors on first. We weren't at such a high completion rate but our skill with the ball let us get away with that," Barrow added. "You don't get that opportunity when you play the world champions. If you're giving cheap ball away, then you're defending. "We've done a lot of work about keeping possession and respecting the ball, but I also think we've got some exciting football in us when we get to the right end of the field to challenge them, so that's our aim." Meanwhile, Australia hooker Keeley Nizza has made it clear they will not take England lightly. "We definitely know about the rivalry," Nizza said. "Last year we played them in Vegas and there was a big score, but I think England are a very different team now." They also have Super League's Woman of Steel Jenna Foubister, 19, and her highly-rated Wigan team-mate Isabel Rowe, who kicked nine conversions alongside a couple of tries to record the highest points tally (26) in a single game by a female England player at a World Cup. title: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat
description: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, This is the first case of Ebola in Nigeria in more than a decade By Simi Jolaoso ,Â Africa correspondent ,Â Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lagos Â and Â Wycliffe Muia Published 23 October 2026, 05:54 BST Updated 44 minutes ago Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed that the woman who has tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria is the wife of a Swiss diplomat. The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national who lives in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, tested positive for the virus on 20 October, becoming the country's first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade. They both travelled to Uganda earlier this month. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, according to the Swiss foreign ministry. The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate. The ministry said the woman had spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja with symptoms before her diagnosis. It believes she contracted the virus while travelling in Uganda, although health authorities have yet to establish the source of her infection. Uganda borders Democratic Republic of Congo, where some 4,600 have died in the country's most deadly outbreak of Ebola. Two people died in Uganda shortly after the outbreak began in May but it has been declared free of Ebola since August. The ministry said the decision not to isolate the embassy's eight Swiss and 17 local employees was taken in consultation with Nigeria's Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO). It added that the embassy remained open and operational, with health and safety measures in place. The woman is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the WHO. She returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. The patient did ânot travel to DR Congo, the Swiss âgovernment told Reuters news agency on Friday, contradicting accounts from Uganda. She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October. Health officials are now investigating whether she may have crossed paths with a Kenyan man who died from Ebola and had travelled through Uganda's main airport on the same day. Investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday. Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established. "One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," he told journalists. The Kenyan man had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He died shortly afterwards, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? Published 2 days ago What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? Published 15 September Kenya has since confirmed nine infections, including the fatal case. Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact. Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source. The WHO said it was too early to determine where the woman in Nigeria became infected. "The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official. He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital. Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help establish whether her infection is linked to other cases. "The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria. Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business. However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country. Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there. Meanwhile, Nigerian authorities are tracing more people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially identified. Kenya's Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission. He urged the public to remain vigilant and not panic but warned: "We are not out of the woods". He said the remaining eight patients were still in isolation and responding well to treatment. The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands cross daily for trade, work and family visits. Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points. The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers. Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu. The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People...

title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
description: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: CCTV vision shows moment quake strikes in Tibet By Laura Bicker ,Â China correspondent, Â and Â Harry Sekulich Published 23 October 2026, 00:22 BST Updated 5 hours ago A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media. The centre of the quake hit BaqÃªn County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau. The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa. Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries. The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas. Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake. Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas. The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km. Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Rescuers search through rubble after Tibet earthquake Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape. Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu told Tibet Daily that she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, her "legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home. Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us". Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet. Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks had been registered since the quake occurred. China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media. Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude, around 4,800m (15,750ft), and prone to aftershocks. The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations. Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (Â£5.6m; $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet. Image source, CCTV via Reuters Image caption, Firefighters are seen helping residents injured by the quake in BaqÃªn, Tibet Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark. These have not been independently verified. The region is prone to devastating seismic activity. In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China. Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing. Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly. In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet. The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area. Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China. With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen. title: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
description: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices Image source, Reuters Image caption, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in India this week By Nikita Yadav & Rachita Prasad BBC News Published 2 hours ago The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit. So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi? The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions â or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs. Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani. It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations. The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies. With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets. And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation. The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Rubio (left) held talks with foreign minister S Jaishankar (right) in Mumbai Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties. The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic. "Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital. "This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai." The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works. But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip. Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms". Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website. It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets. During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani. The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products. Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil. "They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters. Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East. Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer. Image source, Sergio Gor/X Image caption, Rubio's visit to the Jamnagar refinery was closed to the media, with images released afterwards by the Reliance Group Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil. India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022. Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude. In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties. India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority. Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
description: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit Image source, Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images By Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter Published 22 October 2026 Updated 9 hours ago A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December. The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021. Trump cancelled a previous deposition - an interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance". But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", in which the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence. Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition. US Magistrate Judge EnjoliquÃ© Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December or face sanctions - the most extreme of which could be the dismissal of the lawsuit - unless the discovery period is extended. In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. Depositions carry legal weight - they are recorded verbatim by a court reporter and the transcripts can later be used as evidence in trials. They typically take place in a lawyer's office without a judge physically present. In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions. Last week, lawyers asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place. On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year and claimed the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action". Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021. The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action". The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US. In July, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters. Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary". title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skincare sales
description: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skincare sales Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The use of weight loss drugs, known as GLP-1s, has increased in popularity in recent years By Rachel Clun Business reporter Published 22 October 2026 Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skincare sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side-effects of rapid weight loss. The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us". He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular". L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations. The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite. While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side-effect of loose skin - including around the face. Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side-effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss. L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December. Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters. Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler. Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance. Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs. title: Malawi opposition demands answers over president's prolonged stay abroad
description: Malawi opposition demands answers over president's prolonged stay abroad Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year By Wycliffe Muia Published 14 minutes ago Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties. The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips. "Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said. Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum. The professor who beat fraud allegations to become Malawi's presidentâ¦again Published 25 September 2025 Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera. He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020. His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa. On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges. He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs. "The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge." He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency. The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs. Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private." He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration. "That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added. On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe. Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment. Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information. Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well. Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs. Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration. title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
description: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? By Tom Gerken Â and Â Liv McMahon ,Â Technology reporters Published 22 October 2026 Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP. Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades. Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution. There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent. Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out. "The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords. She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied". The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected. A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue". "But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added. Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented". "It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One. But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers. He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected , external had been received and was being acted on. Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb Published 1 day ago What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? Published 23 hours ago Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date. "Hacking has been around for many years," he said. "The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point." Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online. He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long. "MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said. He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers. What is PHP? PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit. When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read. It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today. PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress â the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz , external , which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it. The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP. Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems. Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X , external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added. Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal. 'Serious vulnerability' Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Cyber researchers at Calif and Wiz unearthed the php2shell flaw, theorised by the PHP Foundation in 2024, in part using OpenAI tools While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday. The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday. But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required. In France, telecommunications company Orange also said , external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.
