title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
description: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war rages By Orla Guerin Senior International Correspondent ,Â Reporting from Aden Published 22 October 2026 From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival. They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces. When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks â the twins protected only by blankets. What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden. Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden "It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused." As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhaustedâ¦ there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse." By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs. Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured. Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk. The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet. Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed. The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer. Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz. The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices. The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes. Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away. Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018. "I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself." Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred. "I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]." Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space. Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing." Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut. There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment. That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor. "It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says. "We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them." A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line. Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year. Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon. "Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again." They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics. "Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital." She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them. Image source, Lee...

title: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
description: Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Anti-migrant protesters in South Africa demand that all undocumented foreign nationals leave the country By Ondiro Oganga Published 22 October 2026 A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say. According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established. The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg. Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified. 'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare Published 18 October 2025 The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa Published 18 September 2023 The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year. One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa. Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries. These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence. Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month. Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals. His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated. One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic. "We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme. South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals. The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce. Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence. Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities. title: Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past
description: Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Actor Tiger Shroff, who made his debut in 2014, is known for his action roles By Zoya Mateen BBC News, Delhi Published 23 October 2026, 00:55 BST On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor. Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt . Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies. Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers. The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi , one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years. Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why. The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history. During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip. Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again? To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Watch: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting attempt in Mumbai Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest. D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution. In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt. Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke , a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision. Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle. But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad. "This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else." Image source, Reuters Image caption, Gangster Lawrence Bishnoi has been locked up in prison since 2015 That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online. Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered . Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing. Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety. Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print , external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bishnoi's gang claimed responsibility for killing Baba Siddiqui...

title: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of VuÄiÄ rule in Serbia
description: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of VuÄiÄ rule in Serbia Image source, Reuters Image caption, Young Serbians have been the driving force behind the movement, but none of the candidates are students By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Published 22 October 2026 Updated 4 hours ago Final campaign rallies have taken place across Serbia, ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future. After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar VuÄiÄ's 12 years in power. The main threat to VuÄiÄ's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote. Why is this student movement so important? They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia. The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija SrdanoviÄ said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable." It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people. The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024 What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges. The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by VuÄiÄ, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums. At the last election in 2023, VuÄiÄ's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties. Anger lingers in Serbia after train station tragedy Published 1 November 2025 Who is VuÄiÄ and how popular is he? Image source, Pierre Crom/Getty Images Image caption, VuÄiÄ has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that VuÄiÄ has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017 . The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities. VuÄiÄ has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko MladiÄ, prompting EU anger at his "glorification". Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is VuÄiÄ's biggest challenge since he came to power. "He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President VuÄiÄ isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade. Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections Published 27 September How do Serbia's elections work? Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation. Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday. There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for. Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote. Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List. Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for? Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ilija SrdanoviÄ (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists. They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija SrdanoviÄ is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir StaniÄ and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Å oÅ¡kiÄ. Under an 11-point programme , external , the student movement wants to: eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises VuÄiÄ and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media. How fair will the vote be? European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere". Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned...

title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
description: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's election By Yolande Knell Middle East correspondent ,Â Reporting from Nazareth Published 22 October 2026 At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power. Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. "I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future." Image caption, All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority. If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists. A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values. Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority. Image caption, Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis "After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza." Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending. There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis. Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank. How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders? Published 1 day ago The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government". To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders. Image caption, Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab parties At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party. I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties. "In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel." Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings. These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas. Image caption, United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence" While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc. For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police...

title: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted
description: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted Just now Share Save Add as preferred on Google Gabriela Pomeroy , Hafsa Khalil and Anastasiia Levchenko , Kyiv Watch: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access after row Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits on the satellite uplink had been reversed by Elon Musk. The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations. The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back". Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations. The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks. They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted". Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said. Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield , which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues. The White House has since repeatedly denied deliberately placing limits on the network in Ukraine. Trump refused to say whether he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service when asked about reports to that end on Thursday, but said: "Bottom line, he put it back." Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed. The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. One Ukrainian soldier said there was "simply no alternative" to Starshield, adding that earlier in the week, connectivity had been cutting out when his unit had been travelling in a car at 80km/h (50 mph). "I'll tell you this much: God forbid they shut it off completely - it would be an absolute catastrophe," he told the BBC. "We need a backup option for securing communications and internet." Another soldier said they had reverted to the "proven algorithms" they used before they had Starlink when it initially started playing up, but stressed that Ukrainian forces did need the network, citing its speed. "Even one or two seconds is critical when we can transfer data and orders faster," she said. "You can really feel that advantage on the battlefield." Ukrainian reports of a slowdown to the service came during a tense diplomatic row between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war . Zelensky said the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump later denied. The row prompted a war of words between the two world leaders, with Trump suggesting it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and Zelensky implying Trump was not a real leader. Earlier on Thursday - before Trump's comments - Zelensky had said the speed of the system had still not been restored fully. "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so." The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had told Musk that he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped, and that the system was working closer to normal following that conversation. title: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
description: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018 34 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Freya Scott-Turner Getty Images The Duchess of Sussex has said she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018. In a statement, Meghan said a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police that year and subsequently shared with her. Her comments come after reports that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to her father had been found at his former home in the Philippines, which she said were "deeply" distressing. In an interview with the Daily Mail, Thomas Markle denied possessing child sex images, calling the accusations "sick lies". The duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed." She said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated". She added she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children". This was "to protect them", she said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families". Meghan described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children". title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
description: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say 6 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laura Bicker , China correspondent, and Harry Sekulich Watch: CCTV vision shows moment quake strikes in Tibet A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media. The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau. The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa. Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries. The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas. Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake. Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas. The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km. Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes. Rescuers search through rubble after Tibet earthquake Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape. Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu told Tibet Daily that she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, her "legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home. Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us". Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet. Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks had been registered since the quake occurred. China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media. Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude, around 4,800m (15,750ft), and prone to aftershocks. The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations. Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (£5.6m; $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet. CCTV via Reuters Firefighters are seen helping residents injured by the quake in Baqên, Tibet Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark. These have not been independently verified. The region is prone to devastating seismic activity. In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China. Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing. Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly. In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet. The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area. Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China. With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen. title: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
description: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting 39 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Tom Bennett Jerusalem AFP Photos of one of the suspected attackers were shared by AFP news agency Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say. Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron. In response, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had ordered the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The attack comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time. The two injured Israelis are in critical condition, according to Israel's ambulance service. The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there. Unverified CCTV footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire. The Israeli military said it had begun raids on the homes of the attackers, while far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said he had ordered the demolition of several Palestinian buildings adjacent to the site of the attack. It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis. Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security for Israelis, said that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media. At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN. Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says. title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
description: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan 2 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Koh Ewe AFP via Getty Images Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast. Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday. One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate. Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far. On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) . After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island. Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan. However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches. Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said. Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains. Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island. Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather. Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual. In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company. More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines. Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan. Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties. Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane. While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea. This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms. The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons. Asia Taiwan

title: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
description: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices 2 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Nikita Yadav & Rachita Prasad BBC News Reuters US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in India this week The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit. So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi? The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions – or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs. Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani. It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations. The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies. With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets. And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation. The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now. Reuters Rubio (left) held talks with foreign minister S Jaishankar (right) in Mumbai Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties. The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic. "Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital. "This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai." The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works. But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip. Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms". Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website. It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets. During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani. The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products. Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil. "They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters. Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East. Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer. Sergio Gor/X Rubio's visit to the Jamnagar refinery was closed to the media, with images released afterwards by the Reliance Group Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil. India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022. Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude. In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties. India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority. Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. title: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
description: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial 3 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jim Reed Health reporter Addenbrooke's Hospital Tony Chapman, 75, from Corby in the East Midlands was one of the 1,100 melanoma patients enrolled on the vaccine trial A new personalised cancer vaccine given alongside a widely used immunotherapy drug has cut the risk of patients dying or their skin cancer returning by 42% in a major clinical trial. The researchers involved say the results could mark a turning point in cancer treatment, bringing personalised medicine a step closer. The trial also found that the new drug combination reduced the risk of melanoma, a type of skin cancer, spreading by 38% over two years compared to immunotherapy alone. The drug manufacturers MSD and Moderna say the same approach is already being tested against other tumours, including kidney, bladder and lung cancer. Independent cancer experts described the results as impressive but said longer-term studies were still needed to establish whether the treatment really helps most patients live longer, on average. Personalised vaccine The new approach is aimed at cancer patients who have already had their tumour removed through surgery. In the trial, 1,137 adults were given Keytruda, an established immunotherapy drug which helps the body's immune system find and attack cancer cells. About two-thirds also received an experimental vaccine with the rest being given a placebo or dummy drug. The vaccine, called Intismeran, uses the same mRNA technology as some Covid jabs. It is personalised to each patient, using information from their own tumour to help train their immune system to recognise cancer cells and target them if they return. Two years after starting the treatment, the patients who received the jab were far less likely to have had melanoma come back or see it spread across the body. "Personalisation is the next step up and it's really exciting, it's a fabulous technology," says Prof Pippa Corrie, a consultant medical oncologist who helped run part of the study with patients at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. "The question is how much can we really demonstrate it's worth and this trial was the first proof of principle." The latest checks show that Tony Chapman is cancer free three years after he was first told melanoma skin cancer had spread to his lymph nodes 'What's to lose?' Prof Corrie worked with patients enrolled in the trial including 75-year old Tony Chapman, who was diagnosed with melanoma in 2019. He had the tumour removed from his chest but a lump later appeared under his arm. He was told his cancer had returned and he needed a second operation. He then volunteered to take part in the study but, like all the other participants, he still doesn't know whether he was given the experimental vaccine or a placebo alongside his immunotherapy treatment. "This just seemed like a really good example of moving science forward, as well as getting some benefit for yourself, so what's to lose?" Tony said. Three years on he is now having checks every six months and remains cancer-free. Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer. But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial. Both companies said they were now "engaging with authorities" suggesting they could file for approval from medicine regulators as soon as next year. Widespread NHS use will also depend on cost, given that each individual patient will need to have their tumour genetically analysed and a personalised vaccine made for them. The trial will continue so that the patients involved can be monitored – both to see if the cancer returns over time and to assess whether the drug ultimately helps them live longer. Professor Alan Melcher from the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn't involved in the research, described the results as "very impressive". "It is an important proof of principle for the field, although we shouldn't get ahead of the evidence," he said. "We can't assume from one melanoma trial that the same approach will work across all cancers, and longer follow-up will be important to understand the effect on overall survival." The full trial results are due to be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) cancer conference in Madrid on Saturday. They have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, where they can be scrutinised by independent experts. title: Detective raped by colleague says Met handling of case 'like being raped again'
description: Detective raped by colleague says Met handling of case 'like being raped again' 6 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Daniel De Simone , Investigations correspondent and Nalini Sivathasan Watch: Met chief Rowley not fit for job, says Linda Williams A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again". Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - a serial abuser jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 other women. Linda has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the attack and sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick. The lengthy civil case left her feeling suicidal, she says. The "worst thing", she says, was when lawyers acting for the Met commissioner challenged the severity of her PTSD on the basis that she had been raped only once. The Met has told the BBC it "tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams' welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible". "We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer," the force added. "Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable." Linda, who has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak to the BBC, has settled her civil case and the Met has now paid her compensation without acceptance of liability. In an unprecedented move for a serving officer, she is now calling publicly for Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley to resign. She believes he has failed to change police culture as promised and she still does not trust her own force to handle cases like hers. When he took on the most important job in UK policing in 2022, Sir Mark pledged to change the Met. At the time, the force was viewed as being in crisis - following Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer and other scandals including officers sharing photos of murdered sisters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. PA Media Met Police commissioner Sir Mark Rowley has promised to get rid of officers unfit to serve After Carrick was jailed in January 2023, Sir Mark praised the victims and said: "We have failed and I'm sorry. He should not have been a police officer." Two months later, in an official report by Baroness Casey, the Met was described as a "boys' club", that was institutionally misogynistic and had failed women. Linda contacted the BBC, after seeing Panorama's report last year into a hidden culture of misogyny and racism inside the Met . Since reporting the rape by Carrick in 2021, Linda says it has been "horrific" and she would not report a rape to the Met today "because I don't trust the police and I don't think they deal with it correctly". Carrick was brought to justice by Hertfordshire Police, which investigated the rape of Linda. She reported it to the force after seeing media coverage of the news that Carrick had been charged with raping another woman. Linda was herself a rape investigation officer in the early 2000s. "I supported victims through rape but didn't report myself. I think that says loads. "I'm asking members of the public to report, and I'm there to support them, but I wouldn't do it myself and I didn't do it." She says if a similar attack happened to her tomorrow, she would not report it to the Met, because she has "no faith" that the force would deal with it correctly. Carrick raped her while she was on a three-month attachment with him in south London - miles from where she was normally based. One night, Linda says, Carrick suggested she should stay at his home, so she did not have to drive far late at night only to return early the next morning. He then raped her. When Linda told him no, she says Carrick replied: "It's what I do. I'm going to carry on." She knew that if she fought back then Carrick was going to get violent, she says. Linda Williams Linda has been a Met Police officer for 27 years Afterwards, Linda says she "never told a soul". She says she felt unable to report the rape then, or for years afterwards, because of the culture in the Met. Reporting the rape "would have been the end of my career", she says, because Carrick would not have been charged and she would have been shunned. "I would imagine that if Carrick had been arrested, he probably would have been interviewed and then no further action. So then mud sticks, doesn't it? "Then I'd be the officer that alleges rape, and who's going to want to work with me?" The "very sexist" culture she says she experienced included having her forehead stamped with the words "Property of the Met" and being locked in the boot of a police car for the duration of a shift. Linda, now 60, says the mental and emotional impact of the rape has been vast. She has led a lonely life, she says, focused primarily on her work and pets. She has not had a relationship with a man since the day she was attacked and says she has missed out on having a family. "I still don't feel I could have any relationship," she adds. She feels guilty at not having come forward earlier to report Carrick, she says. Since his conviction, she says the Met's culture has not changed as much as it should have done. "We've not moved on enough in the police to really give victims of domestic violence, sexual offences any [of the] support they really need." title: Final James Bond screen tests to take place this weekend, reports say
description: Final James Bond screen tests to take place this weekend, reports say 1 hour ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Helen Bushby Culture reporter Getty Images Callum Turner and Jack Lowden are both thought to be part of the final auditions to play James Bond Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor are among the actors thought to be taking part in final auditions to play James Bond, according to reports. Screen tests are said to be taking place this weekend, possibly as early as Friday, according to the Hollywood Reporter , with between three and five actors understood to have reached the last stages of the process. The finalists are said to be taking part in auditions with three components - stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Deadline reported the screen tests had been due take place in early October, but had been delayed by scheduling conflicts, while Variety said Turner and Lowden "appear to be in the mix" to replace Daniel Craig. British actors Aaron Taylor-Johnson and James Norton were previously connected to the role, while Irish actor Paul Mescal's name had also been thrown into the mix. Other actors now appear to be in the frame, but reports on the current casting situation vary. Variety suggested Slow Horses star Lowden may now be edging ahead, while Masters of the Air star Turner was speculated about earlier this year, with some fans suggesting his wife Dua Lipa could sing the Bond theme song. Sources told Deadline that at least four final screen test offers have been made, and while unconfirmed, "three of the four expected to test are Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor". O'Connor is best known for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and for starring in 2025's Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, with Craig. Jack O'Connell had been thought to be in the mix, but sources said this may no longer be the case, while Euphoria and Wuthering Heights Star Jacob Elordi is not thought to be testing. Other stars who were previously linked with the role include The King's Man star Harris Dickinson, along with SAS: Rogue Heroes' Jack Barton. Deadline said: "Even with the tests wrapping next week, there is no timeline for when a final decision will be made." Getty Images Daniel Craig served as James Bond across 15 years and five films Amazon MGM Studios, who now control the Bond franchise, announced in May that the casting process was under way, but had no further comment at the time. In August, Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, told Deadline the "end of the year is a good bet" for possible news on who would be playing Bond. "We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow," she said. "And it's got to be something really different that is a stirring and exciting and different." The BBC's Lizo Mzimba reported in September that "for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen". He added: "As the 007 team themselves have explained in the past: 'Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors'." The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered Search for new James Bond officially kicks off as auditions begin Reuters Writer Steven Knight said in September the first draft of the Bond script was done Only six actors have ever played novelist Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series - Sean Connery, Roger Moore, George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig. The last announcement of a new Bond was in 2005 with Craig, who last starred in the role in 2021's No Time to Die, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga. During the equivalent stage of the audition process two decades ago, Superman actor Henry Cavill was widely thought to have also been in the running. "They told me I was close," Cavill told the Happy Sad Confused podcast in 2022. "They told me it was ultimately down to, and this is what I've been told, it was just down to me and Daniel, and I was the younger option. "They obviously went with Daniel and I think it was an amazing choice to go with Daniel," he said. "I probably wasn't ready at the time and I think Daniel did an incredible job over the past movies, so I'm happy they made that choice." The forthcoming film, reportedly out in 2028, will be directed by Dune's Denis Villeneuve , with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight writing the script . Knight told Zoe Ball on Greatest Hits Radio in September that the first draft of the script was completed. Amazon bought MGM for $8.5bn (£6.3bn) in 2021 , which included the rights to distribute James Bond, and they are reported to have paid at least $20m (£14.9m) more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future. Pascal and David Heyman are producing the film, while Tanya Lapointe is executive producer. Knight's final words on the film were about how much he was enjoying working on it. He told Ball: "I'm absolutely loving doing it. It's an honour to be asked. And believe it's going to be so good. I really do believe it's going to be amazing." title: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
description: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich 52 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google James Oliver and Rory Tinman , BBC Panorama Getty Images Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich - his lawyers have said he denies concealing his fortune Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax. Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ). A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit. Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws". The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering. The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed. Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation. A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months. When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved." He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated." Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts. Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT. Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it. title: Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past
description: Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past 11 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Zoya Mateen BBC News, Delhi AFP via Getty Images Actor Tiger Shroff, who made his debut in 2014, is known for his action roles On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor. Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt . Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies. Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers. The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi , one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years. Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why. The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history. During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip. Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again? Watch: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting attempt in Mumbai Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest. D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution. In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt. Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke , a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision. Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle. But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad. "This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else." Reuters Gangster Lawrence Bishnoi has been locked up in prison since 2015 That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online. Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered . Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing. Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety. Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it." Getty Images Bishnoi's gang claimed responsibility for killing Baba Siddiqui (right) in 2024, citing his ties to Salman Khan (left) The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.
