title: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat
description: Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat 32 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Simi Jolaoso , Africa correspondent , Makuochi Okafor , BBC Africa, Lagos and Wycliffe Muia AFP via Getty Images This is the first case of Ebola in Nigeria in more than a decade Switzerland's foreign ministry has confirmed that the woman who has tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria is the wife of a Swiss diplomat. The woman, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born national who lives in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, tested positive for the virus on 20 October, becoming the country's first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade. They both travelled to Uganda earlier this month. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed any symptoms, according to the Swiss foreign ministry. The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate. The ministry said the woman had spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja with symptoms before her diagnosis. It believes she contracted the virus while travelling in Uganda, although health authorities have yet to establish the source of her infection. Uganda borders Democratic Republic of Congo, where some 4,600 have died in the country's most deadly outbreak of Ebola. Two people died in Uganda shortly after the outbreak began in May but it has been declared free of Ebola since August. The ministry said the decision not to isolate the embassy's eight Swiss and 17 local employees was taken in consultation with Nigeria's Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO). It added that the embassy remained open and operational, with health and safety measures in place. The woman is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the WHO. She returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. The patient did ​not travel to DR Congo, the Swiss ‌government told Reuters news agency on Friday, contradicting accounts from Uganda. She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October. Health officials are now investigating whether she may have crossed paths with a Kenyan man who died from Ebola and had travelled through Uganda's main airport on the same day. Investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday. Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established. "One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," he told journalists. The Kenyan man had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He died shortly afterwards, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death. Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed? What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? Kenya has since confirmed nine infections, including the fatal case. Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact. Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source. The WHO said it was too early to determine where the woman in Nigeria became infected. "The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official. He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital. Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help establish whether her infection is linked to other cases. "The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria. Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business. However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country. Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there. Meanwhile, Nigerian authorities are tracing more people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially identified. Kenya's Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission. He urged the public to remain vigilant and not panic but warned: "We are not out of the woods". He said the remaining eight patients were still in isolation and responding well to treatment. The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands cross daily for trade, work and family visits. Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points. The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers. Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu. The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms. title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC finds
description: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC finds 25 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Barbara Plett Usher , Africa correspondent and Mohamed Madi Saudi Hospital medics Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago. UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings. The health minister of the group's civilian-affiliated government dismissed the allegations as propaganda. Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud said it was a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation. Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times. Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict. The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted. "The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC. "The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned." The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military. Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities. El-Fasher residents had little access to healthcare during the long siege of the city In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility. But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query. UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city. The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city. A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023. Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city. Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies. The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher. In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city. The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman. The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says. On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added. The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist. But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office. They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs. "There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners. Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead. "They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me." That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said. The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated. Dr Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base. According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy". In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim. title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
description: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI 3 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Priti Gupta Technology Reporter, Mumbai Mohammed Ashim Mohammed Ashim is paid to film his hands at work Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru. But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work. The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out. "The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working." He wears the camera for five or six hours a day. "It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim. He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities. Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work. That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world. Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data. "Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig. His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work. "For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says. Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says. "We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off." But his customers are getting more demanding. "Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands. "Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people." And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year. Rashdan Technologies Shahil Baig expects dozens more firms to start collecting video of workers Why is such data so important? If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data. Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact. "Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says. And until recently, that data was not available. "There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco. At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia. Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients. "You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US." The factory workers teaching robots how to work like humans But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs? At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai. For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says. The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about. "By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says. Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI. "AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence." 'This is survival' Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development. Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day. Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years. "Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even...

title: Malawi opposition demands answers over president's prolonged stay abroad
description: Malawi opposition demands answers over president's prolonged stay abroad 16 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Wycliffe Muia Bloomberg via Getty Images This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year Malawi's opposition has demanded an explanation for President Peter Mutharika's prolonged stay in South Africa, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, power cuts and economic difficulties. The 86-year-old Mutharika left Malawi on 6 October, for what officials described as a private visit. This is his fifth visit this year, with limited information made public on each of these trips. "Malawi is at a critical moment, and there is a need for decisive action," the opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) said. Information Minister Shadric Namalomba has denied that Mutharika's absence had created a leadership vacuum. The professor who beat fraud allegations to become Malawi's president…again Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera. He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020. His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa. On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges. He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs. "The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge." He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency. The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs. Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private." He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration. "That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added. On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe. Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment. Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information. Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well. Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs. Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration. title: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots
description: Paris extends curfew as Marseille and Lyon ban protests after riots 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jamie Whitehead and Gabriela Pomeroy Reuters Large demonstrations descended into disorder in Paris and across France on Saturday Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected. France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said. Jean-Didier Berger, an Interior Ministry official, said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest. France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise. Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court. Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la République, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday. Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Public transport in Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city. The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses. The prefecture for the Rhône region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT). Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east. Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned." He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm. The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned. Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds. Reuters Unrest spread across several French cities last weekend, including the capital Paris Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests . Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction. Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday. A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year. Correction 23 October 2026: In an earlier version of this story, Jean-Didier Berger was incorrectly described as interior minister, rather than an Interior Ministry official. title: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
description: 'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother 15 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Brandon Drenon Getty Images Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable". Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done." In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody. The ad set off a storm of criticism from members of both parties. On Thursday, US President Donald Trump sought to defend it and Ramaswamy on social media. And at a rally in Iowa late on Thursday, Trump advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it". "Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much'," he added. Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election. In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down. "I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening. "You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad. The last time Acton saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted, according to Acton's campaign. Arthur's husband fled the state before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted and died in 2004. Arthur left with him. In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point". Trump, who has endorsed Ramaswamy,  blamed the press for the negative reaction to the ad, in a long post where he also commended Arthur and Ramaswamy. Trump blasted DeWine, as well. He urged Ramaswamy to keep up his attacks and "let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats and steals!" "I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar and much worse," Trump also posted. In the ad, Arthur repeatedly says Acton lies and asserts she "needs help", but does not discuss anything related to cheating or stealing. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it. Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state. The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet the Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling". On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor. "And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well." MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election. Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad US Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party. David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads were not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense". He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour. A poll by VoteHub released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad. If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades. GUIDE: What are the US midterms? title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
description: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit 9 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December. The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021. Trump cancelled a previous deposition - an interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance". But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", in which the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence. Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition. US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December or face sanctions - the most extreme of which could be the dismissal of the lawsuit - unless the discovery period is extended. In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. Depositions carry legal weight - they are recorded verbatim by a court reporter and the transcripts can later be used as evidence in trials. They typically take place in a lawyer's office without a judge physically present. In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions. Last week, lawyers asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place. On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year and claimed the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action". Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021. The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action". The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US. In July, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters. Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary". title: Gasps as Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
description: Gasps as Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show 13 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Emer Moreau PA Media The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize. During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize. As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa, to cheers and gasps from the audience. They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet". The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films. William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely. There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m. The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November. Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro. The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability. At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible". The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday. title: Watch: 'It's part of the culture' - New York bans horse-drawn carriages after more than 160 years

title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
description: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? 24 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Liv McMahon , Technology reporter and Osmond Chia , Business reporter How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". Cyber-security issue hitting sites worldwide prompts 'millions' of hacking attempts What is PHP? Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server. Developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, PHP still powers lots of platforms today, including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites. When you visit a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read. It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation , composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity". What is the vulnerability? A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet. Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected. Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found". Wiz wrote in a blog post about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites. What websites have been affected? The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. EPA Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on Wednesday A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. What happened after the flaws were exposed? The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said. Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms. The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP. Bloomberg via Getty Images Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X. "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said. Tech companies have also sought to quickly secure their systems. E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue, but its websites were operating as normal. Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, also said it had seen "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced. title: How to make Google put preferred sources up top when you search
description: How to make Google put preferred sources up top when you search 28 January 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google BBC Staff BBC (Credit: BBC) A new feature lets you choose which publishers – including the BBC – appear at the top of your search results. Here's how to use it. Whether seeking the day's headlines or a healthy recipe, turning to Google search inevitably yields almost too much information – and with the recent rollout of AI summaries, trusted sources can sometimes seem lost down the page. With their new Preferred Sources tool, Google has put some control back in users' hands. You can now personalise your Google settings to select the BBC and any other publication or news source you'd most want to see when you visit Google websites and apps. These are your Preferred Sources. Find out more, below. What is 'Preferred Sources'? Preferred Sources are websites you select in your Google settings that Google will prioritise when showing news and content. When you add a site as a Preferred Source, Google is more likely to show you articles, videos and other updates from that site. (Credit: BBC) Where will my Preferred Sources appear? Preferred Sources may appear in the Google Top Stories results on Google search. The most likely place you'll see your Preferred Sources will be in the "from your sources" section nested within Top Stories results, both in the desktop and mobile versions of Google search. What are the benefits of personalising my Preferred Sources? When you personalise your Preferred Sources settings, you're making Google work smarter for you. Choosing the BBC as a Preferred Source means that you see news from your trusted source more frequently. How do I add the BBC as a Google Preferred Source? The fastest way to add the BBC as a Preferred Source is to use this direct link and tick the box next to BBC.com. (If you're not logged in or you don't have a Google account, the link will first ask you to sign in or create an account before bringing you to the selection screen.) (Credit: BBC) You can also set your Preferred Sources while searching: After you search for something on Google, you'll see "Top Stories" next to a starred card icon. Click that icon to add BBC.com as a Preferred Source, then reload the search to see new BBC results. This preference will now be applied to all future Google searches. -- For timely, trusted tech news from global correspondents to your inbox, sign up to the Tech Decoded newsletter , while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. title: Gianni Infantino: Asian football chief gives Fifa president re-election lift
description: Infantino re-election hopes boosted by Asia support after u-turn Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (left) had previously criticised Gianni Infantino over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme By Dan Roan Sports editor Published 4 hours ago Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president have been given a major boost by an endorsement from the head of the Asian Football Confederation. President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa told the confederation's Congress in Tokyo - which was attended by Infantino - that "we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you as you seek a new mandate as president". Sheikh Salman's backing represents a significant u-turn just two months after he signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf criticising Infantino over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. At the time the three confederations accused him of breaking trust "through deception" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, and "a profound failure of judgement...these are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership." But in what appears to be a blow to the rebellion against Infantino, Sheikh Salman told the meeting in Japan it was time "to move forward". "I've spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear," he added. "Yes, we had some issues, we spoke about them in the past, but let's not relate the two things together... "As one Asian family, we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni." Alongside Infantino's power base in Africa and South America, Sheikh Salman's endorsement could be crucial in ensuring the Fifa president secures a fourth and final term. At the election in Rabat in March, Uefa will have 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10. Uefa gives Infantino two-week deadline to release key documents Published 3 days ago Could Wenger really take on Infantino and run for Fifa presidency? Published 15 October The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed. Potential rivals such as Victor Montagliani, the president of Concacaf, and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders. "You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my dear Salman," Infantino said in an address to the confederation's delegates. "You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years." Asked later about Sheikh Salman's comments, Infantino said: "I feel great about the AFC's support." At a meeting of Fifa's Council last week, Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan , but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. He also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (Â£2.6bn). Uefa has since told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by 2 November. Related topics Football

title: The great Ballon d'Or campaign - a race for football's biggest individual prize
description: Pride, prestige, profile - the great Ballon d'Or campaign Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ousmane Dembele won the Ballon d"Or in 2025 and is one of 10 PSG players listed for it this year By Alex Bysouth BBC Sport senior journalist Published 4 hours ago An emotional Ousmane Dembele had barely settled back into his chair at Paris' historic Theatre du Chatelet last September, gold-dipped orb in hand, when campaigns for this year's men's Ballon d'Or prize began to whirr into action. Entourages roused their candidates, media revelled in the hype. Who deserved the award in 2026? A World Cup year, no less, in which the narrative occasionally became not just which players could lead their country to glory, but how doing so would help them secure football's biggest individual accolade. "The Ballon d'Or has been discussed every single day," said European football expert Guillem Balague on BBC Sport's Euro Leagues podcast. "Quite clearly it follows the pattern of society, where it puts a lot of emphasis on the individual - it's harder to understand why a collective works, it becomes very easy to understand why one dribbles or doesn't dribble." Clamour for the spotlight only increased as the red-carpet ceremony neared. "You can't underestimate the PR machine that some clubs and some players are going to use," added French football journalist Julien Laurens. Managers and sporting directors talked up their charges, and questioned why others on their squad did not make the 30-man shortlist. Deco branded it a "huge scandal" that Barcelona pair Raphinha and Pedri missed out, but backed Lamine Yamal as overwhelming favourite to win it. Not, he says, because he is also a Barca player, but "because I like football". Star names have appeared frequently in the media. Lamine Yamal himself insisted he will not "beg for anything" - after last year saying he dreamed of "winning many" - but suggested the prize should not merely go to the top goalscorer. Paris St-Germain manager Luis Enrique confessed he is "bored of the Ballon dâOr" - although with a record 10 PSG players on the shortlist, perhaps he wishes to keep out of the debate. Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia talked each other up to BBC Sport . "We can cut it in two," joked Dembele. "Honestly, he deserves it, the season he had was exceptional." Kvaratskhelia responded: "Of course it's him!" A 'Kvara d'Or' campaign in Georgia celebrated the country's favourite fleet-footed son. "I think for the big nations it's really difficult to understand what [winning] would mean for the small country," the winger explained. Kylian Mbappe, who Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho compared to the original Ronaldo, was less subtle than most in his pitch to win the award for the first time. "I always think I'm the best but everyone has their own opinion," professed the Frenchman, now the all-time World Cup top goalscorer. "Of course, this year could be good for me to win the Ballon d'Or - but journalists vote." Indeed - since a short spell of national team captains and managers also voting ended in 2015 - the 30-player shortlist drawn up by the publications France Football and L'Equipe has been voted on by one journalist from each of the top 100 Fifa-ranked nations . The deadline has passed. The winner has already been chosen. Messi, Ronaldo and social media To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, What does it mean to win the Ballon d'Or? James Kirkham, a sports brand strategist who has worked with top clubs and players, including Harry Kane, says the build-up has had an election feel. "You're going out, canvassing, getting your vote and making sure you shore up certain blocks from certain countries, and why wouldn't you?" adds Kirkham. The lobbying is not for everyone. Max Eberl, Bayern Munich's board member for sport, championed Kane and Michael Olise but said the best players , external "are the ones who don't need to run a campaign". Mbappe's compatriot, Jean-Pierre Papin, winner of the award in 1991, meanwhile told French TV: , external "I like Kylian a lot, he's a record-breaker. However, there comes a point when it's all about me, me, me and me." Mbappe did make an interesting observation, alluding to the dominance of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo - the pair won a combined 13 in a 15-year period between 2008 and 2023. "My idea of the Ballon d'Or comes from the Messi and Ronaldo era - you don't give it to ordinary players, you give it âto players who are different," explained Mbappe. AC Milan's Kaka was the last recipient before Messi and Ronaldo's tug-of-war began, the Brazilian pipping the young pair to the prize in 2007. That was a year after fledgling social media platforms Facebook and Twitter launched to the public. Nokia dominated mobile phone markets, people took digital cameras on nights out. The world had changed immeasurably by the time Messi won for an eighth time in 2023. "Today everything moves at the speed of light," explains former AC Milan chief executive and sporting director Ariedo Braida, who witnessed the club land seven awards, from Ruud Gullit to Marco van Basten's treble, George Weah, Andriy Shevchenko and Kaka. "Fans follow individuals - the players - rather than the club themselves. It's a widespread phenomenon, which we see, for example, in politics too. "Once upon a time, you'd be a Milan fan and go to watch Milan. Today, everything is live and with the Champions League you always get to see all the great stars straight away. "I must say this makes me feel a bit nostalgic, because the event is always immediate. Anticipation creates that sense of longing which has now disappeared." Are fans now more invested in star names than clubs? title: Are Man Utd the unmanageable club?
description: Have Man Utd become the unmanageable club? Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Manchester United are without a win in seven games in all competitions By Phil McNulty Chief football writer Published 4 hours ago The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip. Carrick recreated a familiar scene - the same one acted out by predecessor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after a 4-1 loss at Watford in November 2021 cost him his job - by raising his hands in apology to supporters who had just seen United humiliated by the same scoreline at Como in the Champions League. Carrick is the seventh full-time manager since Ferguson stepped down in 2013 after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge. Since then there have been days of success under Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Erik ten Hag, and moments of hope, but the final outcome is always the same - dismissal. Carrick will need something miraculous to change that storyline, with results poor and revolt within the dressing room as defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the tactics in Como. It hints at something rotten in the state of United. So should it really be crestfallen managers standing in front of those disappointed supporters? Can it really be United's managers every time? Should not even more scrutiny now be aimed at those who appointed them, then decided the direction of the club? Have United effectively, through years of decay, decline and appalling decision-making, become the unmanageable club? There have been those seven full-time managers - David Moyes, Van Gaal, Mourinho, Solskjaer, Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick. There have also been spells as interims for others such as Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher. United's leaders, from former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward to the ruling Glazer family and now part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, have effectively tried every trick in the book to recreate the Ferguson era. And failed miserably. Moyes, an ill-starred appointment led by Ferguson, found the job too big for him after leaving Everton . Van Gaal and Mourinho were tried and trusted operators with stellar track records of success at Europe's superpowers. Solskjaer was effectively the anti-Mourinho without any sort of managerial track record that suggested he would succeed at United, but appointed after a successful spell in temporary charge. Ten Hag got the job on the back of leading a superb young Ajax side to the Champions League semi-final. Amorim was regarded as European coaching's hottest young property when he was lured from Sporting in Lisbon. All ended up sacked. All eventually found the unwieldy beast that is United impossible to tame. Van Gaal won the FA Cup in 2016. Mourinho won the League Cup and the Europa League in 2017. Ten Hag won the FA Cup in 2024 with a landmark win against Manchester City . Slim pickings compared to previous glories. United, however, have not become a bad or dysfunctional club overnight. They have been heading towards this point ever since the succession plan to Ferguson - not easy, admittedly - was botched so badly. Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp all felt able to resist the lure of Old Trafford, leading to what should have been red faces all round in December 2019, when they were all managing within 35 miles of each other in the north-west but none were at United. Ancelotti was at Everton , Guardiola was at Manchester City . Klopp was at Liverpool . United had Solskjaer, an over-sentimental choice made on the back of a feelgood interim spell. He lasted less than three years. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer adopts a similar pose to Carrick after his final game in charge in 2021 With every passing day, Carrick looks like Solskjaer Mark II. Carrick is a former fan favourite who did well in temporary charge, but whose previous managerial career was a sacking at Championship club Middlesbrough. Solskjaer shared that same unwanted distinction, sacked by Cardiff City in September 2014 after only nine months in charge as they struggled in the Championship. It has all brought United to the point where the question must be asked. Since Ferguson's departure, has it ever been worse than it is now? In recent times, has there ever been less hope than there is now? Has morale ever been lower than it is now? United will always find a manager should they require one, but their current parlous circumstances mean they are no longer the attraction they once were. They will not have the pick of the globe's finest. They will need to persuade someone that there is a future at Old Trafford that contains something other than future dismissal, a sobering state of affairs for the self-styled "biggest club in the world". Given the current state of United's squad, there is no guarantee a manager with a high-class track record would have a quick fix, or any fix at all, without huge investment. Carrick is front of house and, on current evidence, will pay the price for United's failings. He is a repeat of the Solskjaer mistake, an easy choice made after taking them back into the Champions League, a comfort blanket with supporters that has now been torn away by poor results. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Manchester United part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in heated discussion with director of football Jason Wilcox - with CEO Omar Berrada in between - at Wolves in December 2025 There are significant culprits elsewhere, led by Ratcliffe. United fans have held regular protests against the Glazers since they took control in 2005, their leveraged purchase loading debt on to the club. They have remained majority owners, despite the level of angered aimed towards them from supporters, unmoved by years...

title: NBA: LeBron James enjoys dream home debut in 76ers comeback win over Cleveland Cavaliers
description: Boos to cheers - James records biggest career comeback win Image source, Getty Images Image caption, LeBron James previously enjoyed two spells with the Cleveland Cavaliers By Elizabeth Botcherby BBC Sport journalist Published 3 hours ago LeBron James says his home debut was "everything that I dreamed of and more" after the Philadelphia 76ers turned boos into cheers by overhauling a 29-point deficit to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106. It is the largest comeback win of James' 24-season NBA career and also the largest comeback by the 76ers in the play-by-play era, which began in 1996-97. Booed from the court after trailing 69-45 at half-time, Philadelphia took the lead for the first time with just under seven minutes remaining in the fourth quarter, with a spell of 15 unanswered points putting them 104-95 ahead. Although the Cavaliers, one of James' three previous franchises, pulled it back to 106-102, the 76ers held firm having emphatically outscored their visitors 69-37 in the second half. James contributed 17 points, 10 rebounds, five assists and three steals while fellow home debutant Jaylen Brown scored 17 of his 21 points in the second half, including 10 in the fourth quarter. Tyrese Maxey top-scored for the Sixers with 32 points, with Joel Emiid adding 24. "We got the boos. That was amazing and we deserved it. And then we got the cheers and almost blew the roof off this thing, in a good way. It was a hell of a night," said James, who joined the 76ers on a two-year contract. The result caps off a thrilling start for James at his fourth franchise, after the Sixers defeated the New York Knicks 106-100 on the opening night of the season to spoil the defending champions' homecoming. However, he also had to respond to criticism from President Donald Trump, who labelled the 41-year-old a "total disgrace" for not standing still during the national anthem before Tuesday's win over the Knicks. "It must be a slow news day at the office," James said on Thursday night. Sixers coach Nick Nurse said his side are used to tuning out such distractions, adding: "I think that goes right in with other outside noise we've already had. "I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor. The focus that they've had and the intent has been outstanding." title: Dream night for Bournemouth - how did the Premier League come to dominate Europe?
description: Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bournemouth have beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now AC Milan in the Europa League By Alex Brotherton ,Â BBC Sport journalist Â and Â Andy Cryer ,Â BBC Sport senior journalist Published 22 October 2026 At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation. That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture. Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final. Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008 , not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts. "It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports. "So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special." To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two). While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point. In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A. The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years. For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare? Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance? Bournemouth sweep aside 10-man Milan in Europa League Premier League sides make strong start English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once. In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them. In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them. Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21. The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams. But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years. So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory? Money talks Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List. It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League. Premier League clubs earn more than Â£1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined. Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30. Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'. Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final. In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively. In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League. All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates. The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of Â£3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues. Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight. You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings. Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent. "With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August. "A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer." While Barcelona, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich all lost to English teams in last season's elongated Champions League league stage, it has been a very different story when it really mattered. title: World Treadmill Championship: Where amateurs compete against the elite
description: The World Treadmill Championship - pitching elite runners against amateurs To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Figure caption, Treadmill World Championship - what are they and how to compete? By Sarah Dawkins BBC Sport senior journalist Published 4 hours ago For decades, treadmill running has been viewed as little more than a training tool for outdoor runners. But that could be about to change, with the launch of the World Treadmill Championship. In this new World Athletics-sanctioned competition, runners around the world log 5km on a treadmill and compete for a prize pool of $100,000 and the title of world champion. Known as Run X, it pitches everyday runners against elite athletes. BBC Sport was invited along to a qualification event at a gym in Southampton to observe runners logging their times on the global virtual leaderboard. Image source, Run X Image caption, The finals for the first ever Treadmill World Championship will take place in Italy in March Among them is British marathon runner Charlotte Purdue. "I think it's good to get people into running. 5km is obviously not too far so people can have a shot at it, there's no pressure," she tells BBC Sport. Purdue, who holds the third fastest British female marathon time, believes the treadmill has been long misunderstood. "I personally love the treadmill and I've always used it in my training. We've got one at home and I find it easy at home and I really enjoy it." But does she think she's got what it takes to be the first ever treadmill world champion? "It's definitely added motivation," she adds. "But I wish it was a marathon on the treadmill, I think I'd have a better chance!" Image source, BBC Sport Image caption, Elite marathon runner Charlotte Purdue logged her 5km time at 18 minutes 15 seconds Runners have until 24 January to complete 5km, for free, at an official Run X centre. They can make multiple attempts, but only their best time will count. There is no official 5km treadmill world record recognised by World Athletics. The men's 5,000m track record is 12 minutes, 35.36 seconds, while the women's is 13:58.06 The men's road record for the distance stands at  12:49, with the women's at 13:54. The top 25% of runners in age categories from 18 to 75+ will represent their nation at the regionals, before the 10 best men and women in each category advance to the world finals in Italy next March. The $100,000 prize pool is split between the men's and women's overall podiums, across seven age-group categories. The exact distribution has not been published. There are currently 20 countries taking part and the list of elite runners registered has not yet been disclosed. Organisers hope to entice more participants with wildcard entries to events like the 2027 World Road Running Championships in China. Despite the treadmill sometimes being referred to anecdotally as the 'dreadmill' due to the repetitive and monotonous nature of indoor running, World Athletics president Lord Coe told BBC Sport it's a "great opportunity" to introduce a new audience to running. "It's across a whole range of age groups. It's very important that we continue to innovate and it's really important that when we innovate, we use technology that attracts more young people into our sport," he says. The ambition for treadmill running doesn't stop there, with hopes the discipline can also be included in Esport competitions in the next five years. "We know there are a lot of long-distance challenges but nothing at that 5km mark which is more accessible and that's the real big starting point," Luke Townsend, education manager at Technogym UK, the co-organisers of the competition, tells BBC Sport. Alongside professionals like Purdue on the treadmills in Southampton were members of the 'She Strides' run club. They usually opt to run together outdoors but wanted to take part in Run X to highlight how important treadmill running is from a safety point of view. "Unfortunately, so many women in the winter have to change their routines of running outside because they don't feel safe," says Hollie Thackway, founder of She Strides. With the clocks going back this weekend, many runners will soon be spending more of their training time in the dark. Thackway added: "By being able to run inside on a treadmill, it means you don't have to stop your training, you can still be on a programme, achieve your goals and not stop running altogether through the winter, so I think this event is great to highlight that."
