title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
description: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis 18 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Orla Guerin Senior International Correspondent, Aden Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war rages From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival. They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces. When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets. What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden. Lee Durant/BBC The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden "It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused." As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse." By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs. Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured. Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk. The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet. Lee Durant/BBC More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed. The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer. Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz. The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices. The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes. Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away. Lee Durant/BBC Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018. "I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself." Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred. "I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]." Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space. Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing." Lee Durant/BBC Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut. There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment. That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor. "It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says. "We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them." A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line. Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year. Lee Durant/BBC Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon. "Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again." They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics. "Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital." She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them. Lee Durant/BBC Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
description: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found 18 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Tom Gerken and Liv McMahon , Technology reporters How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP. Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades. Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution. There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent. Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out. "The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords. She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied". The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected. A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue". "But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added. Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented". "It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One. But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers. He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected had been received and was being acted on. Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date. "Hacking has been around for many years," he said. "The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point." Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online. He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long. "MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said. He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers. What is PHP? PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor. It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit. When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read. It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today. PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz , which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it. The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP. Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems. Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added. Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal. 'Serious vulnerability' Getty Images Cyber researchers at Calif and Wiz unearthed the php2shell flaw, theorised by the PHP Foundation in 2024, in part using OpenAI tools While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday. The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday. But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required. In France, telecommunications company Orange also said it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes. According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally. "The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC...

title: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
description: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning 1 hour ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Gary O’Donoghue Chief North America correspondent, in the Rio Grande Valley BBC Father Roy Snipes is known locally as the Cowboy Priest - he resisted plans to seize chapel land to build Trump's border wall It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel. The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself. As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest. "I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname. In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys. During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). "There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers. Getty Images Donald Trump campaigning in Texas earlier this month - the close Senate race is being hotly contested Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project. "They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing. "But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight." After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said. "The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added. Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy. This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year. Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered. Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate. Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem. "I remember I put out a video… thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all." But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added. Mario Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November Recent polls suggest much of Trump's support among Hispanic voters has ebbed away since 2024. Surveys taken since late summer indicate a majority of Texan Hispanic voters disapprove of the president. They also suggest Hispanic voters are favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin. "When I voted for President Trump, I voted for him because we saw an influx of immigration during the Biden administration," said Mario Guerrero, a young Mexican-American businessman who leads the South Texas Builders Association. It needed to be fixed, he said. "We thought that we were in the right by voting for Trump, and that he was going to do what was best in order to fix the crisis on the border. "And I think to myself, we were really not told the extreme that they were willing to go to make a point," he added, before referencing recent shootings involving ICE agents in US cities. Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues. A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration. Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown. "There's a man that I know that… last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work." Even though...

title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
description: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Yolande Knell Middle East correspondent, Nazareth BBC Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's election At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power. Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. "I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future." All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority. If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists. A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values. Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority. Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis "After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza." Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending. There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis. Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank. How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders? The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government". To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders. Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab parties At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party. I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties. "In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel." Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings. These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas. United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence" While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc. title: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
description: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Reuters Young Serbians have been the driving force behind the movement, but none of the candidates are students Final campaign rallies have taken place across Serbia, ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future. After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power. The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote. Why is this student movement so important? They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia. The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable." It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people. The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project. AFP via Getty Images The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024 What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges. The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums. At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties. Anger lingers in Serbia after train station tragedy Who is Vučić and how popular is he? Pierre Crom/Getty Images Vučić has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017 . The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities. Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification". Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power. "He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade. Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections How do Serbia's elections work? Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation. Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday. There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for. Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote. Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List. Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for? Reuters Ilija Srdanović (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists. They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić. Under an 11-point programme , the student movement wants to: eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media. How fair will the vote be? European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere". Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
description: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow 12 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Liza Fokht Senior reporter, BBC News Russian BBC/Getty Images Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre Lévy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 to 2025, tells the BBC. US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War. But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year. The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion. They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials. Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed. Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia. "There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty." The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls. AFP via Getty Images Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023 Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater. "Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow. Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission. The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution". Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials. One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy. Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect They fled Russia, but the West sent them back Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police. One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear. Not everyone can deal with the pressure. One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months. 'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats' In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre Lévy. He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be. The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible. And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies. Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country. But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning. Reuters Pierre Lévy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024 After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Еven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers. One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'." Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses. A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase. "It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour." title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skincare sales
description: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skincare sales 12 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Rachel Clun Business reporter Getty Images The use of weight loss drugs, known as GLP-1s, has increased in popularity in recent years Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skincare sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side-effects of rapid weight loss. The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us". He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular". L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations. The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite. While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side-effect of loose skin - including around the face. Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side-effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss. L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December. Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters. Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler. Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance. Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs. title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
description: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out 21 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Brandon Drenon Getty Images Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid. "With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MS Now . In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation. The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation". The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya. More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized. Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS Now, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out." Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed. "We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre". The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way". Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one. She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s. The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS. Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating. Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies". Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling" . Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia. He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me". At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster." The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it". "You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported." title: US actor Tom Skerritt, star of Top Gun, Steel Magnolias and Alien, dies aged 93
description: US actor Tom Skerritt, star of Top Gun, Steel Magnolias and Alien, dies aged 93 14 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Nardine Saad REUTERS/Fred Prouser/File Photo Skerritt served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says. Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said, adding: "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives." In a six-decade career, he appeared in the film Mash, A River Runs Through It and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers. His family said he will be remembered "for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose and create change". The moustachioed star of several 20th Century hit films was born in 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles. He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford ​in War Hunt and years later reunited with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt. Skerritt's breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman. Getty Images Actor Tom Skerritt in a scene from the movie 'Alien' in 1979 The hit film, which was released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards and was adapted for television two years later. He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects. "It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with 'Alien'," Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to news agency Reuters. "Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other." Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that "the woman becomes a hero", referring to Weaver's character, Ripley. During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads. He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field's husband in 1989's Steel Magnolias. Getty Images Skerritt starred with Julia Roberts in the film Steel Magnolias As Cdr Mike "Viper" Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise. On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley's drama Picket Fences. The quirky procedural's ensemble cast was nominated for Sag Awards in 1995 and 1996 and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995. Lauren Holly, who played Skerritt's deputy on Picket Fences, described him in a tribute as "our leader". "His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much," Holly wrote. "He cared deeply for his family - both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter." Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09. Getty Images Skerritt was seen with fellow actors Joan Collins, Morgan Freeman and Jessica Tandy and at the 47th Golden Globe Awards in January 1990 He had a six-episode stint on Cheers playing Rebecca Howe's crush-worthy boss Evan Drake. Skerritt's family said that he left behind a "legacy that reaches far beyond the screen". A deep believer in the power of storytelling, Skerritt helped found the TheFilmSchool in Seattle and co-founded the Red Badge Project, which helps veterans work through PTSD, anxiety and depression by writing and sharing their experiences. Inspired in part by his experience filming A River Runs Through It, he also believed in protecting the natural world. He created the documentary series Reflections of the River about America's rivers and supported river conservation. Skerrit is survived by his third wife Julie, five children and several grandchildren. United States

title: Prominent Virginia senator charged over allegations she ran criminal cannabis scheme
description: Prominent Virginia senator charged over allegations she ran criminal cannabis scheme 14 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Kayla Epstein The Washington Post via Getty Images L Louise Lucas has served in the Virginia State Senate since 1992 Federal prosecutors arrested a prominent Virginia lawmaker on Thursday over allegations she oversaw a criminal cannabis enterprise. Democratic state Senator L Louise Lucas and six other people, including her family members, have been charged in relation to a sweeping racketeering case that allegedly involves fraud, drug violations and bribery. Lucas, 82, claimed the prosecution was politically motivated in a statement on X. "I will not be intimidated," she wrote. "I will not be bullied. And I will not back down." While she has not entered a formal plea, Lucas' attorney, Anthony Capozzolo, told the BBC she would plead not guilty. Capozollo said they were "surprised and disheartened" to learn of the indictment and that Lucas "denies these charges in their entirety." Lucas and her alleged co-conspirators are charged with obtaining and illegally distributing large amounts of illegal cannabis. The government has also accused her of using her political influence to benefit herself and her family. Lucas was herself charged with five counts, including racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute cannabis, conspiracy to launder money, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and maintaining drug-involved premises. Other alleged participants were charged with a firearm charge and wire fraud. Lucas is not running for re-election. But her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, who is also charged in the indictment, is running for the city council of Portsmouth, Virginia. "I grew up under Jim Crow," Lucas wrote on X in response to the charges, referencing an era of legal segregation in the US. "I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them. I spent my entire life fighting back, and I'm not stopping now." US Attorney General Todd Blanche accused Lucas of overseeing a criminal "enterprise", arranging for the "acquisition and distribution of marijuana", and using her power as a lawmaker to influence legislation that would benefit her and her family. Lucas has served in the Virginia State Senate since 1992 and assumed the powerful role of Senate president pro tempore in 2000. She has publicly spoken about her cannabis dispensary and her support for legalised usage, as well as her opposition to US President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers. "I'm a 78 year grandma who legalised pot and now has her own cannabis store. And I'm the last thing standing between The GOP and total control of Virginia. That's worth an RT!" she wrote on X in 2022. While small amounts of cannabis are legal in Virginia for personal or medical use, major restrictions remain in place regarding its sale and consumption. Lucas has backed legislation to legalise recreational cannabis. She is an owner of The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth, Virginia, which opened in 2021 after the state decriminalised simple cannabis possession and legalised personal possession of certain small amounts of cannabis, according to WAVY News. The Virginia Mercury reported in 2022 that products sold in her shop may have contained substances and dosages that conflicted with state law at the time. The FBI raided Lucas' office and a cannabis business in May as part of a long-running inquiry, the Washington Post reported at the time. It is unusual for the justice department to announce major actions involving lawmakers, candidates or other electorally sensitive matters in the weeks before an election. Early voting is already under way in the US midterm elections, which are held on 3 November. However, the justice department has announced a series of inquiries against lawmakers and election officials in recent days, including conducting a raid on the home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar as the government investigates her immigration status. Referring to Lucas' case, Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, wrote on X: "The timing of this indictment undermines the US Department of Justice's previously longstanding policy of not taking legal actions - to include indictments or significant investigative steps - close to an election. "And sadly, this timing further erodes the trust the American people deserve to have in the Department of Justice." Virginia Cannabis Legality of cannabis Drug legalisation

title: New York bans horse-drawn carriages after 160 years over safety and abuse concerns
description: New York bans horse-drawn carriages after 160 years over safety and abuse concerns 14 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Madeline Halpert Central Park, New York City BBC Drivers of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park are concerned for their future - while animal activists see the ban as a victory After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked. She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horses, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried. "What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old, referring to Starlight. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?" Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity. On Thursday, New York City Council voted to pass a ban on the carriages, beginning in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry. Several drivers told the BBC that they did not want new jobs and disputed claims their horses were mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban. Horse-drawn carriages in New York City expected to be outlawed "There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing." Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions. New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers. But the ban movement found new momentum this summer. In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park. Mahajan's family was at the city council hearing when lawmakers voted to pass the bill. Council Speaker Julie Menin said the measure would ensure the 18-year-old was "the last soul that we lose to this industry". 'Horses are working animals' Several Central Park horse carriage drivers told the BBC that they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk. Lawson, who was nearby when Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic", but said that if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years. The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision. Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation. "They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals." Lawson says she feels very attached to her horse - Starlight - and to her business as a carriage driver Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke. "I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way." Fidan said he was angry and that officials were passing a ban without talking to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked. The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment. The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling and financial compensation for those in the business. A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (£44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing. But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the law does not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out". The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year. The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work. Carriage owners would be allowed to keep their horses if they choose, said Menin. 'Confining for the horses' Chris Koenigs thinks the horses are "wonderful", but too much of a risk for public safety Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' wellbeing were raised in the city for decades. The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. title: Florida officer accused of stealing dead man's identity and moving into his home
description: Florida officer accused of stealing dead man's identity and moving into his home 14 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Rebecka Pieder Broward County Sheriff's Office Florida police officer Brian Louis Sguros is accused of living the dead man's house for nearly four years, police say. A police officer in Florida has been accused of stealing the identity of a man he found dead during a welfare check call and then moving into his home, authorities say. Brian Louis Sguros, 35, a police officer in Lauderhill, was arrested this week by the Broward County Sheriff's Office. Investigators allege he impersonated the deceased man, Dennis West, moved into the house he found West dead in and then renovated the two-storey south Florida home. Police say he lived there for years undetected. Sguros has not commented on the charges. It's unclear whether he has legal representation yet. He has been placed on administrative leave from the Lauderhill Police Department. In 2022, police were called to check on a 71-year-old resident. Sguros was called in as back-up for the welfare check. When he found West dead of natural causes, he allegedly "created a complex scheme to take control of the individual's home", the Broward County Sheriff's Office said in a news release. Investigators say Sguros told the medical examiner's office he was West's friend, though authorities found no indication the two knew each other, it said. Court documents detail that the officer appeared in body cam footage during the welfare check and did not appear to have a prior relationship with the man. He also allegedly told the county medical examiner that West had no living relatives, which authorities say say was also untrue. Sguros then had West's body cremated, according to the BBC's news partner CBS. Sguros took possession of the home in August 2022 and moved in, according to a joint investigation by the sheriff's office and the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office. Authorities say that in 2025, he allegedly filed paperwork with the property appraiser's office stating that his possession dated to August 2022. Sguros said he took possession of the home because it was hazardous and he wanted to prevent people from squatting, according to court documents. He paid utility accounts that were in the deceased man's name. He also applied for a permit to replace exterior doors and windows, at the cost of $8,000 (£5,970), according to court documents. Sguros claimed he has increased the property's value, spending more than $214,000 on the home, according to the sheriff's office. Sguros faces charges of official misconduct, criminal use of a deceased person's identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. He was released from jail on a $25,000 bond. Local law enforcement were made aware of the situation when West's heirs tried to sell the property, according a police affidavit. Once Sguros eventually returned the keys to the property's rightful owners, he allegedly demanded reimbursement for improvements he had made to the property, court documents state. The Lauderhill Police Department told BBC News that Sguros had been relieved of his duty and was placed on administrative leave with pay. title: Children in care to get £10 a week savings
description: Children in care to get £10 a week savings 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jake Wallace Guernsey Getty Images The States of Guernsey said about 40 people in care will be eligible for the scheme. A new government savings scheme will set aside £10 a week for children in care for them to access when they turn 18. Established by the States' Children and Family Community Services and Guernsey Community Savings, it is designed to give young people a financial foundation when becoming an adult. The States said the scheme will apply to children from entry into the care system and 40 will benefit immediately. Associate director of children services Lucy Cook said the savings accounts would  support young people by "helping them to access opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach." The States of Guernsey said the transition to independent living for people in care can bring "significant financial pressures, from setting up a home to managing everyday living costs". "Having savings of their own can offer greater choice, security and confidence as they take this important step," it said. 'Supported and encouraged' The States will pay a one-off fee to allpay, a payment services company, to establish the scheme. The charity Guernsey Community Savings will then open and manage the accounts, and work with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday. At 18 years old, they will have the choice of opening an account with Guernsey Community Savings or transferring their savings to an account of their choice. Cook said children in care deserve the opportunity to "look ahead with confidence and hope for their future". "This initiative is about giving our care-experienced young people a stronger foundation and recognising our commitment to them as corporate parents. "We want every child in care to know that they are valued, supported and encouraged to achieve their full potential." More news stories for Guernsey Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Chief executive of Guernsey Community Savings Joe Brown said children from care are "particularly vulnerable to financial exclusion when they reach adulthood". "Giving them the opportunity to build up savings, and the financial security that comes with this, can make a real difference as they take their first steps towards independence." title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
description: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Dearbail Jordan , Business reporter and Kali Hays , Technology reporter Getty Images Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires. The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November. The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes. He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure. California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group. The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% each year. Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe. Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board. It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed. In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal. Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday , Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings. Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value. The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California. 'Critically important' Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence." The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii. After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring. Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers. Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools. With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company. Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres . Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year. It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in. And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work. The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday. Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company. title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
description: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Zoe Kleinman Technology and AI editor How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built. We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction. In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building. The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet. There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025. But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution. Less than two months ago , 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI. It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant. The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit. One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult. However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI. The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix. 'A real dilemma' It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked. From that point the clock started ticking. As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site. "There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University. "How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers? "Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out." But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made. We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either. As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success. Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story. "We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4. "We have enormous capability to handle these risks." But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in. Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first. For many it may be a significant repair job, so if there's a web developer in your life you may want to send them thoughts, prayers and maybe a strong coffee. title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
description: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Helen Sullivan and Rachel Flynn Getty Images The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites. Governments and some of the world's biggest companies are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws. The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them. A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement. Amazon said its threat intelligence system identified it was targeted on Saturday. It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted. The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability." PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites. As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like." "They can steal data , they can go to other parts of your network. All sort of things like that - even plant a backdoor to get in later on, so it's pretty serious," Woodward told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Why have websites around the world been taken down? BBC explains Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language. He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI". Austin described PHP as "one of the first web languages that powered the early internet". "It's in a lot of places that you wouldn't expect to be that are basically very core to how the internet runs in a lot of ways. It's like all the old things that are in a house that you know keeps it [running] but you don't really think about," the PHP researcher said. But Austin said this incident is not necessarily bad news because organisations would now "run and patch PHP immediately" if they haven't already. Listen to BBC Radio 4 Today programme on BBC Sounds Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October. In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said. The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said. While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday. In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said. The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning. The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added. The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days". She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said. The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade. Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure. The websites for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors are currently inaccessible. They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it had followed guidance to take its website offline, "in view of the critical security issues affecting PHP". Edinburgh and Oxford council websites also went offline on Wednesday, but are now accessible. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble? The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website. This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed. The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database". It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update.
