title: Malcolm Arnold 'should be better known' - Lloyd Webber
description: Malcolm Arnold 'should be better known' - Lloyd Webber 5 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Pete Cooper and Roberto Perrone , Northamptonshire BBC Malcolm Arnold wrote more than 100 film scores during his lifetime The renowned cellist Julian Lloyd Webber says the Northampton composer Malcolm Arnold should be "much better known than he is". Lloyd Webber will launch the 21st Malcolm Arnold Festival in the Oscar-winning composer's hometown on Saturday. Sir Malcolm, who died in Norwich in 2006 aged 84 , won an Academy Award for his score of the 1957 film The Bridge on the River Kwai, which tells a story of British prisoners of war captured by the Japanese during World War Two. Lloyd Webber, who worked with Arnold, said: "He was a character, and an extraordinary man." The festival first took place in 2006 to celebrate Sir Malcolm's 85th birthday, but he died two weeks before it began. This year there will be a world premiere performance of the composer's unfinished Violin Concerto, orchestrated from his detailed sketches. Lloyd Webber's wife, Jiaxin Cheng Lloyd Webber, herself an acclaimed cellist, will perform the work written by Sir Malcolm for her husband, which he will introduce. Getty Images Jiaxin Cheng Lloyd Webber (right) will perform works written for her husband Julian Lloyd Webber Julian Lloyd Webber, the brother of Lord Andrew Lloyd Webber, retired in 2014 due to a neck injury, which left him unable to play. He said: "Arnold was a really wonderful composer, he should be much better known than he is. "He wasn't the easiest person to work with but he wrote wonderful music." Lloyd Webber said Sir Malcolm "had his problems with the music establishment" because his melodic style was not well received at the time. But he described him as a "genius" at film music, having written 132 scores including Whistle Down the Wind and Hobson's Choice, and said he was a "prolific" composer. "Everyone wanted him, there was a time when all the virtuosos of the time wanted him to write something for their instrument," he said. He said the festival was "keeping Malcolm's name alive and it's introducing people to his beautiful music and they'll be a lot richer for hearing it". Malcolm Arnold's music was not well reviewed at the time but was appreciated later in his life Festival organiser Paul Harris said Malcolm Arnold "wrote music for people to play to other people". He told Bernie Keith on BBC Radio Northampton that he always believed the festival would be well supported in Sir Malcolm's hometown. Harris said: "There is something about Malcolm, his life, the fact he was a Northampton man, his family were in shoes, there is something very personal about [the festival]. "The music, it speaks to people, and people like to be communicated with, it's what draws us in and he knew how to do it." Do you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below. title: Slade star Dave Hill's debut album honours city
description: Slade star Dave Hill's debut album honours city 5 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Oprah Flash , West Midlands and Ed James , BBC Radio WM Anthony Keates Dave Hill, the lead guitarist for Slade, has named his album after a lane near his childhood home Slade star Dave Hill is set to release his debut solo album, paying homage to some of his old haunts in Wolverhampton. Named Dirty Foot Lane, the 10-track album was named after a road near his childhood home and not far from where he lives today. He collaborated with Noddy Holder's son, Django Holder, on the project, his first since the break-up of the band behind hits such as Merry Xmas Everybody. "It's got a lot of depth to it, every one of those tracks is a true story about someone close or someone I've lost," he told BBC Radio WM. Anthony Keates Hill teamed up with Noddy Holder's son Django who produced the album The album blends rock, blues and folk, capturing the energy of Hill's live-performance roots alongside his personal journey, including struggles with mental health and the impact of the Covid-19 lockdowns. "When I started to write, I knew when something was good - it would almost make me cry," the 80-year-old added. He continued: "I was talking to Noddy Holder, [who is] probably one of my best friends in life, and he encouraged me to write my own music. "Wolverhampton was where I lived. [I remember] the council estate and the cinema and growing up in the days when Doris Day was in the charts. I loved her. I used to watch Flash Gordon at the cinema." Hill also teamed up with American country music star John Berry for the album. He also told BBC Radio WM that he has plans to release two further albums in the future. title: What books had people turning pages and turning up the volume this year?
description: What books had people turning pages and turning up the volume this year? 6 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Emma Lennox BBC News NI Getty Images Books with "short chapters" and include "catchy, racy" themes seem to be most popular Thrillers, self-help books and Harry Potter were among the favourites for readers in Northern Ireland this year, according to Libraries NI. For those who prefered to listen to their fiction, Freida McFadden had eight of her titles featuring in the top 10 adult fiction audiobooks borrowed. Jillian McFrederick from Libraries NI said books with "short chapters" and "catchy, racy" themes seemed to be most popular. But when it came to younger readers, there was little change with Harry Potter continuing to be popular - almost 30 years after the release of the first book. This week marks Book Week - a joint initiative between BBC NI and Libraries NI and celebrates books, reading and libraries and everything that they make possible. The data provided by Libraries NI covers a 12-month period from 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026. Jillian McFrederick from Libraries NI said books with "short chapters" seem to be most popular So, which audio books have been the most popular? Audiobooks led the way this year with more downloads than physical book loans. The Housemaid by McFadden was the most listened to, with only Romantasy favourite Fourth Wing by Rebecca Yarros and The Pumpkin Spiced Café by Laurie Gilmore breaking McFadden's hold on the chart. The figures come from Libraries NI as part of Book Week NI 2026 When it came to non-fiction, those listening seem focused on personal development. A best-selling title by Mark Manson, The Subtle Art of not Giving a ... (Google the rest if you wish), topped the non-fiction section, while Atomic Habits and 101 Essays That Will Change the Way You Think followed closely behind. Meanwhile, for younger listeners, the Harry Potter series remained the standout success with all seven books from the series making it into the top 10. Other favourites included classic titles such as Matilda by Roald Dahl, and Diary of a Wimpy Kid by Jeff Kinney. There is still a strong demand for physicals Getty Images Freida McFadden has released 36 books since her first publication in 2013 The Housemaid also topped the charts when it came to physical loans, with the title being borrowed more than 3,000 times. McFrederick said the release of the movie adaptation, starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfield in 2025, had brought a whole new audience to McFadden's work. Niall Williams' historical fiction book based in 1960s Ireland, Time of the Child, came close to beating McFadden with only 15 loans behind. When it came to non-fiction, global best-seller, The Let Them Theory by Mel Robbins came first, slightly ahead of Nobody's Girl by Virginia Roberts Giuffre. The wider top five reflected variety from self improvement to baking, including Mary Berry's very best recipes. Variety continued for junior readers. A Belfast Fairytale led the fiction category with nearly 3,000 loans and the Guinness World Records 2026 took the lead in non-fiction. Finally for eBooks Ebooks showed library users were split between very different reading habits over the last year. In fiction, readers gravitated towards page turners from authors like Virginia Evans with The Correspondent claiming top spot. Richard Osman showed a true favourite with three of the top 10 being written by him. Andy Weir's Project Hail Mary also proved popular following a movie adaption earlier this year. For non-fiction, self-help was a clear winner. Again, Mel Robbin's The Let Them Theory came first, with more than 2,000 loans. McFrederick said the book "struck a chord with people because they're all so stressed and so anxious". Getty Images Mel Robbin's The Let Them Theory had more than 2,000 ebook loans Other popular self-help books were also in the top five including The Psychology of Money and The Courage to be Disliked . Among younger readers, the magic around the Harry Potter series continued with more than 1,500 loans in fiction. Junior non-fiction interests ranged from The Wimpy Kid Movie Diary, Historical Royal Palaces: Ghost in the Walls and 101 Amazing Harry Potter Facts among the most borrowed eBooks. title: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize
description: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize 8 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ian Youngs Culture reporter Alamy Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature. Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship. The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature". Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying. The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m). Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement. "She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said. "She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice." Getty Images Anne Carson pictured in 1998 Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson lives in Michigan and has also held Icelandic citizenship since 2022. Anders Olsson, chairman of the Swedish Academy's Nobel committee for Literature, praised the way Carson has "broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature". "This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms," he said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Carson's win was "an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada". The writer's works feature "wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own," Carney wrote on social media. "She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature." 'Outstanding importance' Carson's notable works include The Glass Essay, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, Nox, Float and The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos. In 2019, her performance piece Norma Jeane Baker of Troy drew a line between famous beauties from different historical periouds - Helen of Troy and Marilyn Monroe. In 2021, she released The Trojan Women: A Comic, a graphic retelling of Euripides' ancient story; and her translation of Elektra by Sophocles was staged starring Brie Larson in London last year. She has been a professor of classics for more than 30 years and her writing is often inspired by Greek literature. Her translations have often given a contemporary twist to ancient works. "Her collaborations with visual artists and choreographers and with opera and theatre directors demonstrate the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems," Olsson said. "It is this that lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene." title: 'The scandal of the century': The English duchess charged with treason and witchcraft
description: 'The scandal of the century': The English duchess charged with treason and witchcraft 55 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Deborah Nicholls-Lee Alamy Eleanor Cobham, Duchess of Gloucester, seemed destined to become queen of England. Then she was convicted of necromancy, heresy and witchcraft, a scandal that led to the Wars of the Roses. Was she a scheming satanist or a political pawn? A new novel tells her story. In 1441, Eleanor Cobham was the wife of Humphrey of Lancaster, Duke of Gloucester, the heir presumptive of the weak and childless King Henry VI. The prospect of becoming queen was tantalisingly close. But as Humphrey's influence at court waned, allegations surfaced that Eleanor had turned to the dark arts in order to shore up his succession. These led to a conviction of treasonable witchcraft that became the scandal of the century and created space for rival claims to the throne. Now, Philippa Gregory's fictional re-telling of Eleanor Cobham's story, Royal Witch, is putting a spotlight on a woman who is remembered for her ambition and beauty but who became a divisive figure. Some believe the evidence against England's first and only convicted royal witch was falsified and that she was a pawn in a political game, but Gregory depicts a more ruthless figure who was the author of her own destiny. "She succumbed to the temptation to use witchcraft to kill the king and to get herself, via her husband, on the throne of England," says the author. "She's one of the very, very unusual women accused of witchcraft who actually did practise witchcraft." For some, this former lady-in-waiting who poached the husband of her mistress, Jacqueline, Countess of Hainault, while still in her service, was a suspicious figure from the start – an unscrupulous interloper whose ostentatious lifestyle caused additional resentment. She needed to be put in her place. Eleanor and Humphrey's interest in the supernatural was visible from the couple's extensive library. But rumours reached the King's Council that Eleanor, eager to become queen, had conspired to prophesise the king's death − with, among others, the wise woman Margery Jourdemayne, known as the "Witch of Eye", and the esteemed scholar and astrologer Roger Bolingbroke. A case for treason was formed. Trumped-up charges? Led by Humphrey's half-uncle and arch-rival, Cardinal Henry Beaufort, 18 charges of necromancy (summoning dead spirits to gain hidden knowledge), heresy, and witchcraft were levelled against Eleanor. These included procuring magical potions, commissioning an astrological chart to predict the king's death and creating a wax figure of the king to cause him fatal harm. Perhaps to fend off the allegations of treason and to suggest that the magic was purely domestic, Eleanor admitted to procuring love and fertility potions from Margery Jourdemayne. I think the allegations are a smear campaign – Eleanor is very much a weak spot for her husband – Dr Euan Roger For many historians, these were trumped-up charges that were politically motivated. As Gemma Hollman notes in her book Royal Witches: From Joan of Navarre to Elizabeth Woodville (2019), astrological prediction to inform important decisions "was no unusual activity, even among royalty". She continues: "If she did try love potions to produce a child, she can hardly have been too different from many other women in her predicament at the time." Alamy A 1431 illuminated manuscript depicting Eleanor, Duchess of Gloucester and her husband Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester (Credit: Alamy) Some commentators feel Eleanor deserves our pity. "I think there's something quite sad about this," Dr Euan Roger, a historian of late medieval and Tudor England, and the principal records specialist at the National Archives, tells the BBC. "I think what is actually going on here, the reason she actually admits guilt to some of the charges brought against her on the witchcraft front, is that she's been trying to conceive a child and resorting to perceived witchcraft in order to do that." The charge of using a love potion gave the royal council the perfect pretext to dissolve her marriage to the heir to the throne, while the accusations of treason made her husband a persona non grata . "I think they [the allegations] are a smear campaign," says Roger. "Eleanor is very much a weak spot for her husband. She's known to have these occult interests and the members of the council see this as a means of targeting her husband." The evidence against her, he argues, is unreliable. "Most of it comes from Bolingbroke's confession, which is almost certainly made public to implicate Eleanor… [and] he's almost certainly being tortured behind the scenes." The case against her By contrast, in the novel Royal Witch, Eleanor is not just the instigator but at the heart of the action, scratching the king's likeness into the wax effigy and laying it among clippings of his dark curly hair. Written in the first person, the book depicts her using magic "not just to get a baby… but to get a king, to save the country, to save the royal family… to make myself great." For Gregory, the case against Eleanor is compelling. "There's a lot of evidence of stuff going on which would be regarded at the time as witchcraft and probably satanism," she tells the BBC. She notes that Roger Bolingbroke "never withdrew his confession" and believes it's telling that the accused did not protest their innocence "more energetically". I don't think anybody would have moved against her without really, really convincing evidence – Philippa Gregory She also stresses that Eleanor's is no ordinary witch trial. "She's at the peak of her success. She's a royal duchess. She's very much in the king's favour and she's in line to inherit the throne. She's in a position of extraordinary power and influence and I don't think anybody would have moved against her without really, really convincing evidence." Gregory gives Eleanor great agency in her novel. "This is a tremendously ambitious woman who really makes her own life," she explains. Eleanor...

title: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline
description: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline 2 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Becca Warner BBC/Serenity Strull (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) Birdwatching can help slow brain ageing and is increasingly being used as therapy for dementia patients. Every week, a group of elderly birders spend hours hunkering down inside a wooden hide in the English countryside, peering through binoculars as they excitedly share what they spot. An oystercatcher's long, bright beak probing the pebbled ground; two great crested grebes bobbing in the water, their plumed heads poised. Most of these birdwatchers have difficulty recalling what happened earlier that day, and might struggle to follow a conversation. But they become animated when swapping notes on the birds that fill the sky around Forge Mill Lake in the UK's West Midlands. Among them is 78-year-old Harold*. He loved the outdoors when he was younger, but more recently dementia has made him withdrawn and anxious. His daughter Lucy* brought him here, hoping that the change of scenery and peaceful lake might be good for him. After an apprehensive start, Harold began smiling when someone pointed out a robin and enjoyed watching the ducks splashing in the water. Blue tits darted between the nearby trees, and Lucy saw Harold laugh for the first time in a long time. "For that moment in time he was present in the moment, he wasn't worried about his memory or his confidence. That is very powerful, in a gentle way," says Jenny Budinger, a community dementia advisor at Age UK, the non-profit that runs the birdwatching group. Birdwatching is increasingly recognised as a valuable way for elderly people and dementia patients to spend their time, with groups set up in nursing homes in the UK, Germany and the US. Paying attention to birds , even through the window, can help older people feel more connected to others, experience more positive emotions and boost memory skills. Now new research shows that birdwatching can reshape the brain, much like learning an athletic sport or a musical instrument – and may even help slow the brain's ageing. Better-organised brains Meanwhile, in the laboratory, neuroscientists are investigating how birdwatching impacts the brain. They tested keen birdwatchers' identification skills to determine who was an expert and who was a novice, then looked at their brains. The scientists found that the very structure of experts' brains was different – and that birdwatching expertise might slow age-related decline by keeping the brain more organised. Erik Wing, who led this research at Baycrest Academy for Research and Education in Toronto, Canada, compared MRI brain scans from bird experts to those of novices while they identified birds. He found that expert brains were wired differently in regions important for functions like attention, visual perception and visual recognition. Among expert birders, these regions showed more activity – particularly when they were asked to identify birds they weren't already familiar with. The findings don't prove whether structural brain differences are the cause or effect of birdwatching expertise. But, Wing says, one explanation is that the areas of the brain used for birdwatching might undergo "neuroplasticity" – the ability to change shape and function over time. BBC/Serenity Strull Birdwatching can reshape the brain and may help slow ageing (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) Wing also analysed how organised the birdwatchers' brains were. Organisation in the brain tends to reduce with age, and lower measures of organisation are associated with reduced cognition . In experts' brains, some regions had higher levels of organisation and coherence than novices of the same age. Some of these regions were also the ones that showed more activity during bird identification. This indicates a "kind of preservation of organisation" in the brains of experts as they age, Wing says. More research is needed to understand the nature of this preservation and how it links to wider cognitive function. But for now, the results may indicate that "acquiring this skill earlier in life might produce benefits that continue through to older adults", Wing says. This is good news for the many Gen Z (16 to 29-year-old) birdwatchers who are getting their binoculars out long before old age sets in. Bird therapy Wing's research looked at birdwatching expertise, but other findings suggest that there may be psychological benefits to birdwatching even for those without special knowledge or skills. In fact, when it comes to experiencing psychological restoration – feelings of calm, freedom and rejuvenation – enthusiasm may be more relevant than expertise . A study of 388 birdwatchers in Poland found that those who say they are more interested in birding than other activities and consider it an important part of their lives are more likely to experience psychological restoration than birdwatchers who are highly skilled but less enthusiastic. Simply choosing to be interested in birds, then, could have its own benefits. Elisabeth Kals, a professor of social and organisational psychology at the Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt in Germany, is interested in how our relationship with nature shapes our life experiences and wellbeing. She studied what happened when people living in nursing homes had the chance to watch the local bird life. Her team installed bird feeding stations outside 65 homes, positioned so that residents could watch the birds from the comfort of the indoor common area, and assessed the residents' cognition, mobility and wellbeing through self-reports and inputs from staff and family. They saw improvements after just a few weeks, and after a month birdwatching explained residents' wellbeing better than their age and care level. "The findings were clearly positive," Kals says. Those who took part in birdwatching became more cognitively agile, she adds – meaning they were more able to follow a conversation and interact with family who visited, remember and recognise birds that had visited before, and show alertness. Nursing home staff were the first to see the difference the birds made. "For weeks, they haven't seen a smile on [a resident's] face, and then they see the smile," Kals says. Some of...

title: The animals you can't outrun - and the ones you can
description: The animals you can't outrun - and the ones you can 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Richard Fisher Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) Ever wondered if you could beat a bear or a horse in a race? What about a rat or a rhino? The answers may surprise you. A few years ago, I was camping in the US, and a black bear happened to pass nearby. As I watched it nose around the camp, I wondered: if I needed to, could I outrun it? Looking up bear speeds afterwards, the answer was clear: absolutely not. Apart from the fact that running away can trigger a chase response, so is not advised , black bears can reach up to 48km/h (30mph). Ever since then though – especially while out for a jog in London – I've found myself asking: what animals could I beat in a foot race? What if I encountered a particularly mean squirrel or badger? Only Noah could have staged a real animal Olympics, but scientists have measured the top running speeds of hundreds of creatures – squirrels and badgers, but also spiders, lizards, rodents, birds, large mammals, and many more. It turns out there are quite a few surprises in the data. So, which land animal would be your own closest competitor? And what would give the world's fastest humans a good race? Muscle mass Over the decades, scientists have measured animals' top speed using differing methods: some more accurate (and ethical) than others. In the 1920s, one naturalist drove his car alongside pronghorn antelopes – North America's fastest land animal – firing gunshots in the air to keep them going. And in the 1980s, researchers realised they could place smaller animals like rats on treadmills . Getty Images A horse trained for endurance should be able to beat most humans in a race (Credit: Getty Images) Nowadays, though, technology like GPS trackers make the task easier, especially for recording animals in their natural habitat at real-world speeds. One recent study that tracked cheetahs in the wild showed they can reach 93km/h (58mph). Previous measurements were based on film recordings, or in one case, artificially inducing the cheetah to chase a hunk of meat held by a stopwatch operator riding in a 4x4. What's your running 'spirit animal'? Many runners might be unsure about their precise top speed, but will know their personal best (PB) over 5km (3.1 miles). That's the distance of a parkrun, a free running event with over 12 million registered participants worldwide. So, if you run a 40-minute 5k, you're matching the top speed of a woodland vole . If your PB is 30 minutes, a rat or a hamster . A time of 25 minutes: that'd be a house mouse or a marine iguana . And 20 minutes? A striped skunk or a groundhog . As for former Olympian Andy Baddeley, who once held the fastest parkrun time – 13 minutes and 48 seconds – his spirit animal would be a ​​ long-nosed potoroo , a small, hopping mammal that lives in Australasia. The good news for the competitive runner is that these are the animals' maximum sprint times, which they couldn't hold, so you'd likely beat them by the finish line. Sometimes, though, simple methods have also worked fine. In another recent study, researchers measured what might be the world's fastest spider (Australia's brown huntsman) by simply nudging it and then video-recording it next to a ruler. While its average pace was around 7km/h (4.3mph), its top speed in bursts was a discomfiting 13km/h (8mph). Over time, researchers have compiled these disparate scientific measurements into larger databases . One of them is biologist Myriam Hirt, now at the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research in Leipzig, who compiled the running speeds of around 350 land animals . In 2017, she and her colleagues were investigating the question of how animal body mass affects their speed . In principle, bigger animals with more muscle mass should be able to run the fastest. "It makes sense when you first think about it, but the data clearly shows that it doesn't work that way," Hirt says. "The largest species are not the fastest. No one knew why." She and her colleagues concluded that the largest animals are constrained from reaching their hypothetical top speeds by the body mass they carry. "You need more time to get a big body moving at the same speed as a small one," she explains, in the same way that big planes need longer runways. (Or as anyone who has ever played Mario Kart will know: tiny Toad accelerates faster than bulky Donkey Kong.) This slow take-off means that big animals begin to fatigue before they reach their top potential speed. "You only have a limited amount of energy available for acceleration. At some point you just collapse, because there's no energy left in your muscles," Hirt says. The slow acceleration of big animals does also mean you might be capable of beating some of them in a race, especially over short distances. For example, an African bush elephant can reach a top speed of 35km/h (21.7mph), but they are slower than humans out of the blocks. As a thin and lanky runner, I'd hoped that a giraffe might be my own closest animal competitor Another animal speed database compiled in 2020, which integrated statistics on animal acceleration , suggests the African bush elephant would reach its top speed in about 7.5 seconds. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests it would therefore run the 100m (328ft) in around 14 seconds. I doubt I could match that time myself, but according to running website Marathon Handbook , it'd be beatable for some well-trained adults. Olympic sprinter Usain Bolt could probably outrun the bush elephant easily – but even he would be overtaken by many other animals. title: 'A masterclass in betrayal': The British double agent who defected to Russia and taught enemy spies
description: 'A masterclass in betrayal': The British double agent who defected to Russia and taught enemy spies 27 July 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Fiona Macdonald Getty Images On 30 July 1963, Kim Philby's defection from MI6 to the Soviet Union was made public. In 2016, the BBC broadcast previously unseen footage of his lecture to Stasi operatives in which he revealed the secrets behind his treachery. "Almost all my life I have spent trying to avoid publicity of any kind," says Kim Philby in a 1981 video unearthed by the BBC from the archives of East Germany's spy service. It's something of an understatement. Philby was a British double agent whose defection to the Soviet Union was made public on 30 July 1963. In the video, he is seen giving a seminar to Stasi operatives on how to succeed at espionage. As the BBC's former security correspondent Gordon Corera explained in his 2016 report on the previously unseen footage, "Philby offers a masterclass in betrayal, from his recruitment by Soviet spies after Cambridge to his joining Britain's secret service MI6, whose secrets he stole." It is the only known video in which the leading member of the so-called Cambridge Five KGB spy ring discusses his betrayal – a rare recording that is revealing on many levels. WATCH: 'My advice to you is to tell all your agents that they are never to confess' "I'm looking back on my career in the enemy camp, this 30-year career in the enemy camp," he says in the grainy video, standing behind a lectern in thick-rimmed glasses and a suit and tie. "Every evening, I left the office with a big briefcase full of reports which I had written myself, full of files taken out of the actual archives. I used to hand them to my contact in the evening. Next morning I'd get the file back, the contents having been photographed, and take them back early in the morning and put the files back in their place. That I did regularly, year in, year out." As part of a circle that also featured Donald Maclean, Guy Burgess , Anthony Blunt and John Cairncross, Philby passed British state secrets to the Kremlin during World War Two and the Cold War, including the period when Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union were allies. Yet there has sometimes been a rose-tinted view of their double-crossing, according to Antonia Senior, the author of Stalin's Apostles: The Cambridge Five and the Making of the Soviet Empire. He had a callous disregard for the men he sent to their deaths – Antonia Senior "The stage and screen portrayals of them, in particular, present them as glamorous rogues," Senior tells the BBC. "In reality they were lying, unpleasant traitors who betrayed the people who loved them as well as their country… This was not a victimless crime. Their betrayals helped Stalin to enslave half of Europe, and the Cambridge Five were enthusiastic in advancing that imperialist project under the guise of world revolution." Philby admits in his Stasi speech that he betrayed a joint CIA-MI6 operation in Albania, which led to hundreds of men being killed. And he described the Albanian agents he betrayed as "just down from the trees" in a 1968 autobiography that was labelled "unrepentant and self-regarding" by the New York Times . He had a "callous disregard for the men he sent to their deaths", says Senior. The Magnificent Five After being recruited as a Soviet spy at Cambridge University in the early 1930s, Philby joined MI6 in 1940, later becoming the agency's head of counter-Soviet intelligence. That position enabled him to feed critical British and American secrets directly to the KGB while sabotaging Western anti-communist operations. His rise through the ranks of British intelligence services was helped by his background and a phenomenon that Senior labels the "chapocracy" – a tight-knit network of privileged men within the establishment who shared the same elite educational backgrounds. According to Senior, this meant that security clearance was granted based on a shared social class and personal charm rather than on merit or rigorous vetting. "The chapocracy brought Philby into the employ of British intelligence at the start of World War Two, when the huge demand for clever chaps to join the Security Services meant that people like him were waved through," she says. In History In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter. By exploiting class biases and institutional blind spots, Philby and the other members of the Cambridge Five were able to gain access "to the deepest secrets of the British and American states during the 17 years they were spying for Stalin", says Senior. "Atomic research. Full UK Cabinet minutes. The secrets of Bletchley Park [the UK's WW2 codebreaking centre]. The private correspondence of Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt. The list is long and utterly flabbergasting – it is no wonder that Soviet intelligence dubbed them internally as the 'Magnificent Five'." After Burgess and MacLean defected to the Soviet Union in 1951, Philby was relieved of his intelligence duties before being dismissed from MI6 in 1955. Yet despite that, he was still able to escape to Moscow in 1963. One possible reason was given in Philby's final piece of advice to the East German spies. "They interrogated me in order to break my nerve and force me to confess. And all I had to do, really, was to keep my nerve. My advice to you is to tell all your agents that they're never to confess. Just deny everything." title: 'Blind alleys are always opportunities': The scientist who developed the polio vaccine
description: 'Blind alleys are always opportunities': The scientist who developed the polio vaccine 6 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Greg McKevitt Alamy On 12 April 1955, Dr Jonas Salk announced that his vaccine was safe and effective. It would go on to save countless lives – but he refused to profit from it. In 1982, Salk talked to the BBC about his breakthrough. "Humanity received some of the brightest news in all its history." That is how one US reporter described the announcement, in April 1955, that Dr Jonas Salk had succeeded in developing a polio vaccine. Polio was a disease which, until then, had no prevention and no cure – and everyone was threatened by it. Interviewed on television that evening, Salk was asked who owned the patent on the vaccine. "Well, the people, I would say," he replied . "There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" Poliomyelitis , or polio, was a public health emergency. In 1952, the US saw a record 57,628 cases of the disease, which causes spinal and respiratory paralysis. Patients would lay confined in large metal ventilators known as iron lungs to help them breathe, which, along with the leg braces worn by children, became polio's enduring symbols. People would fear the approach of summer, the time when outbreaks were more common. WATCH: 'It all happened rather quickly from my point of view'. Every parent knew and dreaded the disease's symptoms, according to Jody Zogran, a ward nurse who worked at the Pittsburgh hospital where Salk and his team developed their vaccine. She told the BBC's Witness History of cases where "a little boy [was] playing football the day before, and here he is encased in this iron lung. He has no idea what's going on and he's screaming, and if his legs aren't paralysed, he's kicking the side of the respirator." Although fewer than 1% of infections led to paralysis, the sheer scale of polio outbreaks meant that large numbers of children still ended up in iron lungs . They might remain encased from the neck down for days, months or even years. The patients Zogran cared for were still contagious, and she and her fellow nurses were told that the only protection available to them was rigorous handwashing. "We washed our hands every time we touched that patient or more, and I can remember going home at night and my hands were so sore and so chapped," she said. While it was primarily children who were affected by polio, no one was safe. Future US president Franklin D Roosevelt, then a rising political star, contracted the virus in 1921 at the age of 39. It left him paralysed from the waist down for the rest of his life. In office, he made combatting polio his own personal crusade, and in 1938, he founded the March of Dimes, a polio charity that would turn the traditional model of fundraising on its head. Rather than seeking big donations from the few, it asked for tiny ones from the very many, and raised hundreds of millions of dollars. Many things appeared that had not been foreseen, and opportunities had to be seized – Jonas Salk By the late 1940s, scientists had shown that polio entered the bloodstream through the gut. At the same time, two researchers emerged to compete in the race for a vaccine, each taking a sharply different path. Dr Albert Sabin , a paediatrics professor at Cincinnati Medical School, had already spent two decades studying the polio virus, and believed in moving slowly and carefully, according to David M Oshinsky , author of Polio: An American Story. "He saw himself as a scientist's scientist… who worked in the lab, never left, and made discoveries one by one, using building blocks," he told a 2014 BBC documentary. Salk, meanwhile, was a fast-moving researcher at the medical school in Pittsburgh, who had already produced a successful flu vaccine for troops during World War Two. Crucially, he had the support of the March of Dimes, which was impatient for progress. Dr Paul Offit of the Vaccine Education Centre in Philadelphia told the BBC how Salk worked with the speed and focus of a pharmaceutical company, a style that challenged traditional ideas of how scientists behaved. He said: "Salk and Sabin had fundamental differences about what would be the best vaccine. Salk thought it would be a virus that would be completely killed. Sabin thought it would be a virus that would be weakened." Testing the vaccine on his family The March of Dimes funding gave Salk a clear advantage. It enabled him to establish his laboratory at the heart of a working hospital in Pittsburgh, surrounded by polio patients. Salk and his team were using a deactivated polio virus to make the vaccine. It was experimental science, with nurses sending down patients' excrement to the basement from the third floor where they worked so that the laboratory could isolate the virus. But Salk and his team still had to prove that the vaccine would stimulate the antibodies needed to fight the polio virus. The development of the polio vaccine, he told the BBC in 1982, came from patient, repeated effort. "There were indications that it should be possible to immunise against poliomyelitis," he explained. "And then [one had] to choose one of the numerous possible alternative pathways. In the course of the work, many things appeared that had not been foreseen, and opportunities had to be seized, so in that sense there were some leaps along the way." Were there blind alleys? "Blind alleys to me are always opportunities," Salk replied. "I've always taken something unforeseen as a cue, and looked quickly to see what the alternative pathways are." title: 'I locked myself in a toilet until we were afloat': The woman who stowed away on a ship to report on D-Day
description: 'I locked myself in a toilet until we were afloat': The woman who stowed away on a ship to report on D-Day 10 June 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Fiona Macdonald Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) American journalist and author Martha Gellhorn tricked officers so that she could write firsthand dispatches from Normandy in June 1944. In 1991, she told the BBC about her daring subterfuge. "Everyone was violently busy on that crowded, dangerous shore," writes Martha Gellhorn in a dispatch from the D-Day landings in June 1944. "We walked with the utmost care between the narrowly placed white tape lines that marked the mine-cleared path… The dust that rose in the grey night light seemed like the fog of war itself." And then, she recalls something that makes the bleakest of moments a little more human. "We got off on to the grass, and it was perhaps the most surprising of all the day's surprises to smell the sweet smell of summer grass, a smell of cattle and peace and the sun that had warmed the Earth some other time, when summer was real." It's an unexpectedly tender insight into the World War Two Allied landings on the Normandy beaches, revealing a quality of observation that marked out Gellhorn's writing. Her gift was to convey both the brutality and humanity of war in vivid accounts that focused more on everyday detail than troop movements or battle logistics. WATCH: 'I just locked myself in a toilet until such time as we were afloat' During a career that spanned 60 years, the Missouri-born journalist and fiction writer covered conflicts including the Spanish Civil War, the Vietnam War, the invasions of Czechoslovakia and Finland, and the liberation of Dachau concentration camp. She also wrote for Vogue magazine and reported on the Great Depression for the US government, travelling through the Dust Bowl with the photographer Dorothea Lange. Gellhorn's firsthand D-Day account came after a daring feat that reveals her strength of character. "I had sneaked on to a hospital ship," she told the BBC in 1991 at the age of 82, during a rare TV interview. "Somebody probably onshore asked me what I was doing, and I said, 'I'm just going on this ship to interview the nurses – a woman's feature.' She didn't allow others to let gender define her and her work – Lyse Doucet "You could always get by with that. It always sounded harmless and idiotic, and it worked a treat. 'I'm just doing the woman's angle,' and nobody's interested anymore. And then I just locked myself in a toilet until such time as we were afloat." That strength of character also meant Gellhorn had an extraordinary personal life. She befriended the Roosevelts and stayed with them at the White House, cadged bed and breakfast from HG Wells, and married Ernest Hemingway – resolutely refusing to live under his shadow. In competition with Hemingway And throughout, she chronicled what happened in the darkest of times, in her own words becoming "a walking tape recorder with eyes" – noticing details that others might have missed in the heat of the moment, and powerfully describing how war affects ordinary lives. Gellhorn had been married to Hemingway for three years when she decided to travel to Europe in September of 1943. During their time living at Lookout Farm in Cuba, while he unsuccessfully hunted for German submarines using his fishing boat, she became increasingly restless. Getty Images Martha Gellhorn and her husband, Ernest Hemingway, both wrote about the D-Day landings (Credit: Getty Images) Hemingway had been the reason she began reporting on war – according to Gellhorn , "I went to Spain in March 1937 and became a war correspondent by accident." Her biographer Caroline Moorhead told the BBC that Gellhorn had travelled to Spain to be with him. "When she got there, Hemingway said, 'Why aren't you writing about the war?' And she said, 'Well, I don't know about weapons and battles.' So he said, 'Write about what you do know, which is people.'" She had funded her trip to Spain in 1937 with payment for a Vogue article entitled Beauty Problems of the Middle-Aged Woman, which involved testing out a harsh chemical peel. Her next published article was called Only the Shells Whine, describing the reality of civilian life under siege in Madrid. She had found her vocation, telling a friend that she would "stick to misery which is my province… and the hell with the flesh". In History In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter. Yet once they were married, in 1940, Hemingway wanted her to remain at home. She accompanied the US Fifth Army to the front in Monte Cassino, Italy in 1943, prompting him to cable her with the petulant question: "Are you a war correspondent or a wife in my bed?" And by the time she returned to Cuba in 1944, the spouses were in competition with each other. Gellhorn had hoped to cover the D-Day invasion for the weekly magazine Collier's, but Hemingway stole the assignment, and while he flew to London, she ended up spending two weeks travelling to Europe aboard a Norwegian freighter filled with explosives. Although the US military refused permission for female journalists to cover the Allied landings, Gellhorn wasn't deterred. "To me, all the people in the rear who make rules, they exist to be thwarted," she told the BBC in 1991. Her defiance meant she was on the first hospital ship to reach Normandy, arriving at Omaha Beach early on the morning of 7 June, and becoming the only woman correspondent on the ground at the D-Day landings. Poetic snapshots and startling details She was arrested by military police once she returned to London for travelling to Normandy without permission, and sent to a nurse's training camp. title: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker
description: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker 24 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Hanna Flint Black Bear Pictures The trailer for this romantic fantasy created an online frenzy thanks to its bizarre premise, about a woman who commissions a basketmaker to weave her the perfect husband. Here's why it has really struck such a chord. Forget about Prince Charming or the rebellious bad boy – there's a new romantic lead women are going wild for, and he is made out of wicker. Back in August, the internet came alive with Gifs, memes and reels reacting to the first trailer of Wicker – a period romantic fantasy with perhaps the year's most bizarre premise. Based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones, it stars Olivia Colman as an ostracised fisherwoman – known only as the Fisherwoman – who commissions Peter Dinklage's basketmaker to weave her the perfect husband. He arrives in the muscular woven form of Alexander Skarsgård, who caters to his new wife's every domestic need and sexual desire, as the village folk watch on with envy. Suddenly, female and gay thirst for Skarsgård's Wicker hunk exploded online. Typical comments on the platform Threads included "Making my husband put a basket on his head to spice things up a bit" and "Insecure men thinking women only want muscles, meanwhile my entire feed is feral for a guy made out of a basket". Then there's been the enthusiastic online reaction to a Wicker promotional popcorn bucket created by Regal Cinemas and suggestively designed from a scan of Alexander Skarsgård's torso, which audiences can print out using a 3D printer at home. What Wicker is actually about The husband-and-wife film-making team behind Wicker, Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, tell the BBC they have been tickled by the responses and understand exactly why so many have fallen in lust with this magical pairing. "They're having sex, the roof is leaking, and he just says, 'I'm going to fix the roof' – then she has a screaming orgasm," Huston Fischer chuckles. "We made him very beautiful," adds Wilson, "but people are noticing that the best thing about the Wicker Husband is that he did something without being asked, and he doesn't require a pat on the back for it." Despite being set in a quasi-medieval fairytale village, the film is tapping into a very current conversation about the imbalance in heterosexual relationships, where women still shoulder much of the household and child-rearing burden. "At the time when we wrote it five years ago, I don't think domestic labour and its mental load was as much in the cultural conversation," says Wilson. She adds that she and Huston Fischer "have a child now so these domestic things you do end up having to negotiate, and now everyone has a lot more language for it". In writing the script, she also wanted to address the "confronting" experiences of women who might be wary of dating and romance. "Entering into the dating pool can invite love into your life, but all of a sudden you're much more examined than you were before," says Wilson. "The Fisherwoman's journey is about what it is to be a woman in this world, struggling with your feelings about yourself and everybody else's feelings about you." The appeal of 'monster'-human romances Wicker sits within the increasingly popular genre of monster-human romances, where relationships between predominantly female humans and male creatures are used to explore societal ills, desires and cultural expectations. From Beauty and the Beast, Shrek and The Shape of Water to Your Monster and Guillermo del Toro's recent take on Frankenstein, they attempt to dissect complicated feelings that people can have about the "monstrous" parts of themselves and the people they desire. Black Bear Pictures Olivia Colman's fisherwoman heroine is as much of a community outsider as her wicker husband (Credit: Black Bear Pictures) "There is a real hunger for seeing imperfect men especially if you're a heterosexual or bisexual [woman], and you're trying to square your attraction to [men] with the fact that they can be very dangerous," Gillian Daniels, author of her own monster-human romance novel Jenny Will Eat You Now, tells the BBC. She refers to the original Beauty and the Beast fairy tale written by Gabrielle-Suzanne Barbot de Villeneuve, which the French novelist wrote after requesting a separation of property from her husband six months after they married. "He was wasting their funds, he was monstrous to live with, so, in many ways, [Beauty and the Beast] became the definitive monster romance after her having this terrible relationship," says Daniels. "There is something there about us trying to square monstrosity, both internal and external, with a healthy hetero relationship or healthy relationships in general." Wicker, however, features a very different type of "monster" – Skarsgård's Wicker husband is the perfect man in many respects, even if because of his unusual provenance, he arouses the suspicions of the rest of the village. "There's also monstrosity in the sense of you're a strange person, you're the weirdo, you're an outsider, but you're mostly innocent – these monstrous narratives are [varied]." In this respect, as a parable of desire and difference, Daniels thinks Wicker might particularly appeal to LGBT and neurodivergent audiences too. How Wicker explores questions of desire In Wicker, the Fisherwoman herself is also a clear outsider, which Daniels appreciates: an autonomous woman who doesn't conform to her community's expectations of beauty, character, and behaviour. "This is not Beauty and the Beast," she notes, where Belle is imprisoned by the Beast before falling in love with him. "[The Fisherwoman] sought out this man to be made for her, she wants a perfect partner, and she hasn't been trapped into this." Indeed, Wilson would never have adapted the short story if the Fisherwoman was presented as a Disney princess character like Belle: "The character is the ugly girl. She has a unibrow,...

title: The simple fitness test that predicts your risk of death
description: The simple fitness test that predicts your risk of death 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jasmin Fox-Skelly Getty Images How quickly your heart rate returns to normal after exercise can reveal a surprising amount about your underlying health. If your heart hammers in your chest when you walk up the stairs, or you need to gasp for air while jogging to catch a bus, it may be a sign that you are not in peak physical shape. Yet what happens after you stop exercising can be just as revealing about the inner workings of your body. Enter the heart rate recovery (HRR) test. This is the difference between your pulse when your heart is pumping hard during exercise, and how fast it beats about a minute after you have finished. Nieca Golderberg, a cardiologist at New York University Grossman School of Medicine, explains that HRR is a good indicator of your cardiovascular health. It can predict high blood pressure and cardiac events . But your HRR is also so much more than that. A poor result can act as an early warning sign, helping to uncover hidden problems with the rest of the body. Crucially, that includes your overall risk of death. Back in 1999, scientists from the Cleveland Clinic, Ohio, published some striking results . They had tested the HRRs of 2,400 adults, then followed them for six years. The team found that people with low heart rate recovery were around four times more likely to die during the study period. Other teams around the world have since found similar results . HRR has emerged as a surprisingly strong predictor of death from any cause, whether there seems to be anything wrong with your heart or not . In young adults and the middle aged, HRR is even more closely linked to your risk of death than high blood pressure. Here's a quick, simple way to calculate your HRR using materials you're already likely to have at home. Finding your rate *It's important to consult your doctor before starting a new exercise regime. If you experience dizziness, chest pain or tightness, or shortness of breath that's out of proportion to the exercise you're doing, stop immediately. This test is not suitable for people with pre-existing heart conditions without medical supervision. The first step is to make sure you have a way of writing down your data and a timer (most phones have one). If you have a smartwatch or other wearable activity tracker, this will be useful. Then you need to calculate your maximum heart rate. If you have a smartwatch or other wearable device, this will be able to tell you what yours is. If not, this is usually around 220 minus your age. Next, it's time to do some exercise. This should be intense enough to raise your heart rate to between 70 and 85% of its maximum . It could include running, cycling, or rowing, depending on your level of fitness. To calculate your HRR, measure your pulse immediately after you stop exercising, when it is still at its highest. The easiest way to do this is with a smart watch or a fitness tracker. Alternatively, you can also hold a finger against your neck and count the beats for 10 seconds. Multiply this number by six for an approximate beats-per-minute. Next, rest for one minute by sitting or lying down and re-check your pulse. Then simply subtract the second number from the first. This is your HRR. An HRR to aim for You want your heart rate to drop back to normal quickly after you finish exercising. The more quickly it drops, the better. A good recovery rate would be one that goes down by at least 18 beats in the first minute. The number can also vary between individuals and depends on factors such as age. However, a HRR of fewer than 12 beats could put you at risk of health problems down the line. Getty Images Your heart rate recovery can reveal how quickly your body returns to a restful state after stress (Credit: Getty Images) An early warning The link between HRR and a person's risk of death is thought to be down to the vagus nerve . This major nerve is a critical link between the brain and the rest of the body, relaying signals to and from the heart, liver, intestines and other organs . It controls whether you are in the more stressful fight-or-flight mode, or the more relaxed rest-and-digest state. "We have these two systems that work on the heart, we've got a brake and we've got an accelerator," says Lindsay Bottoms, professor in exercise and health sciences at the University of Hertfordshire, UK. When you exercise, the accelerator – also known as the sympathetic nervous system – activates, causing the body to enter "fight or flight" mode. Your heart beats faster and your blood vessels dilate, allowing oxygen to be pumped to the muscles. When you stop working out, your body needs to clear out all the metabolic "debris" created during exercise, such as lactic acid and other waste products. This process requires oxygen. "You have to get rid of that out of the muscles, so you still need increased blood flow, and you still need your heart rate to keep high," says Bottoms. When this has been done the body applies the brakes and switches to parasympathetic mode. This is the brake, and it puts the body into the rest-and-digest state. As you get fitter, your body gets better at switching between the accelerator and brakes. This is known as higher vagal tone, and it's known to be highly beneficial. It's linked to better mental health and cognitive functioning , as well as higher immune health and lower inflammation, among other things. That includes a lower risk of death . title: What to eat for younger-looking skin
description: What to eat for younger-looking skin 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Melissa Hogenboom Getty Images One overlooked factor that can help to keep your skin in better shape is what we eat (Credit: Getty Images) Plants, fats, and fermented foods can reduce wrinkles, boost collagen and improve the texture of our skin. Skin is the largest organ in the body and must last us our lifetime. In addition to keeping us looking youthful, well-cared for skin also actively benefits our wider health . But as the barrier between our bodies and the outside world, it takes a battering. Many environmental factors contribute to skin ageing, including air pollution, ozone and a changing climate, says Jean Krutmann, professor of dermatology at the Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine. "For decades we thought ultraviolet radiation was the major driver of environmental-induced skin ageing. We know this is not correct," says Krutmann. " Other wavelengths within natural sunlight can contribute to ageing, for example, visible light and infrared radiation." Even an increase in temperature can contribute to the process, he says. Then there's just time. As we age we gradually lose collagen , the protein that gives our skin its structure, which can result in wrinkles. One overlooked factor that can help to keep your skin in better shape is what we eat. From healthy fats to gut-friendly fermented foods, here's a range to include in your diet. 1. Colourful fruits and vegetables There is abundant research that a diet high in plant-based foods is important for keeping our skin healthy. It helps to aim for colourful fruits and vegetables as they contain powerful antioxidants that help protect the skin from damage caused by pollution and sunlight . Carrots, peppers and tomatoes are rich in carotenoids, including lutein, lycopene, beta-carotene. "They are stored in the fat tissue and protect against UV rays," says Volker Böhm, a professor of food chemistry at the Friedrich Schiller University Jena. While suncream remains important, Böhm says that people tend to apply it during prolonged outdoor exposure rather than every day. Regularly consuming carotenoid-rich foods provides "a continuous baseline UV protection factor of roughly two to three all year round," he says. Adding a small amount of healthy fat like olive oil to tomatoes or carrots helps to make it easier for the body to absorb these antioxidants. Beta-carotene can also be converted into vitamin A , which is important for skin-cell growth and protecting our skin from infection. Carotenoids can help skin cells to produce hyaluronic acid . This molecule helps to maintain skin firmness and elasticity , and is found in many commercially available moisturisers and "anti-ageing" creams. The same pigments may also help to boost collagen. In a small study , women who took a daily carotenoid supplement for ten months showed an improvement in collagen and elastin in their skin, suggesting it could help prevent collagen breakdown. Finally, eating lots of colourful fruit and vegetables has been found to create a healthier looking skin "glow". To gain benefits, we have to eat these foods consistently, says Krutmann. "For whatever antioxidant you are eating, in order to have protection against environmental effects it usually takes eight to 10 weeks before you have a measurable effect." Mangoes have been found to keep our skin looking younger as we age. Take a study of post-menopausal women , led by Vivien Fam at University of California Davis. Participants ate 85g (2.9oz) of mango four times per week over the course of 16 weeks. The researchers found that this reduced the size of existing wrinkles as well as the number of new ones. More research is needed, but the researchers speculated that the beneficial effects could be down to carotenoids, as well as the antioxidants flavonoids and mangiferin. Surprisingly, the study found that eating around 250g (8.8oz) of mango per day increased wrinkles. One of the co-authors of the research, Robert Hackman, a professor of nutrition also at University of California Davis, says it's unclear why this is the case, but it could be due to the high natural sugar content in mangoes. Getty Images Eating antioxidant rich mangos could reduce visible signs of aging, according to research (Credit: Getty Images) "Our proposal is that sugar created some damage to the molecules in the skin," says Hackhan. And while the study was small, follow-up research, which has not yet been published replicated the results, he says. Mangoes and citrus fruits are also rich in vitamin C. This vitamin helps us produce collagen and also acts as an antioxidant, which can protect our skin from sun damage . Studies suggest that vitamin C may help improve skin hydration and reduce pigmentation. For this reason, vitamin C is widely used in skincare products and as a supplement, says Krutmann. 2. Healthy fats I'm not usually a fan of almonds or walnuts but I've started chopping them up and adding them into salads, which I'm enjoying much more than expected. I'm doing so because eating plenty of nuts and seeds could benefit our skin. A small randomised-controlled study found that those who snacked on almonds for 16 weeks had less visible wrinkles compared to those who ate a different snack. Vitamin E, which is abundant in nuts and seeds can also protect the skin from cell damage and ageing. A deficiency of this vitamin can affect skin health , including slower wound healing. Good sources include almonds, hazelnuts, pine nuts and many seed oils. Nuts also contain omega-6 fatty acids , which can strengthen the skin's barrier to keep it more moist. title: The immortal jellyfish can beat ageing. It could inspire treatments for diseases of old age
description: The immortal jellyfish can beat ageing. It could inspire treatments for diseases of old age 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Katarina Zimmer Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) The immortal jellyfish is capable of winding back its lifecycle to become young again. Scientists are unlocking its cellular secrets to find ways human cells could rejuvenate too. The tiny translucent jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii is surprisingly hard to kill. The marine biologist Maria Miglietta of Texas A&M University at Galveston has cut them, boiled them, starved them, overloaded their tanks with salt or plopped them in fresh water – but the nifty creatures seem to cheat death every time. Under duress, they stop in their tracks and fall to the bottom of their tank. Then something astonishing happens: the animals transform into balls of cells that bear no resemblance to the tentacled umbrella shape of adult jellyfish, known as the medusa. Within one to three days, a structure called a polyp – an early jellyfish life stage – buds off from this ball of cells and then grows into a colony, which will eventually sprout new medusae. "From one jellyfish that doesn't die, then you get this colony that can form hundreds more," Miglietta says. And each one of these new jellyfish can, in principle, rejuvenate the same way – exhibiting a seemingly endless capacity to wind back the clock to youth. Miglietta and other scientists are now studying the genetic and molecular processes that make Turritopsis dohrnii's death-defying feat possible. By unlocking these secrets, scientists eventually hope to explore whether they can trigger similar kinds of processes in humans. The goal is not to turn elderly people back into babies, Benjamin Button-style – an idea that's firmly in the realms of science fiction – but to coax cells and tissues into more youthful states to heal wounds and treat age-related maladies. It's comforting to think that nature has found a solution to one of the main problems of humans: ageing and death – Maria Miglietta "The holy grail of this kind of thing, I think, would be regenerative biology: trying to reverse ageing-related degeneration or degradation," says Michael Koldobskiy, a pediatric oncologist and physician-scientist at Johns Hopkins. "We're a long way away from harnessing that for human benefit, but I think understanding these organisms that evolved these processes millions of years ago could potentially really pay off." Alamy A 19th-Century image depicts T. dohrnii, before the extraordinary nature of its lifecycle was discovered (Credit: Alamy) Turritopsis dohrnii's regenerative talents were first reported in 1992 by an Italian scientist who was keeping the animals in the lab and forgot to feed them over a weekend. Expecting to find them dead when he returned, "instead he found new polyps in the container", Miglietta says. Soon, the biologist Stefano Piraino of Italy's University of Salento started to take an interest in what made this feat of rejuvenation possible. As embryos develop, so-called stem cells multiply and morph into the nerve cells, muscle cells and various other cell types that make up the body. Usually, they're stuck in that particular cell type until they age and die. But Piraino discovered that, during the immortal jellyfish's rejuvenation, certain tissues in the medusa undergo a "transdifferentiation" proces s where they revert back to a stem cell-type state and then specialise into other cell types. "Adult cells become 'undifferentiated' and become something else that is needed to form the polyp," says Miglietta, who used to work in Piraino's lab. Turritopsis dohrnii 's ability to rejuvenate earned it the nickname "immortal jellyfish". It is – as far as scientists know – unique in the animal kingdom. While some lizards, worms and amphibians can regrow lost or injured body parts, none come close to reverting adult bodies back into babies. Turritopsis dohrnii is a remarkable demonstration that ageing and mortality is not always a biological inevitability (though scientists can't rule out that it doesn't eventually die naturally). Genetic clues Today, Miglietta and others are working to dissect the genetic processes that allow cells to go back in time. The ultimate dream, Koldobskiy says, would be to identify the molecular "switch" that controls this process. If the same control switch exists in humans, then perhaps it can be triggered to coax human cells to more youthful states. If possible, that could accelerate the healing of wounds or injured tissue after strokes or heart attacks, or perhaps even reverse the damage that occurs in age-driven vision loss or the neurodegeneration that happens in Alzheimer's disease. "We're not going to shrink down to an embryo again and restart," he says, "but at the organ and tissue level, I think it's very much a possibility." The research is young, but is already starting to reveal some clues. In a 2022 study , one team of researchers compared the genes of Turritopsis dohrnii and a related species that is not known to rejuvenate – though it's hard to be certain that it's not capable of doing so, as many jellyfish are understudied, says molecular biologist and bioinformatician Victor Quesada of the University of Oviedo in Spain. Compared to the other species, Turritopsis dohrnii's DNA contained more copies of genes that produce proteins to help repair mutations and other kinds of DNA damage that accumulates with age. The immortal jellyfish also had more copies of genes that produce proteins involved in maintaining structures called telomeres – little caps on the end of DNA strands that protect the genetic material from damage. Normally, telomeres shorten with age, making the DNA more susceptible to damage, but the immortal jellyfish's enhanced ability to repair them could be one key to its longevity, Quesada says. This is just the beginning of understanding the secrets of Turritopsis dohrnii's rejuvenation strategy and whether any aspect of it could be applied to humans, Quesada says. "We assume in many diseases, that there's no way back," he says. "Perhaps there might be a way back, if we [learn] enough about…...

title: I tried eating 30 plants a week. It was surprisingly easy
description: I tried eating 30 plants a week. It was surprisingly easy 12 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Melissa Hogenboom BBC/ Stephen Parker In the end, I overshot my target and ate a grand total of 51 plants. Over the last two years, a new health goal has been growing in popularity. First there was 10,000 steps, then five a day . Now we're being encouraged to eat 30 plants per week. The trend is based on a 2018 study . It found that people who reported eating at least 30 plants per week tended to have more biodiverse gut microbiomes compared to those who ate fewer than ten. Subsequent studies have found that changing your diet to incorporate this much flora each week can improve your microbiome . This has many well-known benefits such as reducing inflammation and helping us to live healthier, longer lives . However, when my editor suggested I give the 30-plants trend a go, it initially sounded extremely intimidating and perhaps impossible. I imagined preparing complicated salads for every meal and struggling with the vast quantities of fibre I'd be consuming. But one week on from my experiment, I can report that it was remarkably easy. So easy, in fact, that I accidentally overshot my goal and ended up eating 51 plants in total. Here's how. More plants, more microbes First up, you don’t necessarily need 30 as your goal. Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation, at the University of California, San Diego, led the research which began the 30-plant trend. He says the number 30 is somewhat arbitrary, especially as there weren't many participants who ate over 30 plants per week in his study. Those who eat 25 or even 20 may also experience similar health benefits, he says. Those who started with a low number of different plants saw the biggest effect. "If you're already eating a moderate number of plants, the effect is not going to be as large by adding more." What counts? As it has grown in popularity, the goal of eating 30 plants has been gamified. Each additional plant earns you a " plant point ". There are six main categories of food we can include, which are: • Fruits • Vegetables • Whole grains • Legumes (beans and pulses) • Nuts and seeds • Herbs and spices Tea, coffee and chocolate count too. All contain compounds, such as antioxidants, which can benefit our health. The fact that spices are included surprised me. Research shows that adding a mix of spices to everyday meals can result in measurable improvements in gut microbes in as little as 48 hours, explains Federica Amati, a nutrition scientist at Imperial College, London. Some sources suggest that herbs, spices, tea and coffee should count as a quarter of a point each. Small changes can quickly affect our "microbe ecosystem" says Amati, but to make this meaningful, we need continued plant diversity. The benefits of focusing on a diverse diet is that it pushes us past simply choosing the obvious, like apples, cucumbers and peppers, says Amati. Research has found that low consumption of whole grains, nuts and seeds is a leading risk factor for an early death. Of course, hitting such a large range of different food items can be expensive if you buy lots of fresh produce, but for my experiment I used a mixture of fresh ingredients, cupboard staples as well as frozen food. BBC/ Melissa Hogenboom I enjoyed experimenting with new recipes such as (L-R) prawn curry, tempeh noodle stir fry, salad and couscous tagine (Credit: BBC/ Melissa Hogenboom) My week of 30+ Each day of my experiment, I ate my usual bowl of overnight oats with chia seeds and yoghurt every morning for breakfast. This week I varied the fruits I added each day. For lunch I rarely have much time, so I ate a sandwich or had leftovers from the night before, which also helped avoid waste. I did put more thought into my evening meals than my usual on-the-day planning, because I was trying not to repeat the same ingredients. I picked recipes not too far from my routine but aimed for those that had plenty of plant-based ingredients. My grocery shop looked slightly more colourful than usual, but it wasn't more expensive. Monday: For dinner I had a chickpea tagine, which was delicious and quick to make. I followed this chickpea tagine recipe from BBC Good Food and added peas for an extra boost of fibre. Plants today: Oats, blueberries, chia seeds, cabbage, peas, chickpeas, couscous, tomatoes, onions, raisins. Also today: Several spices (which I'm listing as one item). Tuesday: Selena Wu, a dietician at King's College London, says that it helps to focus on what extra fibre you can add to a meal. That could involve adding some nuts or seeds into your breakfast cereal or eating a side salad with your sandwich, which is what I did at lunch today. For dinner I made a quinoa salad with green lentils, asparagus and grilled salmon. Plants today: Raspberries, satsuma, apple, quinoa, broccoli, spinach, asparagus, lemon, garlic, spring onions. Wednesday: A simple curry is another staple in my household, but I tried a new recipe this time, adding sweet potatoes and red peppers, served with green beans on the side. The whole family enjoyed this one and it contained plenty of spices. Plants today: Coffee, banana, cashew nuts, coconut milk, sweet potato, green beans, red peppers, brown rice. Thursday: By Thursday I've already hit close to 30 so the pressure is off but I'm still adding as much variation as I can and sticking to my meal plan. Today I chose something easy that I could put together quickly using vegetables and cupboard staples. I made a vegetable soup with onions, garlic carrots, lentils and sweet potatoes and served it with a slice of sourdough bread and a simple side salad.
