title: No cars, no phone signal: Canada's ghost island where guests still check in
description: No cars, no phone signal: Canada's ghost island where guests still check in 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jennifer Bain Barrett & MacKay Once the thriving heart of Labrador's fishing industry, Battle Harbour has found new life as an island retreat with barely a trace of modern life. Several livyers have gathered on the wharf. Sleeves rolled up, four fishermen who "live here" on this remote Labrador island are splitting cod. Behind them, suit-clad merchants and more fishers, some in waterproof oilskins, have arranged themselves for a group photo against a white clapboard building with ochre-red trim. But our ferry approaches the wharf, something seems off. Everyone's as grey as the sky and nobody is moving. I give my head a shake and remember that I'm arriving at a place that proudly describes itself as "nine miles from normal". So, while these fellows were alive in around 1900, when this was the saltfish capital of the world, they've since been plucked from archival photos and turned into life-sized cardboard cutouts. "Welcome to Battle Harbour ," says Peter Bull, the executive director of the Battle Harbour Historic Trust, as we scramble off the ferry on a wooden plank. Jennifer Bain Lifesize cardboard cutouts recreate Battle Harbour's days as a thriving fishing port (Credit: Jennifer Bain) Bull quickly runs through the practicalities. Lunch is in half an hour at 12:30. A tour starts at 13:30. An Arctic fox family lives in the old cemetery. Two historic wireless radio towers need to be saved. There's no mobile phone service and just one communal Wi-Fi spot. Sunrise comes at 06:19. Wanda Fifield will walk me to my room. It's hard to believe that this tiny, half-mile long island was once teeming with fishermen and merchants "This [is the] emergency system – you just turn this button on," Fifield says, stopping at a walkie talkie in the hallway near my room. "If there's a problem in the nighttime, if you're sick or hurt or anything, just press this square button. You tell them your problem. You tell them that you're staying at the Merchant Building because they'll need to know what cottage to go to." With restored wooden houses, weathered fishing stages where catches were once processed and 16 private summer residences, Battle Harbour looks remarkably well preserved. But it has been more than half a century since anyone lived here year-round, and even longer since it was the unofficial capital of Labrador. I've got two nights to step back in time. Battle Harbour Historic Trust Battle Harbour has 16 private summer residences but no permanent population (Credit: Battle Harbour Historic Trust) Getting to Battle Harbour is an adventure in itself. First, you fly to the delightfully named Happy Valley-Goose Bay in mainland Labrador, then drive for five hours along the forest-flanked Expedition 51° highway , hoping to spot a moose and yearning for an outhouse. There are no services for most of the journey. From the wharf in Mary's Harbour, you then catch the daily passenger "ferry" for guests – a lofty name for a boat so small your luggage may be stacked in the bathroom. Plan your trip: When to visit: Battle Harbour is only open from June to early September. Confirm seasonal dates before booking. Getting there: Fly to Happy Valley-Goose Bay, then drive five hours to Mary's Harbour. A passenger ferry (for overnight guests only) departs at 11:00 each day and returns at 09:00 each morning. The journey takes 60 to 75 minutes. Staying overnight: Accommodation is in restored cottages and historic inn rooms. Two-night packages start at C$1,570 (£835; $1,106) for two people, including accommodation, return ferry transfers, meals and a guided historical tour. Taxes and gratuities are extra. Day trips: Separate day trips are also available during the summer season. Check with the operator for current schedules and prices. For 14.5km (9 miles), the boat winds past craggy coastline and near-shore islands, which look otherworldly if it's foggy and desolate if it's grey. Gulls, kittiwakes and gannets may soar alongside the boat and sometimes you'll spot icebergs, humpback whales and minkes. When Battle Island's buildings finally come into view, it's hard to believe that this tiny, half-mile long island was once teeming with fishermen and merchants. In the 1770s, English merchant John Slade established a trading operation on this tiny island that became a gateway to Labrador's rich fishing grounds. Salt cod was processed here and exported to Europe, the Caribbean and beyond. At its peak, there was a hospital, school, church and wireless station, and a permanent population of around 300. Thousands more seasonal fishermen passed through, including floaters who lived on schooners and stationers who built temporary shacks on land. But Battle Harbour's fortunes eventually faded. A devastating fire in 1930, declining fish stocks and a provincial resettlement programme in the 1960s gradually emptied the island. By the 1970s, its last year-round residents had gone. Jennifer Bain Across the tickle from Battle Harbour, Great Caribou Island offers hiking trails and sweeping views of the rocky Labrador coast (Credit: Jennifer Bain) The final blow to the island came on 2 July 1992, when the federal government's cod moratorium closed the fishery and instantly threw 30,000 people across Newfoundland and Labrador out of work. Today, Battle Harbour feels like a ghost island, its restored buildings preserving a world that has all but vanished. Run by a trust, the car-free historic site is only open to guests for around three months each summer, but for those that know it best, the island is anything but forgotten. Bull's connection to Battle Harbour stretches back more than a century, to when his grandfather fished along the Labrador coast. He has worked here since 2013, living on the island for most of the summer and returning to his home in St John's each September with enough cod, squid, mackerel and berries like bakeapple and partridgeberry to get him through winter. title: Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now
description: Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Lindsey Galloway Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) A new global report spotlights the world's emerging urban hotspots. From thriving cultural scenes to changing neighbourhoods, locals reveal what makes them worth exploring now. New York, London and Paris have once again topped Oxford Economics' annual ranking of the world's leading cities . But beyond these familiar names, its 2026 Global Cities Index has identified 28 " cities to watch " – places whose rapid growth and rising fortunes could see them become increasingly influential in the years ahead. These cities aren't just growing economically. New neighbourhoods, thriving cultural scenes and improved transport links are already reshaping the visitor experience and making them increasingly interesting places to visit. We selected five from the list and spoke to people who know them well to find out what's changing – and why they're worth exploring now. Getty Images Toulouse is emerging as one of France's fastest-growing cities (Credit: Getty Images) Toulouse, France With its population forecast to grow by 57,000 over the next four years – more than anywhere else in France – Toulouse is one of Europe's fastest-growing cities and is attracting younger, skilled newcomers with its mild climate, relatively affordable cost of living and high quality of life. You get the energy of a big city, with an incredible food scene, independent cafes, cocktail bars and a growing cultural offering, alongside a much slower pace of life – Elodie Paramelle "Here, you don't have to choose between slow life and fast life," said Elodie Paramelle, who recently returned to Toulouse after 10 years in London. "You get the energy of a big city, with an incredible food scene, independent cafes, cocktail bars and a growing cultural offering, alongside a much slower pace of life." Toulouse has changed significantly in recent years, according to Mélodie Tyler, who moved back here after seven years in Paris. She says the city is much more walkable and bike-friendly, while its food and wine scene has expanded dramatically. And she notes that the buzz is spreading beyond the historic centre. "Ponts-Jumeaux where I live hosts a bunch of festivals, guinguettes [open-air bars] and skateboarding competitions," she said. "The Toulousains love to party and be outside as much as possible!" Beyond its thriving neighbourhoods, Toulouse is also major aerospace hub, home to hundreds of companies, including Airbus's global headquarters. Visitors can explore that heritage at the Cité de l'Espace space-themed discovery centre or Aeroscopia aviation museum beside the Airbus runways. For something more unusual, La Halle de La Machine brings art and engineering together through giant mechanical creatures created by a local street theatre company. Getty Images Ho Chi Minh City's rapid growth is transforming its urban landscape, but its traditional neighbourhoods remain central to its appeal (Credit: Getty Images) Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Vietnam's largest city is on a remarkable trajectory. Oxford Economics predicts Ho Chi Minh City will be among the world's 50 fastest-growing cities over the next five years, with an economy that could rival Berlin's by 2050. Tourism is booming too, with more than eight million international visitors last year, exceeding projections. "The first metro line only opened at the end of 2024, and it's one of the most tangible symbols of how quickly the city is changing," said Meaghan Yash, a travel specialist at tour operator Timbuktu Travel who frequently designs trips here. The 20km (12.5 mile) line runs from Ben Thanh Market in the city centre to the Suoi Tien theme park, with single fares costing less than £1 ($1.33). Yet, Ho Chi Minh's appeal lies in how it balances change with continuity. Chris Buchart, commercial director at Vietnamese hotel company Fusion Group, suggests travellers visit the French-colonial Central Post Office and Opera House , and then the War Remnants Museum for context on the country's history, before turning to one of the city's greatest strengths: its food. Buchart recommends trying bánh mì (Vietnamese baguette sandwich) , cơm tấm (broken rice) and bánh xèo (crispy pancakes), while Yash suggests venturing beyond the usual tourist circuit in central District 1 to quieter, more residential neighbourhoods where leafy streets are ideal for wandering and cafe-hopping. He also suggests Chợ Lớn, the city's historic Chinatown, for its markets, temples and medicine shops, while across the river in Thảo Điền, independent boutiques, galleries and home-grown Vietnamese brands make for excellent shopping. Getty Images Warsaw's rapidly changing skyline reflects the Polish capital's economic transformation (Credit: Getty Images) Warsaw, Poland The Polish capital has made one of the fastest jumps in the Global Cities index, climbing more than 100 places to 61st. Its quality-of-life score now surpasses London, New York and Tokyo, while its economy is projected to expand by around 3% annually – nearly twice the European city average. For Konrad Warzecha, a Polish-Australian whose family home is in Warsaw's Wola district, the transformation has been remarkable. "From our balcony you can see the skyline, and watching the roads, highways and towers go up over 20 years has made the city almost unrecognisable," said Warzecha, who blogs at House Sitters Guide . These days Warsaw is one of the places I recommend most, and not because I am from there. I am proud to have a Polish background – Konrad Warzecha The biggest changes, he says, are on the streets. "As a kid I rode the trams and did not feel safe, and I saw many robberies happen," he said. "Now I have never felt safer. People walk around at night, the streets are clean and trouble gets dealt with quickly." For first-time visitors, Warzecha recommends a walk that takes in both the old and new city. title: 'Leaving something delicious on the plate would be a far worse crime': How Italy's guiltiest food ritual went public
description: 'Leaving something delicious on the plate would be a far worse crime': How Italy's guiltiest food ritual went public 5 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Guilia Crouch Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) Once considered improper, a beloved Italian dining ritual reveals a surprising clash between etiquette and the pleasure of eating. Growing up, I spent a lot of time at my Italian grandparents' house in Kent, where bread was never not on the table. I remember my nonna slicing it into thick chunks and presenting it in a plastic basket lined with kitchen roll. We'd eat it throughout lunch or dinner, but its starring role came at the end: mopping up the last of the pasta sauce or soaking up oil and vinegar from the salad. It was, and still is, my favourite part of any meal. Get to know your expert Giulia Crouch is a British food journalist specialising in Italian cuisine. She regularly visits family in southern Italy and writes extensively about the country's food, culture and traditions. She is the author of The Happiest Diet in the World and a certified olive oil sommelier. These days I'm baffled when my husband leaves good sauce on the plate. "You’ve missed the best bit," I'll cry, tearing off a piece of bread to mop up what's left. It was only when I got older that I learnt that this ordinary habit has a name in Italy: " fare la scarpetta " – literally "to do the little shoe" – using bread to mop up the last of the sauce or juices from a meal. On a recent trip to Naples, I was surprised to see la scarpetta done at a white-tableclothed restaurant as casually as at my grandparents' table. While my Italian dining companion and I were waiting for our pasta dishes to be cleared away, I noticed his eyes darting towards a bit of pesto left on the plate. He eagerly tore off some bread, wiped up every last bit and popped it into his mouth with gusto. He didn't ask if I minded or look up to register any kind of disapproval on my face – not that he'd have found any. He just did it with an uninhibited enthusiasm I found oddly life-affirming. It communicated: this food is good and should be thoroughly enjoyed. On the second course, I followed his lead. So how did a habit once frowned upon in polite company become something Italians now proudly do in public? How scarpetta got its name There are many theories online as to why the ritual is called "little shoe". Some Italians suggest it's because the piece of bread looks like a small shoe or clog; others suggest it refers to being so hungry you'd eat the sole of a shoe. Getty Images Once frowned upon in polite company, la scarpetta is now increasingly embraced in restaurants (Credit: Getty Images) Italian food historian Luca Cesari says neither explanation has much evidence behind it. "Its origin is uncertain, so I'd leave aside the more fanciful theories you find online," he says. The earliest written example Cesari has found is from 1871, in Roman dialect, when a character in the Roman magazine La Frusta asks to make scarpetta with a little sauce left on the plate. The expression also appears in an 1885 dictionary of the Abruzzo dialect, suggesting its roots lie in central Italy. He called it perfectly acceptable – even elegant – as long as it was done with the fingers with nonchalance. As for the name itself, Cesari says the most convincing hypothesis comes from the Accademia della Crusca, Italy's leading authority on the Italian language. In central Italian dialect, fare una scarpetta meant "to go for a little walk" – much like the bread taking a stroll around the plate. Francesca Cipolla, a food content creator from Palermo, Sicily, says scarpetta is instinctive, almost a reflex. "It's not something we consciously perform. If there's delicious sauce left on the plate, I tear off a piece of bread and use it to pick up the sauce. I don't really think about doing it; it's how I grew up eating, and everyone in my family is the same." But the custom has not always been considered good table manners, and attitudes have varied by region, generation and setting. Chef Gaia Enria who grew up in Turin, one of Italy's more formal northern cities, remembers being told off by her parents for doing la scarpetta . "It was viewed as improper back then. I think that was specific to Turin. Times have changed now but I remember it clearly." In Puglia, chef Somaia Hammad remembers almost the opposite. "In Puglia especially, it can almost be considered rude to leave anything behind on your plate, so finishing every last bit with a piece of bread is as much about showing appreciation for the food as it is about not wasting anything." Getty Images Attitudes towards the practice vary, but the pleasure of sharing good food remains central to Italy's dining culture (Credit: Getty Images) Further south in Calabria, the "toe" of Italy's boot, chef Francesco Mazzei of Mezzogiorno restaurant in London, remembers a very different relationship with bread. Bread was a food that commanded deep respect. It wasn't just a vehicle for sauce, it was the integral part of the meal, he explains. In fact, everything else was just a companatico – literally "what you eat with bread". "Our lives centred around bread," he adds "The meal hasn't begun if there's no bread on the table and it can't end without it either." When bad manners went mainstream Cesari cautions, however, that the divide has as much to do with class as geography. He explains that traditional bourgeois etiquette frowned upon touching food with the hands. Even the supposed compromise of breaking bread and spearing it with a fork to mop around the plate could be considered boorish – perhaps more so, because it...

title: The Obituary Cocktail: The 'deadly' drink that symbolises New Orleans
description: The Obituary Cocktail: The 'deadly' drink that symbolises New Orleans 6 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Andrew Nelson BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images (Credit: BBC/ Serenity Strull/ Getty Images) Combining a martini's wallop with one of the world's most notorious spirits, this recently revived cocktail embodies the city's distinctive approach to life and death. Like a rake's progress, it starts with gin. Then vermouth. Then absinthe, delivered by atomiser, eye-dropper or spoon. A lemon twist, with its burst of essential oils, anoints it. My first Obituary Cocktail was in New Orleans, the city that invented it, forgot it and then revived it. In the eight years I lived there, it never appeared on a menu, but savvy local bartenders could make one on request. That evening's details are as hazy as the Wednesday after Fat Tuesday. I could not tell you the year, nor the season. I only remember it was good and that it was sometime after absinthe became legal again in the United States in 2007. I drank it at Cure . Neal Bodenheimer's legendary bar is graced by an enormous scientific print of a palmetto bug, the flying cockroach residents know as the city's native bird. Uplighting shines through the liquor bottles, turning them into bejewelled reliquaries. Chris Granger The Obituary Cocktail has recently started coming back from the dead (Credit: Chris Granger) In a city that uses "costume" as a verb and shimmies into one at the drop of a hat, visuals are important. Poured into a vintage Nick and Nora coupe glass, the Obituary Cocktail is a head-turning drink. It also captures something of New Orleans' carefree approach to life and nonchalance in the face of death, where a clinking glass and party is often a response to worldly travails. "[The Obituary Cocktail] sums up the allure and the appeal of the city," says Clayton Rosenthal, manager and head of the drinks programme at Fives , a cocktail and oyster bar located in a historic 19th-Century building on Jackson Square. Rosenthal uses Old Tom gin, Drapo Dry vermouth and Mata Hari absinthe in his Obituary, warning first-time drinkers: "The first sip can be a bit of a punch in the mouth." It's an appropriate warning for a cocktail that combines a martini's wallop with one of the world's most notorious spirits and then names the result after a death notice. The Obituary's mysterious birth The Obituary Cocktail is a remnant of the louche and bohemian world of the French Quarter in the years following the end of Prohibition in 1933, when artists, writers and creatives like Tennessee Williams and Truman Capote gathered in cafes and bars. According to Sue Strachan, a New Orleans historian and author of The Obituary Cocktail , the drink was likely invented in Café Lafitte on Bourbon Street. She notes that the first known reference to the cocktail was in a 1942 guide to the city called "The Bachelor in New Orleans", which promised to introduce "unattached gentlemen and ladies of spirit" to "the Paris of North America". Alamy The Obituary Cocktail was likely invented in Café Lafitte on Bourbon Street, now known as Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop (Credit: Alamy) But while the drink subsequently surfaced in newspaper columns, nobody seems to have recorded who invented it or who gave it its morbid moniker. "There's no definitive documentation on how the cocktail got its name," says Strachan. "No doubt its powerful punch led to some rough mornings, much like the phrase 'death warmed over'." Absinthe supplied its mystique and maybe a throb in the head. "The Obituary is about intrigue," Strachan adds. "You bring absinthe into the picture and suddenly you have a drink with a little mystery, a little bohemian spirit and a whiff of the forbidden." The drink's "forbidden" ingredient During the Belle Époque (1871-1914), New Orleans was one of the US's greatest absinthe-drinking cities. Ted Breaux, a New Orleans-born historian and distiller who helped return genuine absinthe to the US market after its 95-year absence, says the finest French brands flowed into the city. Alamy New Orleans has had a long and storied connection with absinthe (Credit: Alamy) By the 1890s, absinthe was showing up in New Orleans drinks ranging from the Sazerac to the Absinthe Frappé and Absinthe Suissesse. Then it became notorious, Breaux says. The spirit was blamed for everything from nervous disorders to hallucinations before the US banned it in 1912. The blame, he argues, was its popularity, which encouraged cheap imitations and disreputable ingredients. "You [could urinate] in a bottle and call it absinthe, much to my dismay," he says. Breaux compares absinthe's role in a cocktail with something else New Orleanians understand instinctively. "If you have a bowl of gumbo, what happens when you put in a big dash of Crystal Hot Sauce? It amplifies the flavour and gives it a pop," he says. "That is what absinthe does to [the Obituary Cocktail]. Absinthe is cocktail hot sauce." There was a problem, however: when the Obituary Cocktail was invented, its defining ingredient, absinthe, had already been illegal in the US for decades. Strachan believes Café Lafitte stashed bottles of absinthe smuggled into the country by well-travelled patrons, while other bartenders reached for substitutes. The liqueur Herbsaint, developed in New Orleans after Prohibition ended, replicated absinthe's distinct anise flavours without its prohibited ingredients. Ojen, an Andalusian anise-based liqueur, was also used. But after Café Lafitte moved down the street from its original location (now occupied by Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop ) following a property dispute in 1953 to become Café Lafitte in Exile , the Obituary gradually slipped from view. Fives Fives is one of the bars proudly reviving the Obituary Cocktail (Credit: Fives) New Orleans in a glass When Strachan began researching her book in 2023, she found only one bar – Jewel of the South in the French Quarter – that listed it on its menu. Since then, however, interest in the Obituary has begun to climb with a renewed...

title: 'More audacious than her male peers': The Renaissance woman who was the first female painter of erotic nudes
description: 'More audacious than her male peers': The Renaissance woman who was the first female painter of erotic nudes 7 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Cath Pound Fundación Casa de Alba, Palacio de Liria, Madrid (Credit: Fundación Casa de Alba, Palacio de Liria, Madrid) Late-Renaissance portraitist Lavinia Fontana was the first professional woman artist to paint a nude female figure, many of them more overtly suggestive than those by her male peers. Were these nudes a statement of rebellion against her prudish father, a commercial choice – or a clue to her inner life? There were two sides to the trailblazing artist Lavinia Fontana. The first can be seen in her self-portrait from 1577, in which she sits at the spinet dressed in a fine gown and jewels, the epitome of a wealthy, cultured and virtuous young Italian woman, the easel in the background a proud indication of her chosen vocation. Considered the first female professional artist, she was much sought after as a portraitist and would go on to win important commissions for more than a dozen altarpieces, challenging the view that women were incapable of winning such illustrious assignments, let alone executing them. The second can be seen in the monumental Minerva in the Act of Dressing, in which the nude goddess appears to have been caught unawares as she is about to slip into a finely embroidered robe. Holding the garment carefully in her hands, she turns to meet the viewer with a gaze that is both coy and suggestive at the same time. Accademia di San Luca, Rome In a 1577 self-portrait by Lavinia Fontana, the artist depicts herself as refined and virtuous (Credit: Accademia di San Luca, Rome) The image was painted for Cardinal Scipione Borgese in 1613, a year before Fontana's death; the fact that a woman was behind it would no doubt have added a frisson for anyone who saw it. As would the knowledge that Fontana had a reputation for creating such images, something of which we have only recently become fully aware. Over the past few years, more works have been attributed to Fontana that reveal her to be not only the first female artist to paint the female nude, but also the first to paint erotic works whose subject matter was often more audacious than that of her male peers. Her self-portraits are very proper, so you think you have a very prim woman. Maybe not – Patrizia Cavazzini At first glance it may seem surprising that these two conflicting sides of Fontana existed simultaneously. "Her self-portraits are very proper. There is never a hint of scandal in her life. So, you think you have a very prim woman. Maybe not," says Patrizia Cavazzini, one of the curators of (Woman) Painter at The National Museum of Oslo, where both the self-portrait and Minerva are on display. However, the art historian Elizabeth Cropper thinks we shouldn't necessarily believe that "public social respectability denies private sexual eroticism… We need to allow some complexity in our understanding of Early Modern women," she tells the BBC. Galleria Borghese. Photo by Mauro Coen Fortuna painted the goddess Minerva nude, about to get dressed and gazing at the viewer (Credit: Galleria Borghese/ Photo by Mauro Coen) Whether or not these works are indicative of Fontana's private desires, Enrico Maria Dal Pozzolo, author of Lavinia Fontana: Erotic Paintings, believes there were specific commercial and entrepreneurial reasons for her to paint both sacred and profane works. "In my opinion, she did it to show she was different… and to draw attention to her compositional boldness," he tells the BBC. A veiled Venus Her earliest known erotic work was Venus and Cupid, painted around 1585-90. While a nude Venus is hardly an unusual subject in art, Fontana used jewels, veils and pearls to heighten the sensuality. The trope was repeated a few years later when she painted a recognisable noble woman, Isabella Ruini, as Venus. The half-length portrait, no doubt intended for private viewing only, has Isabella/Venus draped in the flimsiest of gauze wraps, which does nothing to conceal her breasts. Musée des Beaux-Arts, Rouen The noblewoman Isabella Ruini was portrayed as Venus by Fontana, draped in a flimsy gauze wrap (Credit: Musée des Beaux-Arts, Rouen) In Florence and Rome at the time there were whole galleries dedicated to portraits of beautiful women, while in her native Bologna there was great competition between the women. "Many poets wrote about them. They ranked them and said who was the most beautiful, so I think it comes out of that culture of an appreciation of female beauty," says Cavazzini. Three nude noblewomen Fontana's most dazzling work in this genre is the recently attributed Three Female Nudes (c1600), which features three noblewomen dressed in nothing but thin veils and exquisitely observed jewels. Dal Pozzolo speculates that it is a contemporary Judgement of Paris, inspired by the story from Greek mythology in which Paris is asked to choose which goddess – Hera, Aphrodite or Athena – is the most beautiful. The woman on the left is thought to be Clelia Farnese, considered one of the most stunning women in Italy, and both she and the unidentified woman on the right gesture to the clear victor in the centre who is thought to be Maria de Medici. The work is painted on slate, giving it a highly reflective surface, so the latter-day Paris who commissioned it would be reflected in the image as he gazed upon his choice in the privacy of his chamber. Private collection The dazzling 1600 painting of three nude noblewomen in veils and jewels has only recently been attributed to Fortuna (Credit: Private collection) Painting such images was undoubtedly bold, especially for a woman living in Bologna at the time of the Counter Reformation, when the city's severe Archbishop, Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti, was keen to extend the Catholic Church's moralising zeal into the realm of painting. Her artist father Prospero acknowledged that a Christian painter should avoid...

title: 'The 21st-Century gym-toned bodies put me out': Four things Jane Austen adaptations get wrong - according to experts
description: 'The 21st-Century gym-toned bodies put me out': Four things Jane Austen adaptations get wrong - according to experts 23 September 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Molly Gorman Universal/ Alamy (Credit: Universal/ Alamy) A new film adaptation of the English novelist's Sense and Sensibility adds to a long line of attempts to translate Austen's timeless stories to the screen. But these are their common mistakes. Jane Austen's timeless novels are always being re-adapted. And there are two more major adaptations coming this year: Georgia Oakley's film version of Sense and Sensibility and a new TV series of Pride and Prejudice. They add to a long line of attempts to translate the works of the beloved 19th-Century author to the screen. Each generation will have their favourites, and it is a truth universally acknowledged that no film or TV take on a book can ever be entirely faithful to the original text. But there are certain aspects of Austen adaptations that always rile up passionate Janeites. Here are four things they consistently get wrong – according to experts. Alamy Austen knew her books would sell if they included romance (Credit: Alamy) 1. They focus on fairytale romance Romance takes centre stage in most Austen adaptations. But "Austen is much more focused on the heroine", Sutherland says. "She's a psychological novelist... that's what interests her." Austen presents the reader with imperfect heroines who face moral challenges and social obstacles independent of their male love interest – which makes them all the more relatable to modern women. And while Austen may not have the same haunting allure as the gothic Victorian writers who came after her, she does touch on some heavier themes. In Mansfield Park, for example, she explores infidelity and gambling , while she references slavery on multiple occasions across her works (though it's greatly disputed what her thoughts on slavery were). Of course, Austen's fairytale romantic moments are important – like Captain Wentworth's ardent love letter to Anne in Persuasion – but by promoting romance from a sub-plot to the main plot, adaptations can overlook Austen's class critique and her depiction of the bleak reality for women in the Regency era (around 1795-1837). Apart from Emma Woodhouse, the protagonist of Emma, most of the heroines in Austen's stories face financial precarity. "Austen knew her market," says Sandie Byrne, professor of English at the University of Oxford. "And she had to have the girl getting the boy, and the 'happy ever after' to sell her books – but she doesn't make the big kiss, or the proposal, or the wedding the climax of the book, and there's no description of the church and the fuss." Plus a woman's need for security wouldn't have ended after marriage – her security would always rely on her husband's character and how they managed their finances . "The adaptations tend to show a rosy glow – everything's tied up and finished," Byrne says. Universal Elinor and Marianne are often seen with their hair down in the new Sense and Sensibility, ignoring the strict social rules of the Regency era (Credit: Universal) 2. They get the costumes and styling – and teeth – wrong "Where are the bonnets?!" erupted Austen enthusiasts when Oakley's Sense and Sensibility trailer debuted, featuring scenes of 19-year-old Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and 17-year-old Marianne Dashwood (Esmé Creed-Miles) frolicking around with their long hair down. (To confirm, flimsy-looking bonnets do appear, albeit rarely, throughout the film.) In the Regency era, only very young girls would wear their hair down. Older girls would strictly wear a bonnet, says Byrne. "It's a sign of being grown up, that you put your hair up and your hemlines down." Style choices in Austen adaptations are always a point of contention – from costume to make-up and hair. Netflix's 2022 Persuasion featured Anne Elliot (Dakota Johnson) wearing rosy lipstick and mascara, leading to a plethora of online makeup tutorials and accusations of Johnson having "iPhone face" – a slang term used to describe actors in period dramas who look as if they've seen modern technology. "What puts me out is hair and teeth and 21st-Century gym-toned bodies," says Juliette Wells, a professor of literary studies at Goucher College in the US. "And I definitely think about orthodontia and veneers, and what lovely teeth most young actors have, [but] how very few characters in Austen are described as having good teeth. Presumably most of them did not." No matter how accurate the costumes may be, if an actor meets 21st-Century beauty standards, they won't match historically accurate portraits from that period, she adds. "That puts us at a distance from Austen." Films will also often try to be authentic by dressing people in the fashion of the day when the book was published, Byrne says, but most people made clothes last a long time. "If you were very rich, you changed your clothes a lot… [but] most people in the echelon that Jane Austen is writing about didn't have that many clothes. And they made them last. They weren't slaves to fashion." Alamy Netflix received criticism for Dakota Johnson's obvious makeup and "iPhone face" in the 2022 version of Persuasion (Credit: Alamy) 3. They don't capture Austen's language and pacing Austen is renowned for her witty dialogue and sparkling, omniscient narrative voice. "And that's what we read Austen for, isn't it? We read it for the irony, we read it for the humour, we read it for the satire and we read it because it's subtly subversive," Byrne says. But capturing that verbal sophistication is a challenge on screen. And Austen is not a very visual novelist, says Byrne. "That's the odd thing about her. She doesn't encourage you to see things so much as to hear things." However adaptations often take an approach that more closely follows the visual romantic style of Charlotte Brontë, says Kathryn Sutherland, a senior research fellow at the University of Oxford. Oakley's Sense and Sensibility very much plays into this –...

title: 'An object of lust': How the ancient Greek goddess Aphrodite became a controversial symbol of love and sex
description: 'An object of lust': How the ancient Greek goddess Aphrodite became a controversial symbol of love and sex 8 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Matthew Wilson The Ashmolean Museum Praxiteles's Aphrodite of Knidos was lost but later Roman copies like the Capitoline Venus are similar (Credit: The Ashmolean Museum) Artworks depicting Aphrodite, the ancient Greek goddess of love and beauty, have long been branded obscene, objectifying the female body. How did she become one of the most controversial figures in the history of art? The nudity of Aphrodite (or Venus as she was known by the ancient Romans), has been a topic of debate for centuries. In 1880, the shocked author Mark Twain called Titian's Venus of Urbino (1534) "the foulest, the vilest, the obscenest picture the world possesses". In 1914, the suffragette Mary Richardson hacked Diego Velázquez's Rokeby Venus (c 1647-51) with a meat cleaver at least three times in the middle of London's National Gallery. "I didn't like the way men visitors gaped at it all day long," was one of her later explanations. Aphrodite: The Making of a Goddess, a new exhibition at Oxford's Ashmolean Museum , explores the history of the goddess. It helps to explain how she evolved into a lightning rod of such intense cultural controversy. There are two versions of her origin story: a mythological one and a historically accurate one, and neither particularly marks her out as a future troublemaker. In myth, the tale begins with Kronos castrating his father Ouranos and flinging his genitals into the sea; foam began to bubble to the surface, and out of it arose a fully formed Aphrodite. She glided across the waves to the island of Cyprus, where her footsteps caused flowers to bloom miraculously from the land. One of [Aphrodite's] names is Pandemos: the goddess of all people. It's not just the warriors, or the women: love affects everybody and everything. It pervades life – Anja Ulbrich The historical version of Aphrodite's birth also begins on Cyprus, where she emerged as a deity around 1200BC. She was a distinctive new addition to the pantheon but had features that had apparently evolved from older Middle Eastern goddesses like Ishtar, Astarte and Hathor. For these archaic goddesses, "sexuality, love and fertility were their core characteristics," Anja Ulbrich, curator of the Ashmolean exhibition, tells the BBC, "but they all had more than one function". And the same applied to Aphrodite, who in her early years wasn't just a goddess of romantic love, but of all physical love and procreation – in the animal and plant world as much as the human realm. And there are other, perhaps less well-known, sides to her persona. She fought in the Trojan War – and this warrior aspect of her personality led her to be worshipped by the ancient Greek navy. The National Gallery, London In 1914, the suffragette Mary Richardson hacked Diego Velázquez's Rokeby Venus (c 1647-51) with a meat cleaver in London's National Gallery (Credit: The National Gallery, London) Aphrodite can also claim to be the founder of the Roman civilisation, no less. One mythological narrative describes her affair with the Trojan prince Anchises; their son Aeneas fled to Italy after the fall of Troy – and his descendants were said to have established the city of Rome. Following her original appearance on Cyprus back in the 13th Century BC, Aphrodite became a big hit with people, and worship of her spread all around ancient Greece. Why was she so appealing? "Fertility, love, procreation is a topic across humanity, no matter which culture," Ulbrich says. "One of her names is Pandemos: the goddess of all people. It's not just the warriors, or the women: love affects everybody and everything. It pervades life." A new kind of nudity So far, so uncontroversial. For several hundred years, artists didn't make Aphrodite look particularly different from other female Olympian goddesses. And in her early years, they did not typically depict her naked, and certainly never in the more provocative poses we now associate with her. But then, in 350BC, an artwork appeared that changed everything. Praxiteles's Aphrodite of Knidos (c 350BC) was the first completely nude artwork of a woman in ancient Greece. The original sculpture is lost, but we can get a good picture of what it looked like by later Roman copies like the Capitoline Venus (c 160BC). Before Praxiteles, it was only male figures who were shown undressed. "Celebrating physical male beauty through nudity was perfectly normal from the 7th or 6th Century BC onwards," Ulbrich says. So, Praxiteles chose to do the same for female physical beauty. The Ashmolean Museum Praxiteles's Aphrodite of Knidos was lost but later Roman copies like the Capitoline Venus are similar (Credit: The Ashmolean Museum) Aphrodite's nudity was different. If you look closely, you can see how dissimilar the presentation of nudity is in Greek male sculptures: it's all in the body language. Praxiteles's Aphrodite is shown caught whilst bathing. She appears shy and vulnerable, covering herself in shame or embarrassment, whereas the nude male body in Greek art had always been shown as confident and heroic. Ulbrich explains: "It is mostly based on how she's presented in myths, where she is constantly bathing and working on her physical beauty." But in Praxiteles's artwork, Aphrodite's hands are positioned slightly away from her, making it possible for a viewer to see her exposed body if they look at it from different angles. It's an artwork that invites interaction, and rewards the spectator for their sensual curiosity. These innovative artistic techniques would cause heated debate in centuries to come, and a name was coined for the pose of the Praxiteles's sculpture: the Venus Pudica (modest or shameful). The Aphrodite of Knidos was "revolutionary," says Ulbrich. Before Praxiteles, Aphrodite might be recognisable in sculptures from a range of different items of clothing, jewellery and other attributes. Afterwards, he says, "the nudity basically takes over." It's worth acknowledging that a naked body is...

title: 'A window into its soul': The rare elephant behaviour that reveals the depths of their emotions
description: 'A window into its soul': The rare elephant behaviour that reveals the depths of their emotions 13 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen Federico Veronesi Federico Veronesi encountered a female elephant carrying a stillborn calf in Namibia (Credit: Federico Veronesi) The winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year captures a rarely seen elephant behaviour, revealing the complexity of their emotional lives. Photographer Federico Veronesi witnessed a heartbreaking scene while following a herd of elephants trudging along a dry riverbed in the Namibian desert in September 2025. He encountered a female elephant carrying a stillborn calf, its tiny legs wrapped around her trunk and its limp body dangling in the air. "It was an intimate moment, almost spiritual," Veronesi recalls. "The baby was still completely intact and soft. It hadn't stiffened up yet, so it was clearly born in the night, or maybe just a few hours before." At first sight, the poignant scene appeared to show a mother's grief. But as Veronesi would later find out, the rare behaviour he was witnessing had a surprising twist that revealed an even more complex sensitivity than it first seemed. Veronesi followed the herd for several hours and captured some incredibly striking photos, one of which (see the image below) won the grand title prize at the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year , run by the Natural History Museum in London. The female elephant carried the calf for hours, occasionally setting it down to feed or drink, before picking it up again and continuing her journey along the Huab River, Veronesi says. "I thought, 'This is such a sad scene but it needs to be seen by people.' This photo makes it clear how much these elephants suffer, how they have complex feelings, which people perhaps don't associate with animals." It certainly adds another layer to the depth of these creatures' emotions – Federico Veronesi Veronesi eventually found out that the elephant was not carrying her own stillborn calf. "She's not the mother," says Christin Winter, conservation programme director at Elephant Human Relations Aid (EHRA), a non-profit working to protect Namibia's desert elephants. This female, now aged 14, lost her own calf two years ago. Since then, she has been seen carrying the stillborn calves of other elephants on four separate occasions, says Winter. It's the first time that this behaviour has been documented in the area, she adds. This revelation "certainly adds another layer to the depth of these creatures' emotions", says Veronesi. "It's even more poignant how this female has been behaving like that after her loss, as if she is trying to reconnect with her own calf and still not giving up on that loss after many years." Elephant emotions There are a few theories as to why the elephant carried the calf for such a long time. The behaviour may be some kind of "emotional processing", Winter says. "Perhaps it was a way [for her] to process the death and not being able to let go just yet, perhaps she was traumatised by losing her calf and that's why she snaps into this behaviour every time one dies." She may also have been trying to protect the calf's body from predators, Winter adds. Federico Veronesi This photo by Federico Veronesi won the grand title prize at the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year (Credit: Federico Veronesi) Veronesi's photos offer a glimpse into the lives of Namibia's 150 hardy desert elephants that reside along five riverbeds in the Namib Desert and migrate long distances in search of food and water, feeding on the seedpods of Ana trees ( Faidherbia albida ) or on grass in the floodplains. They are not a unique elephant species, but rather an ecotype: a population that has adapted to the arid environment through learned behaviours rather than genetic adaptations, similar to Namibia's desert lions that live along the Skeleton Coast . "It's their knowledge that really makes them special and also very vulnerable, because once that knowledge is gone, it can't be readily replaced," says Winter. Declining species The population has been steadily declining over the past 20 years, says Winter. This is partly due to environmental stress, in particular long periods of drought, but is largely because of heightened conflict with humans, according to Winter. "The conflict is mostly about water." Elephants will come into farms and push over water tanks, pull up pipes and break pumps, "so the tolerance of people towards elephant presence isn't particularly high", she says. "These stories go deep and live on for a very long time." More like this: • The dramatic photo of huskies walking on water • The rare hyena stalking a diamond mining ghost story • 'The moment I made eye contact with a whale' The mortality rate of newborn calves is a major concern, says Winter. "It is extremely high and very scary." Just two calves survived out of a total of 16 between 2014 and 2022, she says. One theory as to why so many desert elephant calves are dying is that they are born premature, "because the females are not fit enough to carry them full term", Winter says. This may be due to the chronic stress from conflict with humans, she says. Research shows that elephants can suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in response to conflict with humans. Whenever the EHRA team comes across stillborn calves, they're very small, Winter adds. Typically, a healthy newborn calf [weighs] between 100 and 120kg (220-265lb), she says. The stillborn calves, meanwhile, are about 60-65kg (132-143lb). EHRA is working with Daniella Chusyd, an elephant expert and assistant professor from Indiana University Bloomington, to analyse how environmental factors as well as chronic stress may be impacting Namibia's desert elephants. They are currently collecting dung samples to test for heavy metals and forever chemicals (such as PFAS), and to check the elephants' thyroid and cortisol hormones, as part of a project running until 2028. title: The US produces millions of tonnes of rice waste each year. Now people are building homes with it
description: The US produces millions of tonnes of rice waste each year. Now people are building homes with it 10 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Nick Aspinwall Modern Mill The recently completed Palisades properties in California are among the new US homes using rice husk panelling (Credit: Modern Mill) A notoriously stubborn agricultural waste product, rice husk is being repurposed as a sturdy and resilient construction material. In 2023, David Fine had a problem. He had been hired to renovate a luxury ski condo development in Park City, Utah, in the US. But the building requirements were proving challenging. The existing condos had begun to rot under the town's famous powdery snow, which piles up for months during the long winters. The homeowner's association had spent a year searching for a material that would absorb moisture while also resisting the increasingly frequent wildfires that threaten the mountaintop locale in summer . They considered products like extruded aluminium, which would protect the condos against fire but appear synthetic. Wooden sidings such as cedar, on the other hand, would achieve a more pleasing aesthetic, but with a weaker fire rating. Finally, they came up with an outlandish-sounding solution: panel boards made from rice husks – a byproduct of rice farming. "Their focus was to find something that looked like wood, that was beautiful, and that was a little better fire-rated than traditional wood siding," Fine says. Rice husk panels, it turned out, "checked all those boxes". Previously viewed as a waste product and even pollutant , rice husks are now attracting attention for their potential as a versatile, sustainable construction material. With hundreds of new homes in the US now using rice husk panelling, and other rice husk products from porches to playgrounds available, why are some developers choosing this agricultural throwaway over classic materials? The house that rice built While growing on the plant, rice husks protect the grains from moisture and pests. But when the crop is harvested, they become one of the most stubborn agricultural waste products to deal with. The world produces around 150 million tonnes (331 billion lb) of rice husk each year, much of it burned on farms or at roadsides , posing risks to both human health and the environment. In the US, which grows some nine million tonnes (20 billion lb) of rice annually , rice husk is sometimes converted into biomass energy , though even then there's not always a clear use for the ash left behind. A pioneering solution kills two birds with one stone – repurposing this agricultural waste as a durable and sustainable building material of the future. Modern Mill David Fine's Sterlingwood Condos in Park City, Utah (Credit: Modern Mill) Alongside the use of materials made from rice husks in panelling and other construction materials, research suggests rice husk ash could provide an alternative to cement , which is responsible for 8% of global carbon emissions . Christopher Guimond first became curious about rice byproducts when he discovered US rice producers let the waste decompose in the ground and release polluting clouds of methane , a potent greenhouse gas . An engineering student, Guimond started to believe that rice husks would make the perfect material to use at scale in construction. "The fascination was to take this thing that was a throwaway and leverage its properties," he says. Guimond is now the founder and chief executive of Modern Mill, the first US-based company that manufactures construction products out of rice husks at scale. The company says it has diverted over nine million kg (20.5 million lb) of rice husks from landfill since it was founded in 2018, including as the panelling for Fine's ski condos. It is often easier to adopt a new floor tile material than it is to adopt a new material for a beam – Sabbie Miller Around the world, other companies including Resysta in Germany and design firm Ricehouse in Italy are producing or using all kinds of construction materials, from decking to paint, made from rice husks. Modern Mill's rice husk composite is even being used to make playgrounds . Rice husks protect the precious grains from wind and rain , and their high silica content allows them to resist moisture and decay, meaning they naturally boast the same properties as many traditional construction materials. "The whole point of the rice husk is to protect the rice while it grows," Guimond says. "What is it protecting it from? Moisture, pests, rot, those types of things." In addition to protecting against moisture, the high silica content means rice husks are surprisingly resilient to fire, according to Fine. Modern Mill's product is designated as Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) compliant, meaning it has passed California's fire safety testing . The benefits of rice husk Timber has long been considered a sustainable building material. It is abundant in continental climates and has comparatively low carbon emissions compared to materials like concrete and steel. But it can also have environmental and financial downsides , from vulnerability to price shocks to the depletion of old growth forests and the carbon they store and absorb . Modern Mill A kitchen in Woodbury, New York, furnished with Modern Mill's rice husk panelling (Credit: Modern Mill) Rice isn't the only unusual alternative building material being tested out. In the Global South, bamboo is increasingly being used as an alternative to concrete and more expensive, slower-growing tropical hardwoods. But the wide availability and low cost of rice husk, added to the fact it is a waste material, gives it a distinct advantage. A recent study found that using the fibrous residues from crops like rice, wheat and maize for buildings, rather than burning them, could produce a significant carbon sink , since the carbon caught in these residues would be locked away for decades. Sabbie Miller, an expert in sustainable building materials and professor in civil and environmental engineering at the University of California, Davis, notes however that whether or not...

title: Why travellers are obsessed with foreign supermarkets
description: Why travellers are obsessed with foreign supermarkets 13 August 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Dayna Camilleri-Clarke Getty Images (Credit: Getty Images) From Tokyo egg sandwiches to Greek dairy aisles, supermarket aisles are becoming one of travel's most revealing and beloved experiences. It's 10:00 in a Tokyo 7-Eleven, and I am standing shoulder to shoulder with a dozen tourists, all clutching baskets loaded with the same things: fluffy egg mayo sandwiches, katsu curry buns, matcha Kit Kats and warm cans of Boss coffee pulled from heated shelves. Behind me, someone photographs their haul before they've even reached the till. Every few seconds, the familiar convenience-store chime announces another arrival. Nobody is here because they have run out of toothpaste. We are all, quite openly, shopping for the experience. It is a travel ritual I've found myself repeating across the globe. I once spent an unreasonable portion of a sweltering Barcelona afternoon navigating the crowded aisles of a basement Mercadona, hunting down jars of pistachio cream. In a chaotic Miami Trader Joe's, I bypassed the groceries entirely and bought six jars of Everything But the Bagel seasoning, then repacked my suitcase around them before flying home. What began as a holiday necessity has gradually become one of my favourite parts of travelling, anticipated and increasingly built into the itinerary rather than squeezed in around it. As it turns out, I'm not alone. Hilton's 2026 Trends Report found that 77% of travellers enjoy visiting grocery stores abroad, while Condé Nast Traveller recently named grocery tourism one of the biggest travel trends of 2026. We might not all be able to afford a Michelin-starred meal or a private food tour, but almost anyone can spend €10 filling a basket with local snacks, unusual drinks and ingredients they've never seen before The industry has noticed too. Earlier this year, K-Supermarket, one of Finland's largest grocery chains, became the first supermarket in the world to officially list its branches as tourist attractions on Tripadvisor . Among them is a Helsinki store built around rooftop beehives that produce their own honey and another lauded for its craft beer selection, with each branch independently run and adapted to its local community. Why supermarkets feel different abroad Away from traditional sightseeing, ducking into a local grocery shop remains a surprisingly raw way to travel. Nothing on the shelves has been curated for out-of-towners or stamped with a tourist board's seal of approval. In an era of timed-entry museums and viral photo spots, wandering the aisles of a neighbourhood grocery store feels wonderfully unscripted Monuments reveal how a country remembers its past, but a supermarket shows how it lives today. You quickly learn what people eat for breakfast, whether nappies are kept behind the counter and just how many varieties of tinned fish a country considers reasonable. The person queuing beside you isn't there to sightsee. They're simply buying dinner. For a few minutes, tourists and locals occupy the same space, following exactly the same routines. Getty Images Browsing supermarket shelves gives travellers a window into everyday food culture (Credit: Getty Images) And there's a scientific explanation for why those convenience store snacks seem to taste so good. When I ask Oxford experimental psychologist Professor Charles Spence why supermarket food seems to take on an almost mythical quality abroad, he points to what he calls a "slightly less glamorous" version of the Provençal Rosé Paradox, the psychological phenomenon whereby a wine tasted on one's summer holidays never quite matches up when opened back home on a cold and rainy winter's night. In the supermarket aisle, context is everything. Most of us have lived some version of it. A flavour of Lay's crisps you've never seen before, eaten on a sunny holiday balcony, somehow loses a little of its magic once it's opened back home. According to Spence, supermarket discoveries work in much the same way. That egg mayo sandwich from Tokyo or a packet of crisps picked up abroad isn't being judged on flavour alone; the atmosphere and environment become part of the tasting experience. Getty Images In Russia, even an ordinary supermarket can offer travellers a surprisingly vast selection of tinned fish (Credit: Getty Images) You don't need a generous budget to take part, either. We might not all be able to afford a Michelin-starred meal or a private food tour, but almost anyone can spend €10 filling a basket with local snacks, unusual drinks and ingredients they've never seen before. Unlike a museum or a guided tour, a supermarket doesn't hand us an experience. We put it together ourselves. The appeal of shopping like a local Consumer psychologist and Humanising Brands founder Kate Nightingale believes the supermarket trend reflects a broader shift in what travellers are looking for. Increasingly, she says, we're seeking moments that feel authentic, participatory and accessible. Rather than simply observing a destination, we want to feel part of it. More like this: • Is it time to change how we buy travel souvenirs? • How convenience store socks became Japan's coolest souvenir • The case for taking the same holiday again and again A foreign supermarket offers exactly that. Its layout and routines are almost universally understood. We know how to pick up a basket, browse the aisles and join the queue. As Nightingale explains, "familiarity frees our brains to become more exploratory, allowing us to notice everything that's different rather than worrying about how to navigate the space". She likens it to the instinct that lets a child confidently run off to explore a playground once they know a parent is nearby. Back home, supermarkets are usually somewhere to get in and out of as quickly as possible. Abroad, they have a habit of drawing us in. We pause over fruit we've never seen before, try to make sense of products from their colours and pictures, or realise we've spent several minutes staring at shelves devoted entirely to seaweed. The weekly shop becomes something we notice rather than simply get...

title: 'What the hell did this?': The orca brothers preying on great white sharks
description: 'What the hell did this?': The orca brothers preying on great white sharks 7 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen Dave Hurwitz/ Simon's Town Boat Company When scientists first found dead great whites around South Africa, they couldn't believe their eyes. All bore the same marks of mutilation – their bodies were torn open and their livers had been extracted – and pointed to the same culprit. These deadly tactics are now seen around the world. On 3 May 2017, a huge carcass of a great white shark washed up on the shore of Gansbaai, a fishing village near Cape Town in South Africa. The female shark weighed 1,100kg (2,425lb) and had a gaping wound on her underside, where her 90kg (198lb) liver had been extracted. "We were like, 'What the hell did this?'" recalls Alison Towner, who led the necropsy on the dead shark. In the months that followed, five more great white carcasses turned up. Their bodies all bore the same distinctive scars; they had been torn open and their livers removed. "It was extraordinary," says Towner, a shark biologist at Rhodes University in Grahamstown, South Africa. "I'd seen hundreds of great white sharks at that point… never had I seen them just wash up one after another, after another." It was the first sign that an underwater battle was unfolding. As she later learned, it would have ramifications across the world's oceans. I'm not talking about a gradual decline of great whites. I'm talking about overnight, gone – Alison Towner Towner carried out necropsies on all the sharks and when she saw the same pattern of mutilation, she immediately suspected two culprits: a pair of orcas nicknamed Port and Starboard. These two male orcas, thought to be brothers, were first seen around Cape Town in 2015 and christened Port and Starboard for their distinctive dorsal fins, which collapsed to the left and right. Shortly after the orca pair were spotted, divers came across a group of dead broadnose sevengill sharks. The stout bodies of these prehistoric-looking sharks were ripped open and missing their livers. "Port and Starboard arrived, right when the divers were pulling the carcasses out of the water," says Towner. "We had the victims and culprits on scene, but at the time we couldn't get our heads around what had happened." Marine biologists and the public continued to see the two orcas up and down the Cape Town coastline, including around Dyer Island, which used to be known as "the McDonald's drive-through for great whites", due to the sharks that patrolled up and down during the winter months in search of seals, Towner says. "There was no doubt that Dyer Island was one of the best places on the planet to see a great white," she says. But suddenly the sharks vanished. "I'm not talking about a gradual decline, I'm talking about overnight, gone." Towner and others had their suspicions, but it wasn't until 2022 that they were able to officially connect orcas with the shark killings. "It was like a crime scene investigation… we were piecing evidence together but we didn't have the silver bullet. Then we got it." Watch orcas hunting a juvenile great white shark in the Gulf of California On 16 May 2022, a hobbyist drone pilot filmed three orcas preying on a 3m (10ft)-long great white shark off the coast of Mossel Bay , 400km (250 miles) east of Cape Town. In the encounter, one of the three orcas used its snout to push the shark to the surface and rolled it onto its right side, before biting into an area near its pectoral fins, releasing a pool of blood. The orca then dived underwater with the shark in its mouth, while another orca appeared to grab the shark's tail before disappearing out of sight. Orcas have now been observed killing great white sharks off the coast of California and Australia too, revealing their remarkable hunting prowess, intelligence and teamwork. With climate change and environmental pressures bringing these species into closer proximity, scientists warn that the battle between the top marine apex predators has dramatic ramifications for life in the ocean. Battle of the apex predators Orcas (also known as killer whales) and great white sharks sit at the top of their respective food chains and play an important ecological role in the ocean. They compete for similar prey, such as seals and dolphins . Killer whales are the only known predators of great white sharks . "They are very selective of the organs that they gain nourishment from and the liver is the most nutritious part of a shark," says Towner. Great white sharks have huge livers which they use as fuel tanks for their lengthy migrations and to maintain their buoyancy . The liver of an adult great white can account for 28% of its body weight, with 90% of its volume coming from high-energy lipids. In Australia, orcas have also been observed removing and eating the lips and tongues of baleen whales as well as the pectoral muscle of penguins, says Isabella Reeves, a marine biologist specialising in orcas at the University of Western Australia. This targeted hunting method is "nutritionally driven", she says. It is difficult to know whether this hunting strategy is a new behaviour or simply being observed more as "there are so many more eyes on the water now" with the rise of underwater cameras and drone technology, says Deborah Giles, an orca scientist at the University of California, Davis, and researcher at the non-profit SeaDoc Society, based on Orcas Island, Washington. "It might simply be that we're looking for it, and we're seeing it." The hunting method reveals orcas' "extreme intelligence, and their ability to take advantage of the prey that is available to them within their home ranges", says Giles. "Great white sharks were thought to be the apex predator in the ocean, but it's very clear that it's actually killer whales that are the top...

title: The five meals Andrew Zimmern will never forget
description: The five meals Andrew Zimmern will never forget 8 August 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Eva Sandoval Courtesy of The Travel Channel The celebrity chef and lifelong traveller has eaten it all, but these are the five meals that he'll remember for the rest of his life. Just by looking at a plate of food, Andrew Zimmern believes you can see a place's history. "Food is the way to understand another culture," says the chef, TV personality, author and lifelong traveller. "If someone from outer space came down and said, 'Show me your hometown', I wouldn't take Mr Spaceman to the museum. If you want to understand a human being, sit down and have a meal with them." The SpeciaList Andrew Zimmern is a television host and food system advocate who has won four James Beard awards and an Emmy. The creator of the Bizarre Foods franchise, he now hosts Curated Journeys, intimate travel experiences focusing on hyper-local food cultures and rare culinary traditions. We asked Zimmern to choose the five meals that have shaped him – no small feat for a man who has been everywhere and eaten literally everything; no organ ever unturned. The result is less a list than an autobiography, tracing a life savoured through food. From the savoury French bite that cemented his destiny, to meeting a culinary hero, here are the five meals Andrew Zimmern will remember for the rest of his life. Andrew Zimmern The extraordinary tasting menu at Restaurant Paul Bocuse cemented the young Zimmern's destiny (Credit: Andrew Zimmern) 1. Liver pâté at Restaurant Paul Bocuse, Lyon, France It was 1976. I was 14 years old, [skiing in Val-d'Isère] with my father's best friend and his family. It snowed for six days straight and we were stuck in the hotel for seven days. The last meal we had before we could leave town was stale bread and sardines. So the seven of us drove to Lyon and I had my first meal at Restaurant Paul Bocuse . I ordered the largest tasting menu: 15 courses. There was chicken cooked inside a pig's bladder, truffle soup with a beautiful puff pastry dome. The fourth or fifth course was a tiny timbale (mould) of liver pâté; warm, with a sauce of wine and liver. To this day it's one of the 10 best things I've ever put in my mouth. The staff was intrigued that a young person would order this. I was asked if I liked it: "Yes, very much. Can I have another?" About two minutes later, Paul Bocuse himself came to the table. "You want another one?" "Yes, please. That's the best thing I've ever eaten in my life." Within seconds, another was at the table. My family just stared at me. [But] I'd never seen a restaurant run that way. It had a garden; you could see women picking vegetables throughout the dinner. They were baking bread during the meal service. The restaurant made its own butter. It convinced me that food had no limits… that there was a sense of craft bigger than I had even imagined. I walked into that meal, knowing that I was going to be in the food business, but I left that meal convinced. Andrew Zimmern Zimmern waited decades to enjoy chef Kiyomi Mikuni's groundbreaking Japanese-French cuisine (Credit: Andrew Zimmern) 2. Grilled aubergine and corn soup at Hokusai Fine Dining on the Mitsui Ocean Fuji, Japan I have been obsessed with chef Kiyomi Mikuni since the early 80s. He started the French-Japanese food mashup. His first cookbook was called the Food Fantasy of Hotel Mikuni. I was a young cook, had spent seven months cooking in Paris, and the book blew my mind. The idea that these two cuisines could be married so perfectly, and that there was a guy only a few years older than me talented enough to pull that off… I fell in love with him, professionally. Every time I went to Japan, I never met him. But I just got back from Japan yesterday, and on this trip, I told the folks who were handling me, "I need to eat [at his restaurant]." He has, like, 12 restaurants, [including one] on the boat that we were taking to South Korea. One seating cost a ridiculous amount of money but there was no way I wasn't eating there. [The menu] was almost straight up French. He spent the whole night talking to us, giving us food. You know how they say never meet your hero? This guy was just so kind, he was so funny. He served grilled aubergine with greens, dressed with olive oil and shallots, then put a piece of grilled eel with a dehydrated and fried eel bone on top. We had corn soup layered on a gelée of beef consommé. Very French, but he used Japanese corn. On top of it, he put a tempura sweet fish, which is very bitter. He told everybody, "You eat it in two bites, head first, and then the rest." Then you wash it down with the soup, and finish with the consommé at the bottom, which was clarified and very beefy, very intense. It's just a beautiful mix of French and Japanese, and it was quite extraordinary. Best food on any cruise line I've ever experienced. Andrew Zimmern Zimmern has returned to Trattoria Sostanza regularly throughout his life (Credit: Andrew Zimmern) 3. Liver crostini at Trattoria Sostanza, Florence, Italy My father, when he was on honeymoon with my mother, went to Trattoria Sostanza in Florence. In the '50s, it was two communal tables, an open kitchen and a hand-written menu. [When] he took me there in the late '60s, one of the waiters who had served him in the '50s was now the maitre d'. [We] went back in '74 or '75, then I went in 1979 with a friend. The waiter-turned-maitre d' was now the manager. He was old. [But] the restaurant hadn't changed. When I...

title: 'NonnaMaxxing': Tourists are paying to travel like grandmothers
description: 'NonnaMaxxing': Tourists are paying to travel like grandmothers 17 July 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Emily-Ann Elliott Alamy Whether it's making pasta with an Italian nonna or sightseeing with a gran in Japan, Gen-Zers and millennials are increasingly seeking out granny-led travel experiences. My cheek presses into a cool mat and a forceful, yet reassuring, pressure travels down my right shoulder blade. Rose, a petite septuagenarian in a loose white tunic, crouches over me, digging her thumbs into my back and speaking in rapid Thai. "She is telling you that this is the line you need to follow," explains a younger woman nearby. Face down, I clumsily attempt to nod, which makes Rose laugh loudly. This is my beginner Thai massage course in Bangkok's Watpo Massage School , where the majority of staff are old enough to be my grandmother. I find that being taught by grandmothers is supremely comforting. They're strict when they need to be, tease us when we make mistakes and encourage us when we doubt ourselves. When I get flustered in the final exam and start to cry, Rose envelops me in a hug. Suddenly, everything feels like it is going to be alright. The rise of 'Grandma tourism' I'm not the only traveller seeking out the comforting embrace of a granny. #Grandmacore, which promotes the benefits of activities like crafting and baking, has almost 800 million views on TikTok. Now, it appears to be influencing "grandma tourism", in which travellers seek out tours and classes led specifically by older women. With more than one-third of Gen-Zers and millennials worldwide saying they often feel stressed , many of us are choosing to spend time with older generations. I've found that their calming presence helps to reduce my own anxiety, and I'm not alone. A report by tour guide company GetYourGuide showed that 76% of Gen-Z travellers from France, Germany, the UK and the US would book a "grandma-inspired" holiday activity, like learning to make pasta with a nonna (grandmother) in Italy and hiring Japanese grannies as their tour guide. For 32-year-old Los Angeles-based fashion stylist Brittany Diego, the maternal warmth she experienced in her nonna-led pasta class was the highlight of her trip to Italy. "There were plenty of pasta-making classes [on offer]," she says. "But learning from an Italian nonna felt like the most authentic option, and it absolutely lived up to my expectations." Diego found that the course, which took place in the nonna's home at the foothills of Rome, felt less like taking a class and more like being welcomed into a grandmother's house. Being engaged with and teaching younger people is extremely good for older people's mood, their health and their longevity "My nonna spoke very little English, but we still connected through smiles, gestures and cooking together. We shared aperitivo and bruschetta before making the pasta." As a solo traveller, Diego appreciated how her nonna created a sense of community before the class even began. She left the experience with a fully belly and, despite the language barrier, new friends. "It was a reminder that genuine hospitality doesn't always require words," she said. Here are some other ways to nonna-maxx on your travels • Bake tarte Tatin and madeleines with French grandmas Mamie Daniela and Mamie Catherine in Paris, France. • Learn the art of making musubi, a Japanese rice and nori sandwich, from octogenarian Kayoko in Tokyo, Japan. • Join Wardandi Bibbulmun Elder Dale Tilbrook, from Swan Valley, Australia, as she shares her knowledge of native foods through bush tucker talks and tastings . • Relax with Zita Pancsovay and her grandmother in their family home in Budapest as they serve up a traditional Hungarian grandma's dinner . • Experience Ayurvedic cooking with Grandma Shyama in her home in Kochi, India. Since her trip, Diego plans to research more granny-led experiences for future holidays, citing the nurturing care as a key part of the allure. "[It] made me feel instantly at home. This showed me that some of the most meaningful travel experiences come from learning directly from locals whose knowledge has been shaped over a lifetime." In my case, learning Thai massage from older women feels like I am benefitting from their decades-long knowledge of the traditional healing system. Learning from women, who have, in turn, learnt from their own mothers and grandmothers, feels very special. And soothing: during our breaks, as we sit sipping small stumpy glasses of Thai iced tea, my fellow classmates and I discuss how relaxing it is to spend time with our instructors. Outside the classroom walls, Bangkok's motorbikes beep and hawkers shout, but inside, there is a feeling of tranquility, thanks to the quiet confidence of our teachers. And, perhaps, being away from our phones. The intergenerational exchange As well as offering feelings of safety and calm, matriarchs can also pass on knowledge, traditional skills and local customs which may otherwise be lost. They may also offer younger travellers the confidence to be comfortable in their own skin. Brittany Diego Granny-led travel activities include pasta making, storytelling and tours (Credit: Brittany Diego) Weeks after my Thai adventures, I find myself in an onsen (outdoor public bath) in Beppu, Japan. Bathing in a Japanese hot spring is something I have been looking forward to my whole trip, but as I undress, I'm suddenly nervous about the ritual of nude Japanese bathing. I'd hoped to slip unnoticed into the bubbling pool, but there is a shriek of excitement. Three older women are enthusiastically beckoning me to join them. How can I refuse? I inch over and lower myself into the piping hot water, before a barrage of questions begins: "Why are you here alone?" "Where are you staying in Beppu?" "Do you know my son? He lives in London!" Thanks to their unbridled joy, my awkwardness soon slips away. It's hard to feel embarrassed when you're squeezed between ladies old enough to be your grandmothers, gently squeezing your cheek and telling you...
